10056-chinese-literature:
This 1900 volume, with critical and biographical sketches by Epiphanius Wilson, gathers five cornerstones of Chinese literature in English. It holds the Analects of Confucius, opening with learning and miscellaneous sayings, and the sayings of Mencius.

Beside them stand the Shi-King, the ancient book of songs, the travels of Fa-Hien, the Buddhist pilgrim, and the Sorrows of Han, a classic drama. Wilson's sketches set each work in its time and place for new readers. Readers new to Chinese letters get a solid first shelf: philosophy, poetry, travel, and theatre in one volume.
10076-lister-s-great-adventure:
Harold Bindloss's 1920 novel opens its first part, Barbara's Rebellion, with Cartwright meddling, a scene in the dark, Barbara vanishing, and a girl on the platform. Shillito gets away, Winnipeg Beach appears, and Lister's dissatisfaction grows toward a test.

Part two, The Reckoning, brings Vernon's plot and its answer, as Lister's great adventure turns from rebellion to reckoning. Bindloss, author of many northern tales, writes of Canada, business, and love with steady craft. Readers get a solid adventure of the prairies and the coast, with a hero who earns his name.
10103-the-great-events-by-famous-histori:
Volume eight of The Great Events by Famous Historians presents world history as complete narratives in the words of eminent historians, arranged in order of time. Its binding, the volume notes, copies a mosaic binding made about 1710 by Antoine Michel Padeloup, royal binder of France and Portugal.

Contributors to this volume include Margaret Oliphant, George Finlay, David Hume, Francis Bacon, Pasquale Villari, Sismondi, and Gaspar Correa, with an outline narrative to connect them. Readers get history told by masters, not summarized by editors, in a volume rich with illustrations. The volume's illustrations add portraits and scenes to the narratives.
10145-turkey-a-past-and-a-future:
A. J. Toynbee wrote this short study in 1917, while the Ottoman Empire was breaking apart in war. He asks what Turkey even means, since the name covers Yemen, Hedjaz, Mesopotamia, Kurdistan, Armenia, Anatolia, and Syria. Each land, he shows, has its own climate, peoples, and past.

Three parts treat the past, the present, and the future, weighing how empire, faith, and geography shaped the region. Toynbee looks past maps to cities, rivers, and trade routes. Readers get a clear, wartime survey of a vast, varied empire on the edge of change.
10394-stolen-treasure:
Howard Pyle published this pirate storybook in 1907, illustrating it himself. Pyle, author of Men of Iron and other classics, wrote four linked tales of treasure, ghosts, and buccaneers for young and old readers. The tone is romantic, clear, and full of sea color.

Henry Mostyn sails under Captain Morgan in 1665 and 1666, Tom Chist finds a treasure box, Captain Brand's ghost returns, and the devil visits New Hope. Each tale turns on greed, fear, and daring. Readers get four well-told pirate adventures from a master of American story and picture books.
10420-the-principles-of-success-in-liter:
George Henry Lewes wrote this classic essay on literary success, first published in the nineteenth century. Lewes argues that literature, like the nervous system in animals, grows more central as society grows more complex. Good writing, he says, both causes and reflects social progress.

The essay traces how literature stores the race's experience, linking past and present, and feeding each new generation. Lewes warns young writers against mere imitation and fashion, urging truth, sincerity, and hard craft. Readers get a clear, thoughtful guide to why some books last and others fade.
1048-the-ruling-passion-tales-of-nature-:
Henry van Dyke was an American minister and writer. He gathers short tales in which one ruling passion steers a life. That passion may be love of the woods, of a river, of a craft, or of a child. The stories move from Adirondack camps to city rooms, and each turns on a choice made outdoors or in the heart.

Van Dyke writes with warmth and a preacher's eye for the moral, but the nature lore is real and the people feel true. Hunters, guides, and anglers share the page with wives and sons. The book suits readers who like gentle, old-style tales where landscape and conscience meet.
10581-uncle-bernac-a-memory-of-the-empir:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote this Napoleonic romance as a memory of the empire, opening on the coast of France. Louis de Laval, carrying his uncle's letter a hundred times read, sits on a lugger and studies the prim, angular hand of a man who began life as a village attorney. The letter, addressed to Ashford in Kent, promises intrigue.

Salt marshes, ruined cottages, men of the night, secret passages, and the camp of Boulogne carry Louis toward Grosbois, cousin Sybille, and Josephine. Napoleon himself, man of action and man of dreams, looms over the tale. Readers get a vivid, romantic adventure of the empire, by the creator of Holmes.
10631-halleck-s-new-english-literature:
Reuben Post Halleck's New English Literature is a school history of English writing from the year 449 to the twentieth century. Chapters move from the Anglo-Saxons and the Norman Conquest through Chaucer, the Elizabethan age, the Puritans, the Restoration, Romanticism, and the Victorians. Pictures, including a facsimile of Beowulf, illustrate the text.

Halleck pairs each period with its leading authors and chief works, and adds lists for further reading. His aim is to help students see literature as the story of a people, not a string of names. The book remains a clear, orderly survey for readers who want the whole shape of English literature at a glance.
10739-the-essays-of-arthur-schopenhauer-:
Arthur Schopenhauer's essays On Human Nature, translated by T. Bailey Saunders, draw on the chapters on ethics and law in his Parerga and posthumous writings. The contents cover human nature itself, government, free-will and fatalism, character, moral instinct, and ethical reflections. Saunders divided the chapters into sections and gave the book its title.

Schopenhauer writes with bleak clarity about motives, habit, and the limits of reason, in prose that is sharp and quotable. The essays suit readers meeting his philosophy in short form. They offer a stern, stimulating view of why people act as they do, and what governments can and cannot change.
10831-the-village-in-the-mountains-conve:
The Village in the Mountains joins two religious narratives: the conversion of Peter Bayssiere and the history of a Bible. The first opens with a Paris merchant visiting manufactories in the mountains of the Loire and the Puy de Dome. He travels back toward Lyons through spring country of peaks, streams, fields, and furnaces. Factories rise among barns, and rural industry meets mountain scenery.

The tales that follow trace faith reaching remote places, through a man's change of heart and a book's long journey. Written for earnest readers, they mix travel description with evangelical warmth. Readers get a gentle, old-fashioned pair of stories about belief in the French hills.
10859-paul-and-virginia-from-the-french-:
Jacques-Henri Bernardin de Saint-Pierre's Paul and Virginia, in this 1851 translation from the French, is a pastoral romance of two children raised together on the island of Mauritius. The translator's preface recalls writing in Paris amid the horrors of Robespierre's tyranny, when reading and writing themselves were dangerous, and a manuscript volume had to be burned after domiciliary visits.

The story follows Paul and Virginia from innocent childhood toward love, parting, and loss, against tropical nature. Its sentiment made it famous across Europe. Readers get a tender classic of innocence and fate, in a translation born under the Terror.
10887-babylonian-and-assyrian-literature:
Epiphanius Wilson assembled this 1901 introduction to the literature of ancient Mesopotamia, centred on the Epic of Izdubar, now better known as Gilgamesh. Hymns, tablets, and cuneiform inscriptions sit beside the epic, with an introduction explaining how scribes wrote on clay with a wedge-shaped stylus. Texts copied under King Assurbanipal preserved much of this material.

Hymns to the gods show the parallelism familiar from Hebrew poetry, while the epic follows a hero's quests, friendship, and search for life after death. Wilson presents the works in English for general readers, not only scholars. The book remains a useful doorway into a literature older than Greece and Rome, written on tablets that survived fire, flood, and time.
10937-the-life-of-st-mochuda-of-lismore:
Reverend P. Power translated this medieval Irish Life of St. Mochuda of Lismore from a manuscript in the Royal Irish Academy library. Power's introduction defends the Lives of Irish saints as valuable history, even when they multiply miracles and paint saints in harsh, almost pagan colours. He urges readers to judge the tales by medieval standards, not modern ones.

Mochuda's story includes robbers who cannot harm him in a mill, where the stones stop while he sleeps and turn while he wakes, and weapons that fail in their hands. Such marvels, Power argues, reveal what monastic writers believed and valued. The book serves students of early Irish Christianity and of hagiography, the literature of saints' lives.
10944-from-a-bench-in-our-square:
Samuel Hopkins Adams wrote these 1922 stories from a bench in a New York square, watching neighbours pass. Peter Quick Banta, a Coney Island sand sculptor turned pavement artist, opens the book, drawing lilacs and butterflies in coloured chalk until a cheeky boy calls his work rotten. Other tales follow a patroness of art, a house of silvery voices, and Mayme, a sharp-tongued girl with a cough.

Adams mixes humour with sympathy, giving street artists, doctors, and working girls vivid voices. The square itself becomes a small world, where art, ambition, and kindness collide daily. Readers get warm, well-made stories of city life in the 1920s, told by an observer who clearly enjoyed sitting, watching, and listening.
11016-the-port-of-adventure:
Charles Norris Williamson and Alice Muriel Williamson wrote this 1913 romance, published in Britain as The Love Pirate. Angela, a woman sailing from the Old World to forget, meets Nick in California, where gardens, missions, and the seventeen-mile drive frame a story of mystery and love. A gold bag comedy, a police mystery, and a box of mystery carry the plot through thirty-two chapters.

Angela's mourning, a man at the wheel, and a door with a red label add suspense to the courtship, while Santa Barbara and Monterey give the romance its setting. The Williamsons wrote popular travel romances, and this one mixes sightseeing with intrigue. Readers get a light, scenic love story, with California itself as a leading character.
11082-old-saint-paul-s-a-tale-of-the-pla:
William Harrison Ainsworth wrote this historical novel about London's plague of 1665 and great fire of 1666, centred on Old St. Paul's. Ainsworth bases the grocer of Wood Street, who victuals his house and shuts his family inside during the worst plague months, on a rare narrative he attributes to Defoe.

Books follow the year month by month: April to December 1665 for the plague, September 1666 for the fire. Leonard, Amabel, Doctor Hodges, and the Earl of Rochester move through coffin-makers, quack doctors, pest-houses, and Paul's Walk. Ainsworth mixes romance with grim detail, giving readers a vivid, if romanticised, picture of London in its two great disasters.
11100-history-of-modern-philosophy-from-:
Richard Falckenberg, professor of philosophy at Erlangen, wrote this history of modern philosophy from Nicolas of Cusa to the present time, translated by A. C. Armstrong Jr. and published in a third American edition in 1893. Falckenberg, a pupil of Kuno Fischer, Erdmann, Lotze, and Eucken, aimed at a manual midway between full histories and meagre short surveys, scientific yet popular.

His method is strictly objective: free reproduction of each system in its original terms and historical connection, without imposing his own moderate idealism. Passages compare empiricists and rationalists on sense and understanding, one calling concepts faded images of sensations, the other calling sensations concepts not yet clear. Students get a reliable, readable survey of modern thought from Cusa through Kant and beyond.
11166-for-gold-or-soul-the-story-of-a-gr:
Lurana W. Sheldon published this 1900 novel, For Gold or Soul? The Story of a Great Department Store. The monster store of Denton, Day and Co. throngs with shoppers, while pale-faced women and narrow-chested men stand behind counters and cash girls with waxen cheeks dart through the aisles. On the fifth floor, anxious girls wait to apply for service.

Mr. Duncan Forbes, junior partner and business superintendent, interviews a beautiful girl of seventeen seeking work as a saleswoman. She has never worked, but begs for a trial, and Forbes, seeing her fine but shabby clothes, rosy cheeks, and graceful carriage, refuses: he wants girls with experience. Later, a store detective watches a poor woman suspected of stealing six pairs of hose. Sheldon's novel exposes department-store labour and the temptations of poverty.
11216-the-happy-venture:
Edith Ballinger Price published this 1920–21 children's novel, The Happy Venture, illustrated by the author. The book opens in rain, with Felicia at the piano singing an old song for the fourth time. Felicia is anxious about their mother, and Kenelm shares the anxiety under a queer code of fraternal secrecy.

Chapters follow tales in the rain, havoc, up stakes, the fine old farmhouse, the wheels beginning to turn, a-maying, work, fame courting, the nine gifts, and roses in the moonlight. The Maestro tells Kirk of a little boy and girl who played in a garden when pools were filled; the girl died, and the boy, who loved the sea too well.
11243-miles-wallingford-sequel-to-afloat:
James Fenimore Cooper's 1863 sequel continues the seafaring life of Miles Wallingford after Afloat and Ashore, opening with a desperate struggle in the water and a rescue aboard the Wallingford. Wallingford narrates his voyages, loves, and losses in the first person, with Lucy and Grace among the figures waiting ashore. Ships, storms, and questions of honor drive the long narrative.

Cooper writes for readers who already knew Miles from the earlier book, and the sequel rewards that familiarity. Its interest now lies partly in its portrait of American maritime life and partly in Cooper's late style, discursive and earnest. The novel is long, but its sea passages still carry the story.
1126-measure-for-measure:
When the Duke of Vienna leaves town, his deputy Angelo enforces dead laws with a zealot's rigor, condemning Claudio to death for a moral fault. Claudio's sister Isabella, a novice nun, begs for his life, and Angelo offers a foul bargain. William Shakespeare's problem play tests mercy against justice.

The Duke, disguised as a friar, watches and steers the plot toward a set of forced marriages and a public unmasking. The comedy is dark, the jokes are grim, and the ending leaves hard questions open. The play still provokes debate on power, sex, and pardon.
1163-adventure:
Jack London sets this novel on a Solomon Islands plantation. Joan Lackland, a bold young American woman, runs the estate with grit and a rifle. David Sheldon, its sick owner, learns to share command with her. Together they face fever, hostile tribes, and scheming traders in the tropic heat.

The tale mixes romance with plantation realism: copra, labor, and the daily fight to hold ground. London, who had sailed these seas himself, writes the islands with heat and color. The book shows his taste for strong women and hard places, and it reads as a vivid period adventure.
11690-calvert-of-strathore:
Carter Goodloe's 1903 novel, Calvert of Strathore, opens at the new American Legation in Paris on 3 February, in a morning of suppressed excitement. Chapters follow the France of 1789, a lass with a delicate air, and afternoons at the Palais Royal.

Mr. Calvert, private secretary, meets old and new friends, attends the king's levee, and watches the fourth and fourteenth of July. Lafayette brings friends to dinner, and Calvert rides down into Touraine. Later he fights a duel, sees a short campaign under Lafayette, and quits the army for a hazardous enterprise. The novel is an American in revolutionary Paris.
11935-mysticism-in-english-literature:
Caroline F. E. Spurgeon's Mysticism in English Literature restricts the crowded term mysticism to its philosophical type, concerned with questions of ultimate reality. Quoting the Phaedo, that many bear the thyrsus but few are mystics, she sets out to consider the subject in English writing with that narrower meaning in view.

The book examines how poets and prose writers approached direct apprehension of reality, rather than treating every religious feeling as mystical. Spurgeon's careful definition gives the study its shape: it is a work of literary criticism and philosophy together, tracing a single idea through English literature instead of surveying religion in general.
12001-studies-in-literature:
John Morley's Studies in Literature, published in 1907, collects articles previously printed in the Nineteenth Century and Fortnightly Review, or in other shapes, with thanks to the proprietors for sanctioning reproduction. Morley, a statesman and man of letters, dated his note October 1890, showing how long some pieces had waited for book form.

Contents include essays on Wordsworth, aphorisms, Maine on popular government. A few words on other subjects, written with Morley's characteristic balance of political experience and literary judgment. The collection suits readers who want criticism from a writer who governed as well as read. Who treats literature as part of public life rather than as an escape from it.
12015-love-under-fire:
Randall Parrish's 1911 novel Love Under Fire, with five illustrations in full color by Alonzo Kimball, opens between the lines, after the despatch-bearer, and with a friend rather than an enemy. Parrish, author of My Lady of the South and Keith of the Border, writes Civil War romance with a soldier's attention to detail.

Later chapters bring the coming of dawn, acquaintances not friends, a bold front, a woman's prisoner. The coming of the enemy, with important news and a Miss Wilton among the characters. The novel's pleasures are those of its genre: danger, divided loyalty, and love tested by war, told briskly and without apology for its sentiment.
12193-the-gentleman-from-everywhere:
James Henry Foss published this autobiography in 1903, dedicating it to his beloved, on earth and in heaven. Foss lived many lives: schoolboy, teacher, preacher, politician, Florida promoter, and town founder, and the book follows him through all of them.

Chapters run from a harsh childhood in a log hut through school days, a disenchanted ministry, marriage and widowhood, political stump speaking, and business ventures that rose and fell. Foss writes with frankness about Christian Science, which he attacks, and about socialist colonies he tried. The memoir is uneven and self-justifying, but its range is rare: one man story of nineteenth-century America, told from the inside.
12229-who-goes-there:
B. K. Benson published Who Goes There in 1900, subtitled the story of a spy in the Civil War. The book follows a young Union soldier drawn into secret service behind Confederate lines.

Chapters run from the advance and a shameful day through breaking his musket, service with a doctor in camp, and the uses of infirmity as cover. Later chapters cross the Warwick line, Fort Willis, and the lines of Hanover, toward battle. A mid-book scene has a general tell the hero he must go into enemy lines, and the hero wonders whether he may decline. Benson writes from a soldier view: spying as duty, fear, and luck, not glamour.
12255-the-egyptian-conception-of-immorta:
George Andrew Reisner delivered The Egyptian Conception of Immortality as the Ingersoll Lecture in 1911. The lectureship, founded by Caroline Haskell Ingersoll will, supports inquiry into human immortality, and Reisner, a Harvard Egyptologist, speaks from excavation and texts.

Reisner traces Egyptian beliefs about the soul, the Osiris myth, and the afterlife. He argues that the Osiris story in its earliest form matches the Tammuz and Adonis story of the Semites, brought into Egypt from abroad. He weighs tombs, inscriptions, and ritual against later Greek and Christian ideas. The lecture is short, scholarly, and clear, showing how archaeology reshaped a theological question. It remains a useful entry to Egyptian religion.
12400-bismarck-and-the-foundation-of-the:
James Wycliffe Headlam's 1899 life of Bismarck traces the statesman who forged the German Empire. Most of the book was finished before Bismarck's death, and Headlam notes the delay that pushed publication back a year. He also weighs Busch's memoirs, judging their value exaggerated except for Bismarck's last years.

Chapters follow diplomacy, war and domestic statecraft, showing how Prussia drew German states together under its lead. Headlam writes as a historian close to his subject, critical where evidence demands it. The volume serves as a clear, contemporary English account of unification, written while its chief maker had only just left the stage.
12482-the-mettle-of-the-pasture:
James Lane Allen's 1903 Kentucky novel opens on a woman in a room, a dark red rose in her hand, glass doors open to lawn, pines and a flower garden beyond. That pastoral setting, an old house, turf, evergreens and house-tops beyond a high fence, sets the tone for a story of country life and feeling.

Allen, known for Kentucky tales such as A Kentucky Cardinal, builds his fiction from landscape, manners and inward choice. Love, family duty and the temper of a place, its mettle, test his characters as seasons pass. The novel offers a slow, atmospheric romance of the Bluegrass region, where a garden and a house carry as much meaning as any speech.
12545-traditions-of-the-tinguian-a-study:
Fay-Cooper Cole, assistant curator of Malayan ethnology, published this 1915 study of Tinguian traditions in Philippine folk-lore. Contents divide into tales of the mythical period, ritualistic and explanatory tales, fables and abstracts. Fourteen principal actors, often under several names in a single tale, lead the myths, and a table sorts their relationships.

The first twenty-six myths form a cycle, secured from six sources, with conflicts in naming that Cole notes honestly. Tales explain custom, ritual and the world, in a people of northern Luzon. The volume remains a classic ethnographic collection, careful, respectful and rich in story.
12578-shakespeare-s-play-of-the-merchant:
Charles Kean's acting edition of Shakespeare's Merchant of Venice, arranged for the Princess's Theatre and first performed 12 June 1858, gives the play with historical and explanatory notes. Dramatis personae list the Duke, the Princes of Morocco and Arragon as suitors to Portia, and Antonio the merchant. Bassanio, Gratiano, Lorenzo in love with Jessica, Shylock played by Kean himself, Tubal and Launcelot Gobbo complete the cast.

Kean's notes explain staging, costume and custom for a Victorian audience, while the text keeps Shakespeare's plot of bond, caskets and courtroom. The edition serves theatre history, showing how a star manager presented a classic. It also records a famous Shylock, played by the editor in his own production.
12670-landmarks-in-french-literature:
Lytton Strachey's 1912 Landmarks in French Literature, dedicated to J. M. S., surveys French writing from origins to criticism. Chapters run from the Middle Ages and Renaissance through an age of transition and Louis XIV to the eighteenth century. The romantic movement and the age of criticism follow, with conclusion, chronological list and bibliography.

Strachey opens with the French nation forming among Roman ruins in Gaul, and a new language slowly evolved, mostly straight from Latin, with little Celtic influence. That linguistic story frames literary history. Strachey writes with wit and brevity, judging authors sharply. The book offers a compact, opinionated guide, still readable as an introduction to French letters.
12834-social-pictorial-satire:
George du Maurier's Social Pictorial Satire, published in 1898, defends and displays the art of pen-and-ink social comedy. Du Maurier, author of Trilby, speaks of the craft to which he gave his best years: portraying life in little strokes, lines, and scratches. John Leech, Charles Keene, and du Maurier himself supply the pictures.

Leech's Mr. Briggs, the hunting gentleman, earns special praise as a creation more winning than Pickwick, made by Leech alone without an author partner. Vulgar cockney snobs on hired, broken-winded horses get no such mercy. The book is a master cartoonist's tribute to his art and his peers.
1286-tales-from-shakespeare:
Charles and Mary Lamb retell twenty of Shakespeare's plays as short prose tales for young readers: Hamlet, Macbeth, King Lear, The Tempest, and the great comedies among them. Each tale keeps the plot, the characters, and the famous scenes, while the verse gives way to plain, clear prose.

The Lambs wrote for children, and their tales have served as a first door into Shakespeare for two centuries. The stories are gentle, vivid, and faithful to the plays' spirit. The book suits young readers and any adult who wants the plots straight before facing the verse.
13029-the-art-of-the-moving-picture:
Vachel Lindsay's Art of the Moving Picture, in the 1922 revision of his 1915 book, argues that film is a new art fit for museums and universities. Lindsay appeals to critics, sculptors, painters, and city builders to take the photoplay seriously. His chapters sort films into types: crowd pictures, patriotic pictures, and religious pictures, with sculpture and painting in motion as higher aims.

Lindsay praises Griffith's crowd scenes while condemning the racial hatred drawn from Thomas Dixon's novel. He also explains film grammar, showing how quick cuts between cottage, field, and mountain can hold a talk between places, not people. The book is a landmark of early film theory, written while cinema was still finding its own language.
13200-act-declaration-testimony-for-the-:
Issued by the Reformed Presbytery, this Act, Declaration, and Testimony defends the Covenanted Reformation as reached in Britain and Ireland between 1638 and 1649. It also testifies against every step of defection since, down to the present day. Texts from Psalms, Isaiah, Jude, and Revelation head the work, urging readers to hold fast what they have.

The presbytery charges the Revolution church with keeping members steeped in apostasy, bloodshed, and cruelty, without public confession or due censure. It argues that magistrates must rule by God's preceptive will, not by mere power. The book is a dense Covenanter manifesto, written for a church that saw itself as a faithful remnant against a fallen age.
13240-a-short-biographical-dictionary-of:
John W. Cousin's Short Biographical Dictionary of English Literature, published by Dent in London and Dutton in New York, lists authors from early times to his own day. Its sources include Allibone, Hazlitt, Chambers, and the Dictionary of National Biography. Each entry gives birth, schooling, works, and a short judgment in compact prose.

One entry follows De Quincey from Manchester Grammar School, which he ran from, through London Bohemian life and first opium, to Oxford in 1803. Another treats James Mill, friend of Bentham, author of Elements of Political Economy and Analysis of the Human Mind, and father of John Stuart Mill. The dictionary is a handy, still useful first stop for English literary lives.
133-the-damnation-of-theron-ware:
A young Methodist minister in upstate New York wins a packed church with his preaching, then meets minds that unsettle his faith. Harold Frederic's Damnation of Theron Ware follows Theron from confident revivalist to a man tempted by science, art, and doubt. A Catholic priest, a doctor, and a worldly woman each pull him in a new direction.

Theron borrows books, questions doctrine, and mistakes flattery for friendship as his certainties slip. His wife Alice watches the change with growing alarm, while his congregation senses a cooling fire. Frederic tracks the fall without sermonizing, letting ambition and vanity do the work. The novel remains a sharp study of faith under modern pressure.
13547-the-rocks-of-valpre:
Ethel M. Dell's 1913 romance The Rocks of Valpré opens with a prologue on the knight of the magic cave, destiny. A rope of sand, and divine magic, then follows Bertrand, Max Wyndham, and a woman whose love is tried and purified. Southey's lines on love indestructible, sown with toil and reaped in heaven, set the tone.

A man confesses dishonour, worse than failure, to a woman who echoes the word unbelieving, his voice choked as he bends over her hand. Max, a Wyndham, tells Bertrand he will play the game with him because he is straight, though such conduct does not run in his family. Dell mixes chivalry, shame, and steadfast love in a high romantic key.
13577-the-meadow-brook-girls-afloat-or-t:
Janet Aldridge sends the Meadow-Brook Girls afloat in 1913 on the stormy cruise of the Red Rover. Harriet and her friends scent a mystery, meet Crazy Jane, set up housekeeping aboard, and face a sudden awakening, a mysterious night journey, and a midnight alarm.

The Tramp Club, invited by Billy Gordon, who owns the launch, spends weeks on the lake with camp equipment while the boys know the water and the girls know camping. George cannot answer how the girls got back into the lake, and laughs with Harriet at the riddle. Aldridge writes a girls' camp story of rivalry, laughter, and a lake cruise that turns stormy.
1368-when-the-world-shook-being-an-accou:
H. Rider Haggard's adventure opens with three English friends, Arbuthnot, Bastin, and Bickley, sailing south after a death in their circle. A cyclone wrecks their plans and strands them on a hidden Pacific island, where a people shut off from the world guard an ancient secret in a tomb.

There they find sleepers from a lost age, a queen of strange power, and a choice between old faith and new science. Bastin preaches, Bickley doubts, and Arbuthnot watches love grow amid peril. The book blends lost-world wonder with a debate on faith, fate, and human pride.
13786-the-influence-of-old-norse-literat:
Conrad Hjalmar Nordby wrote this study of Norse influence on English letters, published in 1901. It was his only literary work, left without final revision and missing a few planned pages. Friends published it as a memorial to his ardent study. A verse from Hávamál heads the book, on fame that never dies.

Nordby traces Norsemen leaving home in the last decades of the ninth century for Iceland. Sixty years to 930 went to settling land, and a hundred years followed for saga growth. He shows how Norse story, myth, and poetry entered English writing. The study remains useful for students of medieval influence. Its unfinished state adds poignancy to its learning.
13844-no-13-washington-square:
Leroy Scott published this 1914 novel about a proud New York household at Number 13 Washington Square. Mrs. De Peyster rules her house with strict ideas of honour and name. Servants depart, an amiable young gentleman arrives, and a honeymoon pair upset the order. Chapters titled Behind the Blinds and The Flight hint at secrets.

Scott mixes comedy of manners with melodrama. Mrs. De Peyster must face the gap between her code and her children's happiness. A reverend, a predicament, and a homecoming test her pride. The novel moves through drawing rooms and city streets with brisk dialogue. It offers a lively picture of old New York society in decline.
1386-lady-baltimore:
Owen Wister's novel of Charleston society follows a young Northern lawyer who falls in love with a Southern girl and must learn the unwritten rules of her world. At the centre stands Lady Baltimore, a cake whose recipe, like the city's code, is prized, guarded, and passed only to those who earn it.

Through balls, calls, and family talk, the hero weighs love against honour, and old Charleston against new money. Wister writes with affection for both sides and a sharp eye for manners. The book is a gentle romance of region, pride, and the small tests that decide a marriage.
13923-the-whitehouse-cookbook-1887-cooki:
Mrs. F. L. Gillette and Hugo Ziemann, steward of the White House, compiled this 1887 household cyclopedia. It covers cooking, toilet and household recipes, menus, dinner-giving, and table etiquette. Care of the sick, health suggestions, and facts worth knowing follow. The volume is dedicated to the wives of presidents.

Recipes range from French chops, trimmed and shaped with care, to cakes, soups, and preserves. Menus and etiquette chapters teach hosts how to give dinners well. Sickroom advice reflects Victorian home medicine. The book became a best-selling American house manual. It still charms readers as a record of Gilded Age domestic life.
1395-letters-on-literature:
Andrew Lang's letters, first printed in the Independent of New York, discuss books with more freedom and bias than a grave essay allows. Each letter goes to an invented friend, yet the subjects are real: Fielding, Longfellow, Keats, Virgil, Lucretius, Richardson, and the French tale Aucassin and Nicolette.

Lang praises, teases, and quarrels with his authors in turn, and adds notes on verse, book-hunting, and tales of American Indians. The letters show a working critic's tastes at close range. Readers get sharp judgments, odd lore, and a sense of how one lively mind weighed old and new books.
13992-kitty-trenire:
Mabel Quiller-Couch wrote Kitty Trenire, a Cornish children's novel of family life and mishaps. Kitty's story opens with fate and a rusty nail on a fierce afternoon. Chapters follow news, a drive, a slice of cake, and storms at home and abroad. Wenmere Woods, tea at the farm, and the Rover's ride home add country colour.

Later chapters bring lessons, alarms, dreadful stockings, and an exciting night. Mokus and carrots, a missing child, and banishment test Kitty's spirit. A sharp-tongued servant scolds Kitty for wanting tea before time. Quiller-Couch writes with humour and affection for Cornish speech. The novel suits young readers who enjoy family stories.
13996-the-divine-fire:
May Sinclair published The Divine Fire in 1904, a novel of a poet and his muse. Rickman, a young poet, writes verse of cold, polished marble, including a poem called Helen. A woman reads it aloud in golden afternoon, building its beauty with her voice. She cannot tell him what she thinks of Rickman himself, but her reading speaks.

Sinclair follows genius, love, and ambition through London literary life. Owen Seaman in Punch praised her sure, leisured style and diffused humour. The novel weighs art against life, and fame against feeling. Its comedy stays quiet and observant. The Divine Fire remains one of Sinclair's most admired early novels.
14045-at-a-winter-s-fire:
Bernard Capes gathered tales in At a Winter's Fire in 1899, most first printed in magazines. Capes thanks editors of the Cornhill, Macmillan's, Lippincott's, Pearson's, and the Sketch for reprint permission. Contents include The Moon Stricken, Jack and Jill, The Vanishing House, and Dark Dignum. William Tyrwhitt's Copy, A Lazy Romance, and Black Venn follow.

A moon-stricken man suffers a frost-bite in the brain, a suspension of intelligence April memory might thaw. His mother tells the story of his collapse. Capes writes ghostly, strange tales with literary polish. Dinah's Mammoth, The Black Reaper, and A Voice from the Pit close the book. The collection suits readers of Victorian weird fiction.
14171-a-man-four-square:
William MacLeod Raine's 1919 western stars Jimmie-Go-Get-'Em, a straight shooter in a crooked cattle country. Chapters move from Shoot-a-Buck Cañon through rustlers' camps, gun-barrel roads, and stampedes. Billie stands pat, Bud Proctor lends a hand, and Peg-Leg Warren crosses the trail. A sheriff functions, fugitives flee, and a mysterious Pete exits in due course.

Tricks and loyalty drive the action. Bud slips to the Elephant Corral by a back way, borrows two horses under a false errand from Mr. Sanders, and whistles Yankee Doodle as camouflage. At a campfire, hungry men trade talk of cattle drives and old-timers like Homer Webb, who knocked the bark off the country. Raine writes clean, fast western prose, and his hero earns the title: four-square in a land of rustlers, double-dealing, and dust storms.
14219-the-helmet-of-navarre:
Bertha Runkle's 1901 romance The Helmet of Navarre takes Macaulay's Ivry as motto: press where the white plume shines, and make the helmet your oriflamme. André Castaigne's pictures show Florentines in the Hôtel de Mayenne and other civil-war scenes. Chapters run from a flash of lightning and the Amour de Dieu inn to rapiers, vows, divided duty, and a matter of life and death.

Lorance de Montluc, a serving girl at the story's heart, blames her vanity for a letter that endangered a boy she loves. She springs to shield him, eyes flashing, then confesses M. de Lorraine played on her pique during five weeks without M. de Mar. Étienne, a trusty messenger, offers to carry a cipher packet to Lemaître, while his master breaks the royal seal and scratches out an initial for safety. Romance, intrigue, and honor braid together in a popular historical tale.
14224-samoa-a-hundred-years-ago-and-long:
George Turner of the London Missionary Society wrote this account of Samoa, first printed in 1884 and reprinted by the University of the South Pacific in 1984. Chapters cover the islands' position, early visitors, names, gods superior and inferior, childhood, food, clothing, amusements, disease, death, burial, and houses. Missionary eyes observe, but Samoan custom leads the narrative.

Marriage and village law receive careful detail. A match needs parents' favor, and families spend months gathering tonga, fine mats and native cloth made by women, for the bridegroom's side. The groom's kin answer with oloa: canoes, pigs, and foreign goods. Village courts punish boldly, and a youth may bite a root five times before chiefs and walk away with mouth afire. Districts of eight or ten villages join for mutual protection. Ethnography and story blend throughout.
1423-no-thoroughfare:
Opening in London on a November night in 1835, this stage drama in prose form follows two men whose lives were swapped at birth. One grows up rich, the other poor, and a dying woman's secret, a stolen identity, and a fortune in dispute set them on a collision course across England and abroad.

Through acts set in London, a Swiss inn, and a lonely house, the plot tightens with chases, disguises, and a final reckoning. The pace is theatrical and the turns are bold. It is a melodrama of birthrights, guilt, and justice long delayed, written for the stage and the page alike.
14252-the-age-of-shakespeare:
Algernon Charles Swinburne published The Age of Shakespeare in 1908, dedicating its verses to Charles Lamb. Lamb, Swinburne writes, rescued Shakespeare's fellows from oblivion when their glory shone round Shakespeare's bright as now. Contents honor Christopher Marlowe, John Webster, Thomas Dekker, John Marston, Thomas Middleton, William Rowley, Thomas Heywood, and George Chapman among others.

Criticism stays vivid and combative. A dialogue between London and Westminster in 1608 strikes Swinburne as windy talk, saved by historic interest and flashes of eloquence. Dekker's pamphlet Work for Armourers sets Poverty against Money in a social fight, with grim humor and sad acceptance. Heywood's plain tale of Elizabeth's troubles, rough but lively, earns praise for pace and spirit. Poet judging poets, Swinburne keeps the age in full, quarrelsome color.
1427-a-drama-on-the-seashore:
Balzac's brief seaside sketch opens with a young man measuring his future against the sea, and a chance meeting on the Breton shore. An old fisherman and his son draw him into a tale of wreck, grief, and a father's crime, told against cliffs, tides, and a lonely house above the waves.

The story is short and sombre, and its power lies in the contrast between the vast sea and one family's guilt. Balzac uses the coast as both scene and judge. It is a miniature tragedy about youth, remorse, and the weight of a past that will not stay buried.
1428-la-grenadiere:
Balzac's short tale takes its name from a little white house above the Loire, a mile below the bridge at Tours. There a widowed mother and her two sons live in quiet retirement, and the beauty of the place. Its river, islands, and cliffs, frames a story of devotion, illness, and a mother's sacrifice.

Told with lyrical care, the tale watches the household through seasons of hope and decline. Its sadness is gentle rather than violent. La Grenadiere is a miniature of Balzac's tender manner, a portrait of a home whose charm cannot hold back loss.
14280-holidays-at-roselands-a-sequel-to-:
Martha Finley's Holidays at Roselands, a sequel to Elsie Dinsmore entered in 1868, follows Elsie's holidays with her papa. Burns supplies the motto: hope not sunshine every hour, fear not clouds will always lower. Morning scenes show Elsie bright after sleep, confident in her fathers' love, while her papa takes her in his arms and kisses her.

Letters test obedience. Elsie pleads in tearful tones for a letter she longs to see, but her papa answers coldly and forbids letters that do not pass through his hands, including any to Miss Allison. Later, reading Elsie's own letter after loss, he groans that she asked his forgiveness while he abused authority, and wishes one hour to beg forgiveness on his knees. Elsie answers with love: she belonged to him, needed correction, and found Jesus when separated from nurse and arms. Pious, tearful, and earnest, the book shaped generations of young readers.
1430-beautiful-stories-from-shakespeare:
E. Nesbit retells Shakespeare's plays as short prose stories for young readers, turning verse drama into plain narrative without losing plot or character. Comedy, tragedy, and history all appear, from mistaken twins and jealous kings to lovers, usurpers, and shipwrecked dukes.

Each tale keeps the play's shape while smoothing its language, so children can follow the action before they meet the verse. Nesbit's versions have introduced generations to Shakespeare. The book is a friendly doorway into the plays, best read as a first map rather than a substitute. Teachers have used it for generations as a first step.
14487-the-lion-s-share:
Arnold Bennett's 1916 novel The Lion's Share follows Audrey, a young woman of the Five Towns circle, through love, money, and wartime London and Paris. Bennett had already made his name with Clayhanger and The Old Wives' Tale.

Audrey visits the Foa household, rides with Monsieur Musa, and weighs suitors and loyalties while the war reshapes her world. Bennett's eye for domestic detail, hotels, and drawing rooms carries the story. The novel is a quieter Bennett, concerned with a woman's independence and the price of taking the larger share of life.
14595-the-soldier-boy-or-tom-somers-in-t:
Oliver Optic's Civil War boys' novel follows Tom Somers, a patriotic young man who leaves a home of plenty to fight for the Union. Hurst published the volume in New York, with a dedication from William T. Adams.

Tom endures sneers from Pinchbrook, calling him a baby, until he earns respect, then marches with a regiment massed around Washington, where fear gives way to hope. Optic consulted loyal and rebel authorities while keeping the tale a romance, not a history. The book is a stirring boys' adventure of the Great Rebellion, moral and patriotic.
14616-thoughts-moods-and-ideals-crimes-o:
W. D. Lighthall, a Montreal advocate, published this 1887 volume of poems, Thoughts, Moods and Ideals, subtitled Crimes of Leisure, at the Witness printing house. Lighthall dedicated it to friends.

The poems open with a dialogue between a young man and a seer on the vision haunting the new Canadian soul, from Breton's shore to Vancouver's strand. Later pieces visit Venice and Florence, watch sunrises, and muse on how familiar things will one day seem antique. The verse is earnest and patriotic, a young dominion's attempt at a national poetry. Lighthall later edited Songs of the Great Dominion.
14637-aspects-of-literature:
J. Middleton Murry's 1920 collection, published by Knopf in New York, gathers essays first printed in the Times Literary Supplement, the Nation, and the Athenaeum. Murry arranged them in order of writing, with two exceptions.

The essays treat the function of criticism, Rousseau's religion, Edward Thomas's poetry, Chekhov, and Keats, whose revised Induction to Hyperion Murry prizes above the Odes. His criticism is searching and severe, aimed at tradition and fashion alike. The book shows a young critic of the modernist years finding his standard of values. Murry later edited the Adelphi and wrote on Keats at length.
14901-epilepsy-hysteria-and-neurasthenia:
Isaac G. Briggs, writing for Methuen in 1921 and dedicating the book to his old schoolmaster Albert E. Woodruff, explains epilepsy, hysteria and neurasthenia for general readers. Major and minor epilepsy, rarer types, general remarks and causes open the volume, with prevention of attacks and first aid to victims.

Neurasthenia, hysteria and advice to neuropaths follow, then first steps toward health: digestion, indigestion, dieting, constipation, general hygiene and sleeplessness. Briggs writes plainly and practically, though his medical advice is now out of date and must not be followed. As history, the book shows how early twentieth-century doctors grouped nervous disorders and counselled patients.
15095-the-story-of-a-picture:
Douglass Sherley's short 1884 tale, subtitled a dainty trifle for his lady love, centers on a colored crayon portrait in a crowded shop window. A youth of the town stops to gaze at a pretty girl in a white gown, holding a letter and pen beneath a marble chimney piece carved with cupids. Treasures crowd the shelf above her.

The youth's hope, the pictured face, and the shop's rare goods weave a slight, sentimental romance about art and longing. Sherley writes in lush, old-fashioned prose, and the tale runs only a few pages. It reads as a keepsake piece, charming in its earnest devotion to beauty and to love.
15108-lazarre:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood's 1901 novel opens in St. Bat's church in Normandy, where a dazed boy sits by a blacksmith's forge. A little girl named Eagle de Ferrier asks his name twice and gets no answer, while hammers echo through the church. The boy, Lazarre, will grow into a life of strange fortune.

Catherwood follows him from that church prelude toward an imperial court, where luck lifts him high. Illustrations by André Castaigne add drama to the tale. The novel blends history, romance, and mystery in a French setting, and it rewards readers who like a slow, rich historical romance.
15153-the-land-of-heart-s-desire:
William Butler Yeats's one-act play, printed here as a Little Blue Book, is set in a Sligo farmhouse kitchen at the end of the eighteenth century. Maureen and Bridget Bruin, Shawn, and young Maire sit by a turf fire as a strange faery child enters their home. The cast list names a priest, Father Hart, among them.

Maire, reading an old manuscript and dreaming of a world beyond housework and marriage, hears the faery call to a land of heart's desire. Her family pleads, prays, and argues against the pull. In short, lyrical scenes Yeats turns a folk tale into a play about youth, faith, and the lure of the unseen.
15204-women-wage-earners-their-past-thei:
Helen Campbell's 1893 study, with an introduction by Richard Ely, traces women wage earners from colonial times to the factory age. Chapters look back at early work, follow the rise of trades, and report wage rates in America, England, and the Continent. Labor bureaus and their work get a full chapter.

Campbell, author of Prisoners of Poverty, writes with reformist zeal and a mass of detail on hours, pay, and conditions. She dedicates the book to Alice, friend, helper, and comrade. The study remains a landmark for labor history and for the story of women at work.
1530-measure-for-measure:
Shakespeare's Vienna problem play opens with a duke who leaves his city in the hands of Angelo, a deputy of strict virtue, and watches in disguise as Angelo enforces laws against lust. Claudio faces death for a lover's pregnancy, and his sister Isabella, a novice nun, pleads for his life at a terrible price.

Angelo's own lust, a bed trick, and a head trick drive the plot toward a final scene of judgment, pardons, and proposals. The play's mercy is as debated as its justice. Measure for Measure is Shakespeare's darkest comedy, a study of power, sex, and law that still unsettles.
15333-the-confessions-of-nat-turner-the-:
Thomas Gray published this 1831 account of Nat Turner, leader of the Southampton insurrection in Virginia, as confessions fully and voluntarily made to Gray in prison. Turner acknowledged them when they were read before the court at Jerusalem on November 5, 1831, with a court certificate under seal. An authentic account of the whole rising follows.

Lists name whites murdered and Black people brought before the court and sentenced. Gray's text, mediated by a white recorder, must be read with care, yet it remains a central source on the revolt. Historians of slavery will find it grim, essential, and troubling.
1537-pericles-prince-of-tyre:
Pericles, Prince of Tyre, follows its hero from Antioch to Tyre, Tarsus, Pentapolis, and Ephesus, through shipwreck, famine, tournaments, and a daughter lost and found. A chorus, Gower, narrates the wanderings, and Pericles endures pirates, a brothel, and a seeming death before a final recognition scene reunites his family.

The play's plot is episodic and its verse is mixed, yet its pathos is real, and the reunion of Pericles and Marina moves audiences still. It is a romance of patience and providence, and a bridge to Shakespeare's late plays of loss and restoration.
15384-the-real-adventure:
Henry Kitchell Webster's 1916 novel The Real Adventure, in book form after a 1915 serial, opens with a point of departure and a beginning adventure. Book one, The Great Illusion, follows Frederica's plan and what happened to it, with Rosalind and others in the cast. An illustration shows a pair who cannot talk where they stand.

Webster traces a young woman's search for a real life beyond illusion, through love, work, and choice, in a thoughtful American style. The novel balances romance with social observation. Readers who like early twentieth-century fiction of manners will find it engaging and humane.
1547-sir-thomas-more:
Sir Thomas More, an anonymous play of the sixteenth century ascribed in part to Shakespeare, follows the lord chancellor from London streets and the Sessions House through his rise, his conscience. His fall under Henry VIII. First printed in 1844 from the Harleian manuscript in the British Museum, it survives as a collaborative text.

More's wit, his mercy to rioters, and his refusal to endorse the king's divorce drive the drama toward the scaffold. The famous insurrection scene, possibly Shakespeare's, pleads for strangers with humanity. The play is a fascinating document of censorship, conscience, and early modern London.
15585-humorous-masterpieces-from-america:
Edward T. Mason edited this anthology of humorous masterpieces from American literature, published in New York and London in 1886 by Putnam's Sons. It gathers short comic pieces by leading American writers, each with dates, so a reader can sample a generation's humor in one volume.

Bayard Taylor, William Allen Butler, and John William de Forest open the set, followed by Trowbridge, Bunce, Warner, and Frances Lee Pratt. Louisa May Alcott, William Wirt Howe, and Artemus Ward follow, with Frank Stockton, Harriett Prescott Spofford, and Mark Twain's celebrated jumping frog of Calaveras County. Fitz Hugh Ludlow and Thomas Bailey Aldrich close the book. The anthology shows American humor before Twain dominated it: local, literary, and fond of tall tales.
15587-macleod-of-dare:
William Black, author of A Princess of Thule and A Daughter of Heth, published this novel in New York in 1883, with John B. Alden. It opens at Castle Dare, on the high rocky coast of Mull, at sunset over lonely western seas. Ulva, Lunga, and the Dutchman's Cap darken on the waters, while the great hall blazes with candles for only three people at a long table.

At the head sits an old lady with silvery hair and proud features, her blue-grey eyes dimmed by sorrow. Later passages follow Sir Keith Macleod and his yacht. Sun-browned, sinewy fellows stand ready to go anywhere at his bidding. Yet he knows too much about tinned meats for a romantic heroine's taste. Black writes a Highland romance of clans, sea, and pride, where old traditions meet a newer, plainer world.
15597-stories-of-american-life-and-adven:
Edward Eggleston, author of Stories of Great Americans for Little Americans, published this school reader with the American Book Company in 1895 and 1923. A preface gives three aims. First, make school reading pleasant with simple, direct, exciting matter. Second, cultivate interest in true narratives full of action. Third, build a preference for fact over fancy in young minds.

Contents range from a white boy among the Indians and the making of a canoe. They run on to kidnapped boys, the last battle of Blackbeard, an old Philadelphia school, and stories of whaling. Later tales include witchcraft in Louisiana, a story of Niagara, among the alligators, Elizabeth Zane, and river pirates. Eggleston writes for boys and girls whose pulses are quick with youth, in short tales meant to wake attention and teach American history by adventure.
1560-the-san-francisco-calamity-by-earth:
Compiled from eyewitness accounts, this large volume tells of the San Francisco earthquake and fire of 1906, when a great city shook, burned, and emptied in days. Reports describe the quake itself, the fires that followed, the panic and lawlessness, and the plight of some 300,000 homeless people.

Later chapters add the worldwide rush to the rescue, with relief trains, camps, and rebuilding, plus accounts of other great earthquakes and volcanic eruptions for comparison. The prose is urgent and often graphic. The book is a period record of disaster, valuable as a first draft of a city's worst week.
15678-the-house-that-jill-built-after-ja:
E. C. Gardner, author of Homes and How to Make Them and Home Interiors, published this book on home architecture in Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1896, with W. F. Adams Company. The title jokes that Jill builds after Jack's house has proved a failure. Fifteen chapters or more run from a wise father and a glad son-in-law through moral suasion for malarial marshes to a first visit and sage advice.

Later chapters weigh many fires against small dividends, floods and rains, and Jill's wisdom in the kitchen. Be honest and keep warm, truth, poetry and roofs, and professional etiquette follow. Questions of fire and water, what to stand upon, and economy, cleanliness, and health close the set. Gardner writes a practical, witty guide: how to build a sound, healthy, honest house, with the housewife's sense at its center.
15749-the-interest-of-america-in-sea-pow:
A set of essays on naval power by Captain Alfred T. Mahan of the United States Navy, issued in London in 1897. Mahan, author of a famous study of sea power in history, argues that trade, fleets, and bases shape a nation's fate. The essays first appeared in magazines and reviews, then were gathered here with a preface. Readers at the time took Mahan as a voice on strategy.

Mahan presses America to build a strong navy, guard its coasts, and think hard about canals, colonies, and trade routes. He weighs Britain's example, the Pacific, and the Caribbean as tests of policy. The tone is firm and practical, not dreamy: ships cost money, but weakness costs more. The book matters as a record of how America debated its rise as a sea power.
15792-folk-lore:
A study of folk belief in the west of Scotland by James Napier, Fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh. Alex. Gardner issued it in Paisley in 1879. Napier, author of notes on Partick, gathers superstitions he knew within his own century. An appendix links Christmas, May Day, Saint John's Day, and Halloween to ancient sun and fire worship.

Chapters treat birth and childhood, marriage, and death, then witchcraft, second sight, and the black art. Charms, counter-charms, and divining follow, with superstitions of daily life. Napier writes as a collector, not a scoffer, saving beliefs before they fade. The book still serves folklorists: a careful record of what Scots feared, hoped, and practised.
15867-the-little-colonel-s-chum-mary-war:
A children's novel by Annie Fellows Johnston, author of the Little Colonel series, issued by L. C. Page and Company in Boston in 1908. Etheldred B. Barry supplied the pictures. Mary Ware, the Little Colonel's chum, takes the lead in this volume, her keen gray eyes sweeping a newcomer in one pictured scene. A twenty-third impression followed in 1944.

Mary's friendship with Lloyd, the Little Colonel, faces tests of loyalty, temper, and growing up. Kentucky homes, schools, and country pleasures fill the chapters. Johnston writes with warmth for girls who grew up with the series. The book delights as a friendship tale: two girls, different in temper, true to each other through it all.
15982-woman-as-she-should-be-or-agnes-wi:
A novel by Mary E. Herbert, author of Aeolian Harp and Scenes in the Life of a Halifax Belle, published by the author in Halifax, Nova Scotia, in 1861. Miles and Dillingham printed it in Cambridge, Massachusetts. A Wordsworth epigraph pictures a spirit, yet a woman too, with household motions light and free. Agnes Wiltshire embodies Herbert's ideal.

Agnes moves through praise, blame, love, kisses, tears, and smiles, never too bright or good for human nature's daily food. Herbert writes for readers who prized domestic virtue. The novel shows a mid-century ideal of womanhood: gentle, capable, and true. It still interests students of Canadian letters: a woman author, shaping her own heroine.
16055-shakespeare-and-precious-stones-tr:
George Frederick Kunz, the famed gem expert, wrote this study of every known reference to precious stones in Shakespeare's works. The book asks what Shakespeare knew of gems, where his material came from, and what stones meant in his plays and poems. Contents divide the references between the plays and the poems, with illustrations including the Droeshout portrait and a diamond cutter's shop.

Kunz also sets out the lore behind the stones: their symbolism, superstitions, use as talismans, and ties to birth months and planets. The result joins literary study with the history of jewels, showing how deeply gems ran through Elizabethan life and speech. Shakespeare lovers and gem lovers alike will find fresh detail here.
16056-a-soldier-s-sketches-under-fire:
A book of war drawings by Harold Harvey, a private soldier, issued in London by Sampson Low, Marston and Company. A frontispiece shows Private Harold Harvey himself. Harvey's forenote calls the volume an unpretentious book of annotated drawings, plain about its scope and limits. Faked pictures of the war, he notes, are plentiful.

His sketches were taken on the spot they depict, sometimes by a hand that had momentarily laid down a rifle to draw them. A draughtsman who drew under fire made every picture. Captions explain each scene with soldierly brevity. The book stands as a true record of the trenches: art made between shots, honest because it was made there.
1607-a-journey-in-other-worlds-a-romance:
John Jacob Astor sends travellers in a romance of the future to Jupiter and Saturn, imagining life on other worlds with Victorian science and wonder. The journey, written in 1894, predates much modern science fiction. Astor, heir to a great fortune, wrote the novel in 1894, before his death on the Titanic.

Astor pictures advanced beings, strange landscapes, and moral lessons drawn from other planets. The novel charms as an early space romance, and as a view of what a wealthy American imagined for the future. His Jupiter and Saturn, imagined with canals and strange beings, reflect Victorian astronomy.
16246-a-very-pleasaunt-fruitful-diologe-:
Erasmus of Rotterdam wrote this dialogue called The Epicure, newly translated into English in 1545 and dedicated to the young Prince Edward. Its preface warns Christians not to be deceived by false doctrine or vain talk, but to hearken to the Gospel. The dialogue then argues that dignity, riches, kinship, worldly pomp, and renown neither make men better nor happier, against the blind judgment of most people.

Erasmus turns Epicurus into a Christian teacher, finding true pleasure in a good conscience and a godly life rather than in luxury. The old spelling and quaint phrasing give the text a Tudor flavor. Readers of Renaissance humanism will find a short, surprising defense of pleasure rightly understood.
16295-the-vedanta-sutras-with-the-commen:
George Thibaut translated this first part of the Vedanta-Sutras with the commentary of Sankaracarya, a core text of Hindu philosophy. The volume belongs to the Sacred Books of the East series. Its contents run through the first two books of sutras. Each book is divided into four sections, with an introduction on Vedic literature. A note on transliteration guides readers through the Sanskrit terms.

The introduction explains that Vedic texts, to be understood, must be read with running commentaries, since memory alone cannot unlock them. Sankara's commentary gives the sutras their classic Advaita reading, arguing for the unity of self and ultimate reality. Students of Indian philosophy will find a foundational translation, dense yet indispensable.
16412-a-study-of-shakespeare:
Algernon Charles Swinburne sorts Shakespeare's plays into three broad periods in this study: lyric and fanciful work first, then comic and historic plays, then tragic and romantic ones. He opens with a long sea image, likening Shakespeare to an ocean that two hundred years of scholars have sailed, from small boats to great ships like Coleridge and Goethe.

Notes on King Edward III, a report from the New Shakespeare Society, and late corrections round out the volume. The prose is rich and warm, full of praise for the plays and their makers. Readers who know the plays well will find a poet's reading of them, not a dry list of dates.
16594-a-short-history-of-english-agricul:
W. H. R. Curtler traces English farming from the manor to modern times in this 1909 Oxford history. Early chapters cover communal farming, manor organization, and prices, then the thirteenth-century manor at its height, the Black Death, and the Statute of Labourers. Later chapters treat enclosure, the Peasants' Revolt, corn laws, and the golden age of the labourer.

Curtler writes as a clear, scholarly guide, with centuries laid out in order. The book suits students of rural history and readers curious about how England fed itself. It remains a compact, readable survey of a thousand years of farming change.
16612-the-lee-shore:
R. Macaulay's 1912 novel follows Peter Margerison from a school term where Urquhart steps in, radiant, to a life shaped by loss. Chapter titles chart the course. A hereditary bequest, the choice of a career, the hopes, and the complete shopper lead on to the loss of a profession, an idea, a goblet, the single state, and a wife. A new life and a last loss close the tale.

Macaulay writes with wit and a sharp eye for class, money, and the line between those who have and those who have not. The novel's losses pile up with quiet irony. Readers of early Macaulay will find a clever, sad comedy of a young man learning what the shore leaves behind.
16632-over-here:
Edgar A. Guest gathers home-front poems in this 1918 volume, dedicated to the mothers over here. The index runs from The Alarm and America through The Boy Enlists and The Call to Service. The Chaplain, Christmas 1918, The Flag on the Farm, The Girl He Left Behind, and The Gold Givers follow. Fathers, mothers, and boys at the front fill the verses.

Guest writes in his plain, heartfelt style, meant to comfort and rally families waiting at home. The poems are short and direct, with no high artifice. Readers of wartime verse will find a sincere record of American home feeling in the last year of the Great War.
16715-sir-walter-scott-as-a-critic-of-li:
Margaret Ball wrote this 1907 Columbia University Press study of Sir Walter Scott as a critic of books. Chapters move from Scott's life and his gifts as critic into his work on medieval verse and drama. Dryden, Swift, and the novelists of the 1700s follow. His views of his own age and his own work close the book. Footnotes sit at the end.

Ball shows Scott as more than a novelist: a scholar-editor who shaped how Britain read its past. His work on border minstrelsy, romances, and lives of novelists set the taste of his day. The book suits readers of Scott and of criticism, giving a clear, scholarly portrait of a writer judging other writers.
16736-books-and-culture:
Hamilton Wright Mabie wrote this 1896 book on how books shape a life, issued by Dodd, Mead in New York. Twenty-four short chapters move from method and place, through meditation, delight, and the feel for verse, to fiction, action, ideals, and a final look back. Each chapter takes one facet of reading and turns it over.

Mabie holds that books free a reader from his own time and place, widen feeling, and teach through tragedy and tale. He urges slow, thoughtful reading over fast skim, and links books to deeds, not just dreams. The book still speaks to readers who want reading to count for more than pastime.
16809-the-story-of-grenfell-of-the-labra:
Dillon Wallace wrote this 1922 boy's life of Wilfred T. Grenfell of Labrador, issued by Fleming H. Revell in New York, Chicago, and London. It follows Grenfell from the sands of Dee and North Sea fleets, down to Labrador, where a ragged man in a rickety boat and a fall overboard test him. Pictures mark each stage.

Wallace tells a young life of sea, medicine, and mission work on a harsh coast, in short chapters made for boys. Grenfell grows from a lad at sea into a doctor who serves fishers and folk of the far north. Young readers get a stirring, true-life tale of courage and service, told without gloom and with plenty of sea air.
17100-beatrix-of-clare:
John Reed Scott's 1907 romance sets a young knight, a bold countess, and the court of Richard of Gloucester in late medieval England. The tale opens with archers on a path and moves through captures, favors lost and won, an inn at Northampton, royal Windsor, and a judgment by the king. Beatrix of Clare herself, red-haired and sharp-eyed, steers much of the plot.

Sword play, chases, and court intrigue fill twenty-six chapters, with Clarence Underwood's pictures to match. Scott writes in the old cloak-and-sword mode, where honor, love, and loyalty clash at every turn. Fans of historic romance will find a fast, colorful tale with a strong heroine at its heart.
17101-anglo-saxon-literature:
John Earle, Rawlinson Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford, wrote this 1884 survey as part of a series on the dawn of European literature. He calls Anglo-Saxon the oldest vernacular literature of modern Europe, nursed by Latin and rising out of it. Chapters cover the heathen period, Kent schools, Anglian verse, West Saxon laws, chronicles, Alfred's translations, and Aelfric, ending with the Norman Conquest.

Earle wrote for students and general readers, with a preface noting new books he could not yet use. His survey is clear, orderly, and full of names and works. Readers new to Beowulf's world will find a solid first map of Old English letters, from rune and riddle to law and chronicle.
17144-the-house-of-the-vampire:
George Sylvester Viereck's 1907 novel opens at a New York concert, where a freakish Sicilian conductor waves his wand over music and clatter. Reginald Clarke, silvered and subtle like a Borgia cardinal in evening dress, leaves with a wistful young poet at his side. Clarke's smile is that of a conqueror, and the boy's soft eyes mark him as a dreamer.

The tale turns on a vampire of art: a master who drains young talent to feed his own work. Viereck writes in lush, decadent prose, with New York society as its stage. Horror fans will find an early, literary vampire tale where the bite is on the soul, not the neck, and youth itself is the prey.
17154-the-condition-elevation-emigration:
Martin R. Delany's 1852 book sets out the condition, elevation, emigration, and destiny of Black Americans. Early chapters weigh the state of many classes in Europe. They then compare the lot of colored people in the United States, with chapters on colonization, claims as citizens, warriors, businessmen, mechanics, and literary men and women. Farmers, herdsmen, and students of the professions each get a place.

Later chapters turn to national disfranchisement and to emigration: Liberia, the Canadas, Central and South America, and the West Indies. Delany's tone is firm and practical, urging self-reliance and organized action. The book stands as a landmark of Black political thought before the Civil War, and it still rewards careful reading today.
17244-french-art-classic-and-contemporar:
W. C. Brownell's 1892 survey, dedicated to Auguste Rodin, traces French painting and sculpture from classic roots to his own day. Classic painting runs from Claude and Poussin through David and Ingres; romantic painting follows Gericault and Delacroix; realistic painting covers Courbet, Manet, Monet, and Degas. Sculpture moves from Goujon and Houdon to Carpeaux, Chapu, and Rodin.

Brownell treats French art as a national expression, judging each school by its own aims. His prose is learned and firm, with long views rather than gossip. Art students and museum goers will find a solid Victorian guide to the French schools, still useful for names, order, and taste.
17504-the-mintage-being-ten-stories-one-:
Elbert Hubbard published this set of eleven short pieces in 1910, taking his title from Goethe's line about the mintage of the mind. The contents run wide. They include Five Babies, To the West, Simeon Stylites the Syrian, and the Battle of the Little Big Horn. Cleopatra and Caesar, Uncle Joe and Aunt Melinda, Billy and the Book, John the Baptist and Salome, and a closing piece called The Master follow.

Hubbard, the Roycroft printer and essayist, tells each story in his plain, aphoristic manner, mixing history, legend, and moral point. Readers get a sampler of his popular philosophy, where famous figures and homely folk alike serve a lesson. The book suits anyone curious about the homespun essay trade of early twentieth-century America.
1761-my-buried-treasure:
Richard Harding Davis calls this a true story of a search for buried treasure, with only one name changed: the man who led the expedition would not let Davis write it otherwise. Davis and his partner fit out a schooner, study old charts, and sail for a coast where earlier seekers made mistakes that cost lives.

The plan, Davis explains, is to avoid those mistakes and so avoid the killing that followed them. The tale is told with a reporter's briskness and a sportsman's humor. Its charm lies in the gap between the romance of treasure and the practical work of finding it: provisions, crews, and a map that may mean nothing at all.
17689-sea-warfare:
Rudyard Kipling published this war book with Macmillan and Company in London in 1916. Its contents gather three pieces: The Fringes of the Fleet, Tales of the Trade, and Destroyers at Jutland. The first, dated 1915, opens in Lowestoft, where a boat built for the herring trade is sent out roving with government coal and a quick-firing gun at bow and stern.

Kipling writes of trawlers, drifters, and destroyers turned to war work, and of the men who sailed them. Readers get wartime prose and verse from Britain's most famous living writer, close to the naval war. The book suits readers of Kipling and of the Great War at sea.
17740-the-chemistry-of-hat-manufacturing:
Watson Smith, fellow of the Chemical Society and of the Institute of Chemistry, delivered these lectures on the chemistry of hat manufacturing before the Hat Manufacturers' Association. Smith was then lecturer in chemical technology at Owens College, Manchester, and lecturer of Victoria University. Albert Shonk revised and edited the lectures for publication in London in 1906, with sixteen pictures.

Lectures open with textile fibres, chiefly wool, fur, and hair, then turn to water, its chemistry, impurities, and tests of purity. Acids and alkalis, boric acid, borax, and soap follow. Readers get a trade chemistry manual, precise and practical. The book suits readers of industrial history and of the hatting trade.
17741-pieces-of-eight-being-the-authenti:
Richard Le Gallienne wrote this 1918 tale of a treasure found in the Bahama Islands in 1903, now first given to the public in full. The book claims to rest on a dead pirate's own account, told on his deathbed in 1859, and on the author's own hunt that followed.

A secretary at Nassau, a ship called the Maggie Darling, sharks in the shallows, and an enchanted fish all play their parts. Le Gallienne dedicates the tale to his sailing friends, in the hope each finds his own treasure. It is a light, sunlit hunt story, part pirate yarn and part holiday, best read for fun rather than fact.
17997-contribution-to-passamaquoddy-folk:
J. Walter Fewkes wrote this paper on Passamaquoddy folk-lore, reprinted from the Journal of American Folk-Lore for October to December 1890. Fewkes worked with the Hemenway Southwestern Expedition, and he sought a truer way to record Native stories than the loose retellings of travelers.

He warns that no two tellers tell a tale alike, and that a listener tends to add his own thoughts. His cure is to give the speaker's exact words, with care for sounds, stress, and signs. The paper is short but weighty, a landmark in the move toward faithful field notes, and a useful start for students of Wabanaki lore.
18164-potash-perlmutter-their-copartners:
Montague Glass wrote Potash and Perlmutter in 1910, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap, with pictures throughout. Abe Potash and Morris Perlmutter, cloak and suit men of New York, are among the most famed comic partners in American letters.

The book opens with Abe paying his lawyer a hundred and fifty dollars to end the firm of Vesell and Potash, vowing never to take a partner again. Fate, of course, joins him to Perlmutter, and deals, quarrels, and laughs follow. Glass writes in rich, comic dialect. It is a funny, old New York tale of trade, friendship, and the art of the deal.
18252-hertfordshire:
Herbert W. Tompkins wrote this county guide to Hertfordshire, with pictures by Edmund H. New and from photographs, plus two maps. Methuen published the first edition in March 1903 and a revised second edition in 1922. Charles Lamb's line, hearty, homely, loving Hertfordshire, stands on the title page, and Tompkins dedicates the book to his wife.

The opening chapters treat situation, extent, and boundaries, physical features, climate, flora and fauna, population, communications, industries, history, antiquities, and celebrated men. A long alphabetical description of places follows, from St. Albans Abbey Church onward. Readers get a walking and reading companion: a county mapped, pictured, and described parish by parish.
18298-essays-in-natural-history-and-agri:
Thomas Garnett of Low Moor, Clitheroe, wrote these essays in natural history and agriculture, published in London at the Chiswick Press in 1883 after his death. The volume gathers facts, letters, and papers from a country naturalist who watched fish, birds, and fields with a farmer's eye. Its first part treats the salmon in rivers, its breeding, and the laws for its preservation.

Letters on farming follow, on growing wheat on the same land year after year, on gravelling clay soils, and on cotton. Papers on natural history close the book, with wrens' nests, the long-tailed titmouse, the stoat, the marsh titmouse, the creeper, and the dates of spring birds at Clitheroe in 1832. Readers get Victorian field science: close watching, plain notes, and practical advice for river and farm.
18384-studies-in-early-victorian-literat:
Frederic Harrison published this set of studies in early Victorian literature with Edward Arnold in London and New York in 1895. The essays first appeared in the Forum of New York and in London during 1894 and 1895, revised and partly rewritten after suggestions from England and America. Harrison aims at a mature estimate of the permanent influence and artistic achievement of the principal prose writers of the early Victorian age.

Harrison treats no living authors, and no poetry, philosophy, or science. His subjects run from characteristics of Victorian literature to Carlyle, Macaulay, Disraeli, Thackeray, Dickens, Charlotte Bronte, Kingsley, Trollope, and George Eliot. He finds the age brilliant, diverse, and complex, with genius more scientific than literary and greater in discovery than in abstract thought. Readers get Victorian prose judged by a contemporary critic: ten writers, weighed for what would last.
18421-bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-kee:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this children's book, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1922, with pictures by Walter S. Rogers. Hope also wrote the Bobbsey Twins and Six Little Bunkers series. Bunny Brown and His Sister Sue Keeping Store opens in a summer storm, while Bunny and Sue press their faces to the windows. Bunny boasts he can make his nose flatter than Sue can.

Chapters follow a grand crash, feeding alligators, and something in a desk. The corner store, a new pupil, and a busy buzzer follow. Later chapters bring the barn store, a hole, a ladder, a legacy, the last day, watering the garden, helping Mrs. Golden, and the cross man. A broken window and a window display close the fun. Children get shopkeeping as play: a store of their own, customers, and the small business of being kind and busy.
18441-bright-wits-prince-of-mogadore:
Burren Loughlin and L. L. Flood wrote this children's fantasy, published by H. M. Caldwell in New York and Boston in 1909. It tells of Bright-Wits, a prince of Mogadore, whose marriage to the beautiful Azalia depends on tasks, riddles, and trials in a kingdom that cannot be found on any modern map.

The prince arrives in Parrabang, solves the riddle of the rug, learns of three fountains and three gates, and faces the villainy of Garrofat and Doola. The tale is a chain of clever tests, where wit rather than force wins the day, and where each solved puzzle brings a new task.
18495-the-drama-of-the-forests-romance-a:
Arthur Heming wrote and illustrated this book of the Canadian forests. Doubleday, Page published it in Garden City and Toronto in 1921.
