Its pictures reproduce his paintings owned by the Royal Ontario Museum. Heming dedicates the book to Mr. and Mrs. David A. Dunlap, with whom he spent many happy seasons in the woods. A frontispiece shows a strange winged, tailed apparition crossing a lake on long upturned feet, carrying what might be a trident.

Chapters give romance and adventure, a quest for treasure, Oo-koo-hoo's El Dorado, Oo-koo-hoo playing the game, a meeting of wild men, wild animals and men, and life and love returning. Business and romance close the set. Readers get the north woods through a painter's eye: lakes, lynx, snow, York boats shooting cataracts, and the people who lived by trap and paddle.
18499-suzanna-stirs-the-fire:
Emily Calvin Blake, author of Marcia of the Little Home, wrote this children's novel, published by A. C. McClurg in Chicago in 1915, with pictures by F. V. Poole. Suzanna Stirs the Fire opens with Suzanna up at six, drawing a curtain to let in sunshine, while her sister Maizie still lies blurred with sleep. A frontispiece shows Suzanna telling Mrs. Reynolds she has come to stay.

Book one follows the tucked-in day, the only child, time with father in the attic, a new dress, and Suzanna coming to a decision. Later chapters bring her entry, regrets, a character met, a leaf missing from the Bible, and a picnic in the woods. Book two adds an Indian drill, a stray dog, a Lent mother, and Suzanna aiding Cupid. Young readers get a lively girl stirring a quiet household into warmth, mischief, and kindness.
18639-the-victorian-age-in-literature:
G. K. Chesterton wrote this short survey for the Home University Library in 1913, published at New York by Henry Holt. The editors warn it is not an authoritative history but a free, personal statement of views, made at their invitation. Chapters cover the Victorian compromise and its foes, the great Victorian novelists, the great Victorian poets, and the break-up of the compromise.

Chesterton opens by arguing that growth draws life from roots, not from leaving home behind, with Chaucer, Shakespeare, Johnson, Cobbett, and Dickens sharing a national note. His judgments are bold, witty, and often contrary. The book remains a lively, opinionated guide to Victorian letters.
18728-the-well-of-saint-clare:
Anatole France wrote this set of tales, translated by Alfred Allinson and published at London and New York in 1909. A prologue sets the frame: the narrator, at work in Siena's archives, meets Father Adone Doni on evening walks toward Monte Oliveto. Tales follow on San Satiro, Guido Cavalcanti, Lucifer, loaves of black bread, and the merry painter Buffalmacco.

Longer pieces include The Human Tragedy, with Fra Giovanni and a seraphic doctor, plus the Lady of Verona, the Mystic Blood, and Bonaparte at San Miniato. France mixes medieval Italy, wit, and gentle irony throughout. The book is a fine entry to his storyteller's art.
18818-on-the-evolution-of-language-first:
J. W. Powell's Smithsonian study, printed in the Bureau of Ethnology's first annual report, asks how a few old words can serve a world of new ideas. Drawing on Native American languages, Powell argues that new words rarely arrive from nowhere; old material is combined and reshaped instead.

He names four grammatic processes: joining words side by side, compounding them, fusing them by agglutination, and changing them by inflection. Chinese shows juxtaposition, while English pairs like house-top and truthful show compounding and fusion at work. The essay gives students a plain frame for watching languages grow, from small stocks of roots to full sentences that carry complex thought.
18833-with-clive-in-india-or-the-beginni:
G. A. Henty wrote this historical adventure about India in the days of Robert Clive, when Britain and France fought for power on the subcontinent. A young Englishman travels out as a writer for the East India Company, survives brushes with privateers and pirates, and reaches Madras as Clive arrives. The chapters then follow sieges, battles, and marches across southern India.

Arcot, the Black Hole of Calcutta, Plassey, and the sieges of Madras and Pondicherry all appear in turn, mixed with tiger hunts, escapes, and rescues. Henty aimed to teach history through a stirring personal story. Readers get a fast-moving introduction to the wars that laid the groundwork of British India, told from a young hero's viewpoint.
18916-daughter-of-the-sun-a-tale-of-adve:
Jackson Gregory published this adventure novel in 1921, first serialized as The Treasure of the Hills. Its hero is a young American known as Headlong, who plays dice with a figure in man's clothing who is not a man. From that strange game grows a spell, an expedition, and a tale of Aztec treasure. Zoraida Castelmar, daughter of the Montezumas, fronts the book.

Chapters promise an earthly paradise that proves quite another sort of place, a queen lady's command, a girl held for ransom, and eyes that hold a mystery. Gregory mixes lost-world romance with western adventure. Readers get a colorful quest tale, with treasure, captivity, and a proud heroine, in the author's popular romantic style.
18954-tom-slade-with-the-boys-over-there:
Percy K. Fitzhugh published this Boy Scout novel in 1918, with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. Its hero, Tom Slade, leaves home for service overseas during the First World War, the France that Americans then called Over There. The book is dedicated to the real Tom Slade, whose own adventures Fitzhugh says put these storied exploits in the shade.

Tom carries scout skills into wartime work: finding his way, helping comrades, and keeping steady under fire. The story treats scouting as training for real duty, not only for camp games. Readers get a wartime boys' book that mixes adventure with patriotism, and a snapshot of how the Scout movement presented itself to young readers in 1918.
19652-a-ball-player-s-career-being-the-p:
Marshalltown, Iowa, opens this baseball memoir, praised as a handsome town of some thirteen thousand people. A Ball Player's Career presents itself as the personal experiences and recollections of its player-author. Books of this kind came from the first stars of professional baseball. They let fans hear the game described by a man who played it.

Readers get the early pro game from inside: travel, pay, crowds, and clubhouse life. Such memoirs helped turn ballplayers into national figures. They also fixed stories that later histories would test. The value here is the first-hand voice from baseball's rough early decades. Few records of that era feel this direct.
19734-the-fairy-book-the-best-popular-st:
The Fairy Book promises the best popular fairy stories, selected and rendered anew. Its preface speaks plainly to parents and children. In real life, it warns, beautiful people are not always good. Ugly people are not always wicked either. Elder sisters are not all ungenerous, nor stepmothers all cruel. Tender young hearts, it says, are reached by fancy as soon as by reason.

Retellings shaped how generations first met fairy tales. Editors softened some cruelties and kept the wonders. A preface like this one argues for the tales' honesty. It defends fancy as a teacher in its own right. The stories inside are the shared stock of childhood. This book shows Victorians handing that stock down, carefully.
1983-monsieur-beaucaire:
Booth Tarkington sets a short romance in eighteenth-century England, where a French barber at Bath turns out to be far more than he seems. His skill at cards first exposes a cheating duke, then draws him into a duel of manners and rank. Tarkington, an American novelist of manners, sets the tale in Bath, the spa town where rank and gossip ruled.

Beaucaire courts a lady above his supposed station while his true birth stays hidden, and the plot turns on who knows his secret and when. The tale is light, brisk, and fond of period detail, with a hero who wins by wit and poise. The comedy turns on politeness itself, as Beaucaire's perfect manners prove stronger than any sword or title.
19908-essays-on-scandinavian-literature:
Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen published Essays on Scandinavian Literature in 1895. His Henrik Ibsen chapter, he explains, grew into its own book. That three-hundred-page study appeared the year before. It must be read as supplementary to this volume. His Björnson chapter nearly suffered the same expansion. Only heroic condensation kept it inside these covers. Boyesen, a Norwegian immigrant, interpreted the North for America.

Boyesen taught literature at Columbia and wrote novels too. He knew Ibsen's Norway from inside its culture. These essays carry Scandinavian writing to English readers early. Ibsen, Björnson, and their peers get full, serious treatment. The book marks America's discovery of modern Northern letters. Its enthusiasm still instructs and persuades.
19914-arabic-authors-a-manual-of-arabian:
Arabic Authors is a manual of Arabian history and literature by F. F. Arbuthnot. It hopes for a day when Oriental languages fill leisure hours. So much is to be learnt from Oriental literature, the author argues. King's College, London, is praised as full of promise for such study. A future generation thirsting for knowledge might study Arabic as a pastime. The manual itself opens that door for English readers.

Arbuthnot translated and promoted Eastern literature in Victorian Britain. His manual surveys poets, historians, and storytellers of Arabia. Short lives and work-lists guide beginners through centuries. The Thousand and One Nights looms over such surveys. This one stays practical, a handbook rather than a romance. It shows Oriental studies entering general culture.
19998-rural-architecture:
Lewis F. Allen wrote Rural Architecture to improve American farm buildings. Friends solicited the book, Allen says, believing he could help landholders. Without their urging, these pages would probably never have appeared. Practical farmers are his declared audience throughout. Plans for farmhouses, barns, and outbuildings fill the volume. Allen was a noted New York stock breeder and agricultural editor.

Farm architecture was a reform cause in the 1850s. Bad barns wasted stock, feed, and labor visibly. Allen gives designs, costs, and siting advice in full. His own farming success backed the authority claimed. The book belongs with Downing's country-house movement. It shows the model farm becoming an American ideal.
20101-under-fire:
Under Fire is a tale of soldiers, home, and the pride of a plains family. A soldier son comes home with an honored name in his trade. His parents glow with pride to have him under their roof again. Two sturdy, plains-bred little Cranstons add noise and joy to the house.

War still hangs over such a homecoming in the tale. Health, fame, and family love meet the strain of service life. The book shows how frontier homes bore the costs of war. Readers get a warm, tense story of return after danger and long absence.
20131-the-mask-a-story-of-love-and-adven:
Arthur Hornblow published The Mask in 1913, a story of love and adventure. News breaks of a huge gem found after blasting at some rocks. The land sits next to tracts of the Americo-African Mining Company. Some say the firm is already buying the ground for itself.

If true, the giant stone means a windfall for its Yankee owners. Diamonds, deals, and desire drive a tale set around African mines. The mask of the title hints at hidden faces and false shows. Readers get romance and risk in the world of gems and gold.
20406-epic-and-romance-essays-on-medieva:
W. P. Ker, a leading scholar of old literature, wrote Epic and Romance to explain the great stories of medieval Europe. The essays treat heroic poems, sagas, and romances as serious art. Ker writes for readers who want the old tales understood, not merely retold.

One essay wrestles with the Icelandic historian Sturla and the rivalry of a king and his father-in-law, Duke Skule. Ker praises the work of his friend Dr. Björn Magnússon Olsen on these hard problems. The book remains a guide to how epic strength and romance wonder grew side by side.
20572-marie-claire:
Marie-Claire is Marguerite Audoux's novel of a French orphan girl, drawn from the writer's own hard childhood. Marie-Claire grows up in a convent orphanage and goes out to work on farms and in service. The telling is plain, close, and quietly heartbreaking.

She remembers her sister's torments in their childhood games. The girl used to collect earthworms and hold them up close to her face. When she claimed she was no longer in pain, their keeper sent them both outdoors. One day her sister threw a handful of earthworms onto her dress. Such small cruelties mark the book's truthful eye.
20631-chosen-peoples-being-the-first-art:
Chosen Peoples, published in 1919, was the first Arthur Davis Memorial Lecture, delivered by Israel Zangwill. Zangwill, the Anglo-Jewish novelist, took up the hard idea of the chosen people. He spoke just after a war that had shown where racial pride could lead.

The recent show of racial arrogance in Germany, he notes, has handed the Allies a new weapon. An American writer in the Bookman declared that Germanism is Judaism. The proposition, Zangwill warns, contains just that dash of truth which is more dangerous than a falsehood. The lecture untangles that dash with care.
20657-tales-from-shakespeare:
Charles and Mary Lamb wrote Tales from Shakespeare to retell the plays as stories for young readers. Charles took the tragedies and Mary the comedies, in retellings first published in 1807. Their versions brought Shakespeare into the nursery without flattening his plots.

The Tempest opens the book. There was once an old man whose name was Prospero, and his daughter Miranda, a very beautiful young lady. She came to the island so young that she had no memory of any human face but her father's. The Lambs' plain, warm style has carried readers into Shakespeare for two centuries.
2066-wildfire:
Zane Grey sets a western romance at Bostil's Ford, where eighteen-year-old Lucy Bostil longs for something wonderful to break her quiet life. A forbidden ride, a wild horse, and a stranger soon answer that wish. Grey wrote Wildfire for readers who loved horses as much as romance, and Lucy shares that love.

Lucy, who loves every horse except her father's racer Sage King, finds herself at the heart of races, rivalries, and danger in the sage country. Grey writes the desert in warm colour, and the story moves between love, horses, and open land. The desert of southern Utah, with its sage and coloured cliffs, gives the story its glowing backdrop.
20702-a-general-plan-for-a-mail-communic:
A General Plan for a Mail Communication by Steam proposes regular steam packet routes to carry Britain's mail overseas. When sails ruled, letters waited on wind and season. The plan argues that steam can give the mail fixed days and faster passages between Great Britain and its distant ports.

It leans on expert proof. Mr. Napier of Glasgow, called an able and practical engineer, told the Post Office Commissioners in 1836 what steamers could do. Boats of 240 horsepower and 620 tons, he said, could be furnished at known prices. Such pamphlets helped push Britain into the steam age of world mail.
20733-critical-miscellanies-vol-1-of-3-e:
Robespierre and the close of the Reign of Terror open the first essay in Critical Miscellanies. The writer takes up a new French book on the fall of Robespierre. Those events bear the calendar name of Thermidor, in Year Two of the French Republic.

Victorian essay craft is on full show here, with long views of men and ideas. The piece weighs how a revolution turned on its own leaders. Later essays in the set treat other great figures and books. Readers who like bold, old-style literary essays will find strong opinions, wide reading, and prose built for argument rather than speed.
20740-myths-and-legends-of-all-nations-f:
Prometheus and Epimetheus, Forethought and Afterthought, open Myths and Legends of All Nations. The two brothers were sons of Titans who fought Jupiter and were chained below. Yet the brothers, for some reason, escaped that harsh fate.

Famed tales from Greece and other lands fill the book, retold in clear prose for general readers. Gods, heroes, gifts of fire, and hard lessons follow one after another. Such sets once served as a first door into world myth for many homes. The simple retelling keeps the old plots clear while trimming the hard parts of the source tales.
20784-eighth-annual-report-of-the-bureau:
Pueblo building in Tusayan and Cibola leads the eighth annual report of the Bureau of Ethnology. Victor Mindeleff studied those towns of stone and adobe in close detail. James Stevenson adds a study of a Navajo rite and its mythic sand painting.

Staff work by Cosmos Mindeleff, Garrick Mallery, James Mooney, and Jeremiah Curtin fills the report. The bureau sent trained men to record native life before it changed. Their plates and plans keep much that would else be lost. This 1886-87 volume is a rich trove for students of the native Southwest and its old towns.
20902-the-clyde-mystery-a-study-in-forge:
Plates from Gillen, learned boards, and Scots societies crowd the thanks in The Clyde Mystery. Andrew Lang turns to finds claimed as relics near the Clyde. Forgery and folklore, his subtitle warns, both haunt the case at hand.

Lang, a famed folklorist, tests stones and tales said to prove old Scots glory. He weighs proof with wit, lore, and a sceptic's sharp eye. The Clyde finds had stirred pride and doubt in learned Scotland. His study shows how scholars sort true relics from fond fakes, a craft as gripping as the finds themselves when told by Lang.
20953-by-the-christmas-fire:
Turning a sword to a pruning hook takes a smith, but a bayonet to a poker takes none. Samuel McChord Crothers opens By the Christmas Fire, from 1908, on that fireside thought. Severed from its rifle, the blade's new work is to coax winter flames.

Crothers, a beloved essayist and preacher, gathers warm talks for the Christmas season. Home, giving, faith, and good humour glow through his gentle pages. His essays were famed for kindness lit by quiet wit. This book suits slow winter reading, each piece a small fire of its own against the cold and dark outside.
21053-an-anthology-of-german-literature:
Sixty-nine lines of alliterative verse are all that survive of Germany's oldest heroic song, Calvin Thomas notes. The Kassel manuscript of the eighth or ninth century keeps that fragment safe. Its tongue mixes Low and High German, with gaps and doubtful words.

Thomas's anthology of German literature spans that fragment to near his own day of 1906. Poems, plays, tales, and essays appear in English versions with learned notes. He built the book for American students new to German letters. It maps a vast literature in one volume, from heroic lays to Goethe and beyond, with a teacher's steady hand.
21090-brief-history-of-english-and-ameri:
Henry A. Beers combined his outline sketches of English and American literature into this single brief history. It was published in New York, with copyrights running from 1886 to 1897. John Fletcher Hurst added an introduction and extra chapters on religious and theological writing in both countries. The book was aimed at students and general readers.

Beers moves through the main writers and periods of two literatures in a compact survey. Hurst argues that preachers and students of religion alike need real knowledge of literature. Indexes and page markers help readers use it as a reference. It shows how the two literatures were taught side by side in its day.
21098-the-independence-of-claire:
Claire Gifford has lived for three years in a Brussels pension when Mrs George de Horne Vaizey's novel opens. She stands in the salon asking herself one question: can she marry the man proposed for her? Her brain says she must, out of duty to her family, while her heart rebels.

Vaizey writes about young, well-brought-up women of Edwardian times, their money worries, clothes, parties, and marriage choices. Claire seems headed for a big mistake before matters sort themselves out. The title points to her real struggle, which is less about one suitor than about standing on her own feet and choosing her own life.
21214-the-law-and-lawyers-of-pickwick-a-:
Frank Lockwood, a Queen's Counsel and Member of Parliament, delivered this lecture in York and then in London in December 1893. Its subject is the law and lawyers of Dickens's Pickwick Papers. Lord Russell of Killowen, then Attorney General, introduced him at Morley Hall in Hackney. The Roxburghe Press printed the lecture in 1894.

Lockwood, himself a witty advocate, examines Sergeant Buzfuz and the famous trial of Bardell against Pickwick. That breach of promise case turns on chops, tomata sauce, and comic cross talk. He explains the real law behind Dickens's fun. An original drawing of Buzfuz fronts the little book.
21303-devon-boys-a-tale-of-the-north-sho:
Three boarders at Barnstaple Grammar School spend their summer holiday on Devon's north shore in George Manville Fenn's tale, set in 1752. Bob Chowne is a doctor's cross-grained son, and Bigley Uggleston is a fisherman's pleasant boy. Sep Duncan, the narrator, is a naval officer's son whose father has just bought a stretch of cliffs.

The boys blast a rock from the cliff top and uncover a rich vein of galena, lead and silver ore. Sep's father opens a mine on the spot. Escapades follow: rescues at sea by a French smuggler and a French attack aimed at twenty boxes of silver bullion stored from the mine.
21390-the-golden-grasshopper-a-story-of-:
Ernst Verner, a Dutch boy, tells his own tale in W. H. G. Kingston's The Golden Grasshopper. His parents died in Holland for their Protestant faith, and he reaches an England split by creed. Between King Edward, Queen Mary, and Queen Elizabeth, belief could cost a life.

The story first came out in 1870 as The Royal Merchant, in the days of Sir Thomas Gresham. Gresham, the great London merchant, stands at the heart of the tale's world of trade. Boys on the run, a hostile priest, and slow Channel crossings add the peril. Kingston revised the book near the end of his life.
21404-from-powder-monkey-to-admiral-a-st:
Three boys join the navy at its lowest rung in W. H. G. Kingston's From Powder Monkey to Admiral. Kingston wrote the story for the Boys' Own Paper when that paper first started. His aim was to show how a plain lad might climb to the top rank.

Powder monkeys ran powder to the guns in battle, small targets who often lived through fights. Real men like Benbow and Hopson had made just that climb before. The three boys share the usual run of Kingston sea adventures. Only one of them, though, wins his way to the quarterdeck and a midshipman's place.
21724-the-handbook-of-soap-manufacture:
Two chemists, W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, wrote this practical handbook of soap making, published in London in 1908. The opening chapter defines soap and explains how it cleans, through the splitting of fats by water and alkali. Later chapters take up the make-up of oils and fats and how they turn into soap.

The authors cover old research, modern methods, and the tools and tests a working soap maker needs. Twenty-seven pictures help show plant and process. The book was made for the trade, not the home kitchen. It gives a clear snapshot of factory soap making at the start of the twentieth century, chemistry and craft side by side.
21908-chums-of-the-camp-fire:
Bullfrog hunting opens Chums of the Camp Fire, a 1915 boys' book by Lawrence J. Leslie. Steve, Toby, and Max count thirteen frog saddles and aim for twenty before they quit. Toby stammers his tallies while the boys dream of the Dismal Swamp, where a bushel basket might be filled. The chapters roll into the woods: a terrible roar, a mysterious ham thrower, and a wild animal trap.

A strange disappearance and a plot against the missing link raise the stakes before the last camp fire. Leslie writes in the brisk series style, each chapter a small adventure with a hook. The frontispiece shows Max sure they can capture the monkey. It is cheerful outdoor fiction for boys of the camping age, all appetite and schemes.
21957-the-psychology-of-singing-a-ration:
Singing teachers are put on trial in David C. Taylor's The Psychology of Singing, first published in 1908 and reprinted in 1922. Taylor calls his book a rational method of voice culture built on a study of all systems, ancient and modern. In no art, he says, do art and nature seem so one as in singing. A perfect voice hides its own art completely.

Part one surveys modern instruction: breathing, registers, resonance. Part two attacks its fallacies one by one, from breath control to nasal resonance and mechanical management of the voice. Part three seeks the basis of a real science of voice. Taylor writes as a reformer with a laboratory mind. The book remains a sharp, readable argument that singing is guided by the ear and mind, not by throat tricks.
22071-marjorie-dean-college-sophomore:
Pauline Lester sent her heroine back to Sanford College in Marjorie Dean, College Sophomore, published in 1922. Marjorie and her friends return for their second year full of plans. Jerry speaks for them all: whose fault is it, she retorts, that she and Muriel have lost last year's trusting faith in reception committees? As freshmen they stood on the station platform like dummies, with no one to bid them the time of day.

The slight rankles, and the Sans Soucians, the campus society at the books' centre, must mend its ways. Lester's Marjorie Dean books followed their heroine through high school and college. This sophomore volume mixes friendship, snobbery, and reform in the series' earnest style.
22211-gilian-the-dreamer-his-fancy-his-l:
Neil Munro, the Scottish novelist of John Splendid, published Gilian the Dreamer in 1899. His subtitle promises Gilian's fancy, his love, and adventure. The book opens by a Highland river as rain beats on plane and beech leaves. The scent of the blossoming gean-tree hangs sweet and haunting round the road.

Gilian is a dreamer in a hard, practical world of Highland trade and kirk. Munro follows his fancies, his love, and his brushes with rougher men. Mist, hills, and old woods colour every chapter, as the opening sigh of wind suggests. The novel is a tender, melancholy piece of the Scottish literary revival.
22218-the-street-that-wasn-t-there:
Clifford D. Simak and Carl Jacobi wrote The Street That Wasn't There for Comet magazine in July 1941. Mr. Jonathon Chambers leaves his house on Maple Street and finds the world subtly wrong. Chambers was once a professor whose book cost him his university post in a scandal. What he taught has been forgotten, but it was revolutionary enough to ruin him.

Now the forgotten theory seems to be coming true around him. Streets, neighbours, and his own past refuse to stay fixed. Simak and Jacobi build the unease quietly, in a small town at evening. The story is a neat early tale of reality slipping, by two masters of the pulp magazines.
22255-the-counts-of-gruye-re:
Mrs. Henry de la Pasture translated The Counts of Gruyère from the French history of the Swiss counts. The book opens on a green plain where the first steps of the Alps rise like an amphitheatre. A little castled city on a solitary hill has watched the scene for a thousand years. That city is Gruyères, and its counts ruled the valley for centuries.

The history follows the counts through crusades, wars, debts, and marriages. The last count, Michael, lost the county in the 1500s, and the castle passed to Fribourg and Bern. De la Pasture, herself a novelist, made the dry records readable. The volume is Swiss local history in its romantic vein.
22280-views-and-reviews-essays-in-apprec:
W. E. Henley, poet and editor, gathered his criticism in Views and Reviews: Essays in Appreciation in 1890. Henley was a formidable judge with a wooden leg and a thunderous taste. On Dickens he is deliciously severe by proxy: Andrew Lang, he notes, mocks those who cannot read Dickens, yet loves only the humourist. For Dickens the artist in drama and romance Lang has as little sympathy as the most practical reader.

Henley himself reads generously and judges sharply. Essays on novelists, poets, and dramatists fill the volume. His criticism is personal, quotable, and often unjust in an interesting way. The book is a monument of the 1890s literary battlefield, where reputations were made by fighting.
22281-the-facts-about-shakespeare:
William Allan Neilson of Harvard and Ashley Horace Thorndike of Columbia wrote The Facts about Shakespeare as a plain handbook. They begin with an England in motion. When Elizabeth came to the throne, England was still largely Catholic after nine centuries. When Shakespeare died, it was Protestant and turning Puritan, and religion, politics, literature, and commerce had all changed around him.

Against that moving background the professors set the documents: baptism, marriage, will, and the Stratford monument. They separate record from legend with scholarly care. The book was written for students who wanted the evidence without the fog. It remains a sober, useful life in brief, all facts and no Bardolatry.
22303-personality-in-literature:
Personality in Literature is a critical essay preserved from Project Gutenberg, with no author named in the record. It opens at an exhibition of Post-Impressionist pictures. The writer walks the show with an artist who helped create it.

Forced to speak in questions, the writer faces a canvas that looks formless and ugly to untrained eyes. That awkward scene sets up the larger topic named in the title. The essay asks how the maker's own character shows through in creative work. Readers get period criticism in a personal voice, caught between polite manners and honest doubt about new art.
22318-crocker-s-hole-from-slain-by-the-d:
Crocker's Hole is one of R. D. Blackmore's tales from Slain by the Doones. Where other Doone stories chase outlaws, this one slows down for water. Its quoted passage follows small streams with loving patience.

Tricklets slip through water-grass, make moss, and forget themselves in the ooze. Kettles are filled from the same small flows at cottage doors. One and all, Blackmore writes, they come to the same thing at last: the river. That gentle close shows his gift for West Country landscape. Readers get a quiet nature piece tucked inside a book of rougher tales.
2238-measure-for-measure:
Vienna is rotting under lax rule when its duke steps aside and leaves the strict Angelo in charge. Measure for Measure follows Angelo as he revives old laws against vice, then falls prey to the very desires he punishes, blackmailing the novice Isabella over her brother's life. Shakespeare balances the grim plot with a comic underworld of pimps and fools.

The duke, watching in disguise as a friar, steers events toward mercy and exposure rather than revenge. Questions of justice, chastity, and power stay unsettled even at the end. The play fascinates because it refuses easy answers and mixes farce with moral dread.
22752-the-pirate-of-panama-a-tale-of-the:
William MacLeod Raine wrote The Pirate of Panama, a 1914 tale of the fight for buried treasure. Raine, a prolific western novelist, here trades the range for the sea roads of Panama, where tales of pirate gold still drew adventurers in the canal years. His subtitle promises the fight, and the book delivers it.

The opening is all weather and nerves: a chill wind swept the city and cut to the marrow. From a hilltop the narrator watches his car sliding down toward him as he clings to the curb, postponing the plunge into the flowing street. Modern streets give way to older, bloodier trails southward. Raine writes clean, fast adventure in his western manner, transplanted to treasure country.
22866-an-ounce-of-cure:
A doctor's warning opens An Ounce of Cure, a short story about health and denial. Fifty-five is a dangerous age, he tells his patient gravely. He asks about a cough, heartburn after dinner, and sleeping propped on pillows. Then comes the sigh. The man has gone ten years without a checkup.

The tale builds its tension from that ordinary neglect. Prevention, the old proverb promises, beats any cure, and the story tests the proverb on a man who would rather not know. Its setting is the modern clinic rather than the sickroom of older fiction. Readers get a compact, pointed piece of mid-century magazine storytelling, with a moral carried by scene and dialogue rather than lecture.
22996-the-rover-boys-on-snowshoe-island-:
Arthur M. Winfield races his Rover Boys across the ice in The Rover Boys on Snowshoe Island, published in 1918. On a Saturday in early winter, Colby Hall's cadets pack the smooth ice of the lake beside their school. Tag, hockey, and snapping the whip fill the hours until Gif Garrison, head of the athletic association, suggests a race.

Snowshoe Island and an old lumberman's treasure box wait beyond the schoolyard fun. Winfield, writing as the Rover Boys' chronicler, delivers the series formula, sport, mystery, and clean rivalry in equal parts. The cadet setting updates Tom, Dick, and Sam's world for a new generation. Millions of boys read these books, and this volume shows the machine working smoothly.
23014-a-soldier-of-the-empire:
Thomas Nelson Page guards a New Orleans quarter in A Soldier of the Empire. Neighbors came to treat the old Sergeant as the Quarter's true keeper of order. He preserved its quiet better than every gendarme ever posted inside its bounds. And thus the children all knew him.

An old soldier of Napoleon, settled in Louisiana, gives Page his figure of honor out of place and time. The empire fell, but its discipline keeps one neighborhood safe. Page tells the tale in his elegiac register, loyal to lost causes and the men who served them. Beneath the sentiment sits a shrewd portrait of authority earned by character. It is among his characteristic short works, compact and carefully warmed.
23044-the-merry-wives-of-windsor-the-wor:
Textual trouble heads The Merry Wives of Windsor in this Cambridge Shakespeare volume. The editors print the play's early text exactly as the 1602 quarto gives it, using Capell's preserved copy. They check that text against the second quarto of 1619 throughout.

That fuss exists because the Merry Wives survives in two very different early texts. The play inside is Shakespeare's sunniest piece of town comedy, Falstaff scheming after two merry wives who out-scheme him at every turn. Laundry baskets, jealous husbands, and a midnight fright at Herne's oak fill the plot. The edition lets readers enjoy the farce and inspect its foundations on the same page, a double pleasure this series made normal.
23141-the-island-treasure:
Captain Snaggs shouts orders in The Island Treasure. Captain Snaggs barks his orders in quick succession, hoarse words ringing fore and aft until the deck fittings seem to jingle. His drawl carries a strong nasal twang, as though half the speaking came through his nose.

A treasure island, a nasal captain, and a crew under full sail give this sea tale its classic furniture. George Manville Fenn, to whom the adventure is credited, stocked dozens of boys' books with just such gear. Storms, charts, and buried wealth turn the pages in order. The Snaggs portrait alone, all voice and authority, shows a practiced hand.
2415-the-mutiny-of-the-elsinore:
Jack London's Mutiny of the Elsinore strands a narrator aboard a ship where the crew, a collection of misfits and madmen, rises against its officers. The novel follows the voyage from Baltimore around Cape Horn, with London's sea knowledge giving every storm and mutiny real force. The narrator, a literary man, must learn to act or die.

The book's grim view of human nature and its vivid shipboard life divide readers, but its power is undeniable. London wrote it from his own sailing experience. Sea story fans will find a harsh, compelling voyage.
2424-black-bartlemy-s-treasure:
Jeffrey Farnol's Black Bartlemy's Treasure is a pirate romance in which a young man inherits a map, a mystery, and a dangerous enemy. The story follows the hero from an English village to the sea, through duels, storms, and a hunt for buried gold, with Farnol's lavish period prose dressing every scene. Black Bartlemy himself, the pirate of the title, haunts the plot.

Farnol was a master of the historical swashbuckler, and this novel shows his flair for action and atmosphere. Readers of pirate fiction will find a rousing, old-fashioned adventure. It pairs well with his other romances.
2460-the-madonna-of-the-future:
Henry James's tale The Madonna of the Future follows an American artist in Florence who has spent years preparing to paint his masterpiece, a modern Madonna, and never begins. The story watches the gap between ambition and achievement, with James's irony gentle and devastating by turns. The narrator, a fellow American, sees the dream curdle into self-deception.

The tale is a fable about art, procrastination, and the romance of Italy. Its ending is quietly devastating. James readers will find an early masterpiece of his short fiction. James wrote the tale in 1873, during his early years in Italy.
2463-the-prophet-of-berkeley-square:
Robert Hichens's Prophet of Berkeley Square is a comic fantasy. A society man, told by a prophet that he will commit a murder, tries to dodge fate and fails in the funniest ways. The novel mixes London high life with supernatural prediction, as the hero's attempts to avoid his destiny keep pushing him toward it. Hichens writes the farce with a light, knowing touch.

The story's pleasure lies in its paradoxes and its elegant setting. Readers who enjoy Edwardian comic fantasy will find a witty, unusual novel. It anticipates later comedies of fate and free will.
2548-the-poor-clare:
Elizabeth Gaskell opens this tale on December 12, 1747, with an old man looking back on a family history that began before he knew its people. At its center stands a great old hall in the Trough of Bowland, Lancashire, and a young woman named Lucy whose life is shadowed by an old wrong.

A curse laid in anger follows Lucy's line, and love, guilt, and faith collide as the past returns. Gaskell writes with gothic feeling but keeps her people human and tender. The story blends a ghostly mystery with a plea for mercy, and it ranks among her most haunting short works.
2566-how-to-fail-in-literature-a-lecture:
Andrew Lang gave this lecture at the South Kensington Museum to aid the College for Working Men and Women, and later rewrote it for print in 1890. Lang begins from a plain fact: most who try their fortunes in letters will fail, as the bookseller's yard can testify.

With wit and mock advice, he shows the traps of vanity, imitation, and chasing fashion, and the habits that doom a young writer. The lecture charms as a backhanded guide, teaching success by mapping failure. Aspiring authors will laugh, wince, and perhaps dodge a few of the pitfalls Lang names.
2687-the-snare:
Rafael Sabatini sets this romance of intrigue in motion with an affair at Tavora, an ultimatum, and Lady O'Moy. Count Samoval, a fugitive, Miss Armytage's pearls, and an ally follow, with an intelligence officer and a general order tightening the net.

A stifled quarrel leads to a challenge and a duel, then to a champion, a wallet, and bitter water, until fool's mate gives way to truth. Sabatini writes with his usual dash, and the snare of the title closes on more than one neck. The novel delights as a swift tale of honor, spies, and swordplay.
2763-the-world-s-desire:
H. Rider Haggard and Andrew Lang wrote this romance of Odysseus together, opening on a silent isle with a vision of the world's desire. The slaying of the Sidonians, a blood red sea, and Meriamun the queen follow, with the queen's vision and the lore of ka, bai, and khou.

Odysseus, weary of wandering, seeks Helen and a final home, while Egyptian priests and prophets shape his fate. The collaboration blends Haggard's adventure with Lang's scholarship. The book offers a late classical romance, where myth, Egypt, and longing meet. Lang's hand shows in the Egyptian lore and quiet scholarship.
2861-the-sleuth-of-st-james-s-square:
Melville Davisson Post wrote The Sleuth of St. James's Square as a set of detective stories linked by a great investigator and his cases. The contents run from the thing on the hearth, marked by a woman's bare footprint, to the lost lady and the cambered foot. Later cases add the man in the green hat, American horses, spread rails, and a pumpkin coach. Each case turns on a small physical clue read with care.

Post's detective works by reason and by homely detail, as when a father tests a quill pen and writes a dozen formal words about contests in court. The stories favor quiet deduction over chase and violence. The collection appeals to readers who enjoy classic puzzle mysteries in an Edwardian London setting.
2870-washington-square:
Henry James published Washington Square in 1881, setting it in the New York of the first half of the nineteenth century. Dr. Sloper, a respected physician, guards his plain and wealthy daughter Catherine against Morris Townsend, a handsome suitor the doctor believes is after her fortune. Morris swears his affection is pure and disinterested, and the doctor takes note while refusing to believe him.

The novel turns on Catherine's slow growth from obedience to judgment, as her father's cold certainty meets her steady love. James keeps the action within drawing rooms and family talks, letting small speeches carry large stakes. It stands as one of his most accessible novels, sharp about money, pride, and a father's power.
3015-the-man-made-world-or-our-androcent:
Charlotte Perkins Gilman wrote Our Androcentric Culture, or The Man-Made World, as a feminist analysis of a society shaped by men. Chapters take up humanness, the man-made family, health and beauty, and men and art. Masculine literature, games, ethics, education, fashion, law, crime, politics, industry, and a human world beyond follow. Gilman begins, inoffensively, with sheep.

The sheep, familiar from religious imagery and painters' stock, introduces her argument that male dominance distorts even familiar things. A later chapter notes that games remain vital to human life, yet in a two-sex society where one sex dictates terms, play is divided with great inequality. The book remains a foundational feminist text, clear, systematic, and still provocative.
3109-fashions-in-literature:
This posthumous set gathers Warner's essays on reading and writing. An introduction recalls that readers had known him for thirty years and more. Since My Summer in a Garden, it says, his name alone had been introduction enough. His fame had mellowed into memory by the time these pieces were collected.

Clarity of mind and lucidity of style marked his work, joined to sincerity and urbanity. The essays weigh literary fashion: what lasts, what merely passes, and how taste forms around new books. They give a working critic's view of American letters at the turn of the century, in prose free of the jargon it gently mocks.
3269-the-autobiography-of-mark-rutherfor:
Mark Rutherford's autobiography arrives edited by his friend Reuben Shapcott, at least in the book's own frame. The 1913 Hodder and Stoughton edition gives the chapters in order: childhood, preparation, and Water Lane, then Edward Gibbon Mardon, Miss Arbour, and Ellen and Mary. Emancipation closes the arc the contents reveal.

Rutherford's story is one of religious doubt and slow liberation. A dissenting upbringing, a ministry tried and left, and friendships that widen the mind carry the narrative. Doubt and slow liberation carry the narrative to its emancipation, without a sermon in sight.
3290-valerius-terminus-of-the-interpreta:
Francis Bacon's Valerius Terminus survives only in fragments, and this volume gathers them. A preface by Robert Leslie Ellis explains the state of the text. The pieces first appeared in Stephens's Letters and Remains in 1734. They hold detached passages and an epitome of twelve chapters of the first book of Bacon's proposed work on the interpretation of nature.

The detached passages give the first, sixth, and eighth chapters whole, with parts of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and ninth. Readers meet Bacon planning his great instauration: a new method for reading nature, against scholastic habit. The fragments suit students of science's history, showing a system still forming, in notes rather than in finished argument.
377-kansas-women-in-literature:
Nettie Garmer Barker profiles Kansas women writers in this early survey, opening with a verse praising the state and its daughters. Each short sketch gives a life, a list of works, and a taste of the writer's voice. Teachers, poets, novelists, and lecturers appear side by side, many born in Kansas and some adopted by it.

Barker stresses work done in schools, papers, and homes, not only in books. Her sketches show how Kansas women wrote through farm life, town life, and public service. The volume now serves as a first map of a state literary scene that later histories often passed over.
3778-the-interdependence-of-literature:
Georgina Pell Curtis sketches a subject no schoolman had treated alone, the way the literatures of all ages and peoples borrow from one another. She opens with De Quincey's split between the literature of knowledge, which teaches like a rudder, and the literature of power, which moves like an oar or a sail. Chapters then range from Babylonian and early Hebrew writing through Sanskrit, Persian, Egyptian, Greek, and Roman letters to heroic poetry, Scandinavian, Slavonic, and Gothic tales.

Later sections follow chivalry, romance, drama, and the Arabian, Spanish, Portuguese, and French traditions, with German mysteries giving way to opera and then to Goethe. Curtis writes in narrative style rather than as a textbook. Students of comparative letters will find a lively outline, meant to wake interest for a larger history still to come.
4211-the-treasure:
A novel called The Treasure follows Owen Sargent, Sandy Salisbury, and Mrs. Salisbury in the town of River Falls. Owen's constant visits would have filled Mrs. Salisbury's heart with wild maternal hope, had Owen and Sandy been a few years older.

As it is, with Sandy barely nineteen and Owen not quite twenty-two, their friendship gives her more tantalizing discomfort than satisfaction. Owen is a dear boy, queer but fine, and Sandy the prettiest girl in town. Readers who enjoy gentle domestic fiction will find a quiet story of youth and watching mothers.
4256-stammering-its-cause-and-cure:
Benjamin Nathaniel Bogue wrote this book from experience. He had been a chronic stammerer for almost twenty years. He then devised the Bogue Unit Method and founded the Bogue Institute for Stammerers. The first part tells his own life as a stammerer.

It covers early attempts at a cure and the hunt for work. It covers failures that taught him what helped. Later parts define stuttering and stammering and discuss their causes. They discuss effects on mind and body, and set out his method for setting the tongue free. The book speaks directly to sufferers and their families, mixing memoir with practical instruction.
4515-the-golden-snare:
James Oliver Curwood sets this northern tale among the forests and rivers far north of the settled lands, where trappers, traders, and wild animals live close together. Bram Johnson, a huge man raised in that hard country, stands at the centre of the story. The book traces his family back three generations, showing how the north shaped his temper, his strength, and his way of dealing with other people.

When a young woman and a rival enter Bram's lonely world, pity and menace mix in everything he does. Curwood follows hunts, traps, flights, and confrontations through snow and timber country. Readers get a fast-moving adventure about a man who is both pitiable and dangerous, and about the claims of love and loyalty in a place with little law.
4612-the-altar-fire:
Arthur Christopher Benson published The Altar Fire in 1907, with a Latin epigraph on fire falling from the Lord and devouring the burnt offering. His preface warns that the book may truly be felt as morbid, since it deliberately pictures a diseased spirit. Yet a pathological treatise on cancer or paralysis, he argues, is not necessarily morbid, and bodily ailments are now rightly seen as natural phenomena, not hidden away in attics and bedrooms.

Benson extends that plea to the heart and soul: suffering there is still treated as unreal, imaginary, or hypochondriacal, and thought curable by a little resolution and cheerful society. By foolish, secretive reticence, he says, much is lost. Readers get a serious Edwardian study of a troubled mind and spirit, written with candour about faith, illness, and inner life, and best read slowly, without expecting a light tale.
4746-kennedy-square:
F. Hopkinson Smith opens Kennedy Square with an author's preface on the place in the late fifties. Rough stone seats stood among birds, trees, and blossom, while vine-heavy bowers drooped over earth tracks edged with boxwood. Tall magnolias scented the enclosure, and roses clambering over a decaying fence vanished and reappeared between its bars.

Youngsters laughed on shaded paths, playing with hoops and balls while old Black mammies in pale aprons and bright headscarves watched. Quiet nooks sheltered lovers talking together, weary travellers taking rest, and elderly men absorbed in books for long stretches. Beyond the turf edge and a shaky wooden barrier, a bumpy walkway lay dappled with shade and flecked with green mould. In summer a melon seller halted his cart beside it, and in winter Moses stopped his own cart there. Readers get a nostalgic Baltimore novel of an old square and its people.
4934-the-natural-history-of-wiltshire:
John Aubrey's natural history of Wiltshire gathers antiquarian notes, wonders, and weather from an English county and beyond. The sample chapter ranges past Wiltshire itself to hurricanes and hailstorms across England and Italy, including the great tempest linked in legend to Oliver Cromwell's death.

Aubrey, writing in the seventeenth century, records what he heard and saw with a collector's appetite for the remarkable. The volume mixes county lore with natural marvels, storms, and local custom. Readers get a cabinet of curiosities from an early naturalist, valuable as much for its period voice as for its facts.
4994-five-thousand-miles-underground-or-:
Professor Amos Henderson calls for Washington across a big shed full of machinery, and this underground adventure answers with a joke. Washington hides beneath iron, steel, and aluminum. He replies in grand speech that he will attend to the professor's orders at the appointed time. Henderson wishes he had started when he began talking.

The professor's subterranean vessel carries the party five thousand miles underground toward the mystery of the earth's center. No byline appears in the catalog record. Readers get a boys' scientific romance of drills, caverns, and wonders below, in the tradition of voyages to places no one had ever seen.
5161-the-treasure:
Selma Lagerlof's short novel, The Treasure, opens at Solberga parsonage in the days of King Frederik the Second of Denmark. Its ten chapters move from the quays and the town cellars to moonlight, haunting, unrest, and Sir Archie's flight over the ice, as a buried treasure draws thieves and lovers toward ruin.

Lagerlof tells a dark tale of greed and guilt in a coastal town, with the sea's roar closing the story. The book shows her gift for legend-like narrative, where landscape and conscience press together, and it offers a compact, haunting read for lovers of Scandinavian fiction.
5168-the-land-of-heart-s-desire:
W. B. Yeats's one-act play, first performed in 1894, is set in a cottage in County Sligo, where the Bruin family gathers around the hearth. A faery child enters their home and tempts the young bride, Mary Bruin, away from marriage, work, and mortal sorrow toward the land of heart's desire, where beauty never fades.

Yeats wrote the play from Irish folklore, and its short scenes carry his early themes: the pull of the otherworld against ordinary life, and the price of longing. The play is brief, lyrical, and strange, and it offers a fine first taste of Yeats as a dramatist before his later Abbey Theatre work.
5169-hardscrabble-or-the-fall-of-chicago:
John Richardson's Hardscrabble tells of the fall of Chicago in 1812. It opens on an April day in a farmhouse beside the Chicago River's southern branch, four miles from the fort. Four people rise from a midday meal by a blazing fire, unaware that war with the surrounding tribes is about to destroy their settlement.

Richardson, who knew the frontier wars first hand, writes a tale of Indian warfare, siege, and flight, grounded in the history of Fort Dearborn. The novel offers readers a dramatic, if dated, account of a famous frontier disaster, told from the settler side of a conflict that ended in massacre and captivity.
518-the-enchanted-island-of-yew-whereon-:
L. Frank Baum tells of Prince Marvel on the Enchanted Island of Yew in this fairy tale. A fairy gives Marvel a year in mortal form, and he roams with Nerle, meeting a king of thieves, gray men, a royal dragon, and the twin rulers of Twi. A tyrant, a magic book, and enchanted mirrors test his knightly heart.

Baum writes with gentle humor and bright invention, in the vein of his Oz books. Marvel wins fights by courtesy as much as sword. The book charms young readers as a quest where kindness, not force, proves the truest magic, and where a year of wonders ends in a hundred years of peace.
5202-the-golden-lion-of-granpere:
Anthony Trollope's novel is set in Granpere, a village among the Vosges mountains of Lorraine, near the baths of Plombieres. Its inn, the Golden Lion, is the centre of village life. The story follows its keeper's family, their hopes for marriage, and the arrival of outsiders who disturb a close community.

Trollope, writing of French provincial life, mixes romance with his usual close observation of money, pride, and family feeling. The novel is quieter than his English Barsetshire books, and it gives readers a charming picture of a mountain village where an inn's fortunes and a family's honour rise and fall together.
5418-the-home-acre:
E. P. Roe wrote The Home Acre as a practical guide for people who dream of a country home. He opens with tree-planting, arguing that land hunger is a natural craving, and that city breadwinners often dream of a rural house as the crown of their working lives. The book then works through the whole smallholding in order.

Chapters cover fruit trees and grass, the garden, the vineyard and orchard, raspberries, currants, strawberries, and the kitchen garden. Roe writes plainly, for beginners who want food and beauty from their own acres. Readers get a friendly nineteenth-century handbook, useful as history and still clear about the work involved.
5429-preface-to-shakespeare:
Samuel Johnson wrote this preface for his annotated edition of Shakespeare's plays, published in 1765. He opens by complaining that praise is lavished on the dead and honors paid to mere antiquity, by critics who hope to seem clever through paradox. Johnson then turns to Shakespeare himself, judging the plays on their merits rather than their age.

The preface defends Shakespeare's mixture of comedy and tragedy, his characters, and his language, while admitting faults where Johnson finds them. Selected notes on plays such as Hamlet, King Lear, and Othello follow. Readers get a landmark of literary criticism, still readable as an argument about why Shakespeare endures.
545-at-the-earth-s-core:
Edgar Rice Burroughs sends two men into a hollow Earth in this adventure, told by a narrator who met the survivor in the Sahara. A drilling machine meant for coal bores past the crust into Pellucidar, a world lit by a central sun, ruled by winged Mahars, and full of ape men and dinosaurs. Dian the Beautiful, a captive, stirs love and revolt.

Burroughs writes at a gallop, with escapes, temples, and pursuits. His hero must learn Pellucidar's ways or die in them. The book charms as pure lost-world fun, where science serves as a door to a stranger, older Earth within our own.
5672-the-voice-on-the-wire:
Eustace Hale Ball wrote The Voice on the Wire as a mystery opening in a club grill-room. A large man awkwardly follows a servant downstairs, feeling every man at the Flemish tables must ask what he is doing there. He wishes Monty Shirley would meet him in the back room of a ginmill, where he would feel comfortable, rather than this classy joint, but that is Shirley's game to play.

Reaching Shirley, he exclaims eagerly that he is glad to find him, fearing he might arrive too late. Chapters titled When Three Is a Mystery and The Fleeting Prompter follow. Readers get a brisk early mystery of telephones, clubs, and tangled lives.
573-tales-from-shakespeare:
Charles and Mary Lamb retell Shakespeare's plays as short stories for young readers in this classic primer. The Tempest, A Midsummer Night's Dream, King Lear, Macbeth, Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet, and Othello lead the set, with comedies such as Twelfth Night and The Taming of the Shrew. The Lambs keep Shakespeare's words where they fit the tale.

A preface explains their method: tragedy lends itself to retelling, comedy less so, since dialogue resists turning into narrative. The tales aim only as a first taste, not a substitute for the plays. Generations of children have met Shakespeare here first, and then gone on to the plays themselves.
581-ginx-s-baby-his-birth-and-other-misf:
Edward Jenkins follows a foundling through Victorian charity, church, parish, and politics in this satire. Ginx's baby, born to a poor father named Ginx, is passed from hand to hand: first his father, then charities and churches, then parish guardians, then clubs and politicians. Each part asks what its keepers did with him.

Jenkins writes with sharp, comic anger, mocking laws, sects, and reformers who debate while a child waits. A preface stages a critic who calls the tale improbable, answered by an author who insists it may be true. The book endures as a witty indictment of how societies fail their poorest children.
606-indian-why-stories-sparks-from-war-e:
Frank Linderman retells Blackfeet why stories from War Eagle's lodge fire in this volume, dedicated to Charles Russell and George Bird Grinnell. Tales tell why the chipmunk's back is striped, why the curlew's bill is crooked, why the deer has no gall, and how Old-Man stole the sun's leggings. A preface praises Indian lore's closeness to nature.

Linderman writes in plain, warm prose, keeping the tales' childlike simplicity. Birds, beasts, winds, and moonlight explain the world in fanciful reasons. The book serves as a treasury of Montana Indian folk tales, saved before the blanket Indian and the buffalo vanished from the plains.
6066-king-of-the-khyber-rifles-a-romance:
Talbot Mundy opens with the song of the Indian Secret Service. Its men are eyes of empire, skinned and puckered and quick to see. They shun display, yet stay hot on the trail of ties and pullers of roots of ruction. The men who govern India are few, while those who stand in their way with floods of words are a host.

Athelstan King might claim to know a little. Mundy answers cries that India is a home of thugs and hungry millions. He claims instead that she is the original home of chivalry. The romance follows King on the frontier, where loyalty, daring, and secret work decide the fate of border tribes and empire.
6074-lady-clare:
Alfred Tennyson's Lady Clare comes illustrated by Alfred Fredericks, Granville Perkins, Frederic Schell, Edmund Garrett, F. S. Church, and Harry Fenn. The plates mark the poem's turning points: lilies blowing, a lily-white doe, old Alice the nurse entering, and a cry of falsely, falsely have ye done.

Lady Clare speaks of birth and love, asking whether she is loved for herself and declaring, if I'm a beggar born, she will face it plainly. She clothes herself in a russet gown, while Lord Ronald steps down from his tower. Tennyson's ballad turns on rank, truth, and a nurse's secret, told in swift, musical verse.
6112-nature-and-human-nature:
Thomas Chandler Haliburton's Nature and Human Nature dates from 1855. It promises surprises, clippers and steamers, and a woman's heart. A critter with a thousand virtues and but one vice appears, with a new way to learn Gaelic. Wounds of the heart, fiddling and dancing, stitching a button-hole, and the plural of moose follow.

Later chapters give a day on the lake, a betrothal, and a foggy night. Female colleges, gipsying, the world before the flood, lost at sea, and holding up the mirror follow. Town and country, honeymoon, clams, the devil's hole, and cucumber lake close the miscellany. Haliburton catches manners living as they rise, with humor.
6143-essays-on-work-and-culture:
Hamilton Wright Mabie dedicates Essays on Work and Culture to Henry Van Dyke. It opens with the line that along slender wires of speech some message from the heart is sent, though none can tell the whole that's meant. His contents ask tool or man, the man in the work, and work as self-expression.

Pain of youth, a year of wandering, the ultimate test, liberation, larger education, fellowship, and work and pessimism follow. Later essays treat training, concentration, relaxation, recreation, imagination in work, character, and freedom from self-consciousness. Mabie treats work as a path to culture and character.
6368-here-there-and-everywhere:
Lord Frederic Hamilton, encouraged by the kind reception of The Days Before Yesterday, ventures into print again with personal experiences in many lands, seen from unaccustomed angles. This is less a book of reminiscences than a recapitulation, he says, and its chapters range from big game shooting at Cooch Behar to Himalayan sunrises. A confidential elephant named Chota Begum, a first tiger, a leopard and an orchestra, and a charging rhinoceros fill the Indian chapters.

Jamaica and Barbados planters, East India soldiers and civil servants shaking the pagoda tree, and merchants retiring to England with yellow faces and torpid livers give the book its wider sweep. Hamilton writes as a traveller who has lived in the places he describes, with humour and a sharp eye for ceremony, sport, and empire's odd corners. The volume is anecdote as history, told by a man who was there.
6423-history-of-american-literature:
Reuben Post Halleck, author of a History of English Literature, writes its American companion after earnest requests from readers across the United States. He followed his rule of careful first hand study, which delayed the book, and plans it on the same model. Colonial literature opens the story, for American letters did not begin independent: colonists brought English language, books, and modes of thought.

Shakespeare had died four years before Pilgrims landed at Plymouth, Halleck notes, and an American in Paris without French can neither read books nor talk with citizens. Later chapters cover New York and New England groups, southern and western literature, and eastern realists, with Cooper's Leatherstocking Tales as a peak. Leatherstocking, Hawkeye, Natty Bumppo, embodies pioneer fearlessness and rugged honesty. Halleck writes a school history, clear and patriotic.
6436-castle-nowhere:
Constance Fenimore Woolson sets Castle Nowhere on the northern curve of Lake Michigan, a shore that was wilderness not many years ago and still shows on school maps as empty waste. Pale, cold yellow paper runs from Point St. Ignace to the iron ports on Little Bay de Noquet, a hundred miles of nothing, according to map makers who know nothing of the region. Long legged tribal names stretch across townless territory farther west, but not here.

This northern curve is and always has been a place apart, the book's opening insists, withholding even the names other regions get. A mid scene finds Waring holding a girl wrapped in furs, while an old man chafes her icy hands and feet. He cries that if she but comes back to life he will say not one word more. Woolson writes lake country romance with wilderness, rescue, and a father's remorse.
6439-nan-sherwood-at-rose-ranch-or-the-o:
Annie Roe Carr sends Nan Sherwood to Rose Ranch for an old Mexican's treasure, after school reopens and introductions at Lakeview Hall. Laura Polk, of irrepressible spirits and flamboyant hair, drawls that a Rhoda from the rolling prairie will ride up on a pinto pony, gun at belt and lariat swinging, to rope Dr. Beulah and bear her captive to a lair. Amelia Boggs corrects her metaphors: only four legged beasts bear victims to lairs.

Rhoda, red haired, answers that movies show more wonders in the wild west than philosophy dreams. Later, a tennis ball from a court whizzes over the back stop and bangs a grey pony on the nose. The beast leaps all four feet in air at once, crazy in an instant. Carr writes a girls' school and ranch tale, where jokes, ponies, and a Mexican girl's treasure braid into a summer's adventure.
6440-elsie-dinsmore:
Martha Finley opens Elsie Dinsmore with Mrs. Welby's verse on an eye bright and soft, swimming in liquid light and tears. The school room at Roselands is pleasant, though its ceiling runs lower than the modern portion, since its wing dates before the Revolution. Windows reach floor to ceiling and open on a veranda over a flower garden, with fields, woods, and hills beyond, and rosewood desks inside.

Within this pleasant apartment the story's young heroine takes shape, a girl of feeling and conscience in a grand southern house. A mid scene shows Adelaide urging Elsie to hurry for a party, sure her papa never said she should not go, until Mr. Dinsmore steps from the library and answers dryly that Elsie is not to go. Finley writes a girls' story of duty, family rule, and a child's tender heart.
6614-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-v:
Captain Kidd leads the ninth volume, which asks where buried treasure might lie between Key West and Halifax. Skinner notes that if Kidd saved his pirate gains with care, pots of gold could hide at Gardiner's Island, Dunderberg, Coney Island, Cape Cod, and a dozen more spots. Hope of such finds has cost real wealth in the search.

Storied waters, cliffs, and mountains follow, with sea serpents, stone-throwing devils, lovers' leaps, and gods on high peaks. The volume mixes greed, wonder, and caution in equal parts. As to Buried Treasure is a fun, skeptical tour of America's gold fever and its watery myths.
6700-sidonia-the-sorceress-the-supposed-:
Volume one of William Meinhold's Sidonia the Sorceress opens with a portrait of Sidonia von Bork in her prime. Golden hair lies under a gold net. Jewels cover her neck and arms, and she wears a purple bodice with an azure velvet robe. Behind her beauty, the painter adds a second, spectral Sidonia in death garments, a sorceress in white with black stripes. The contrast sets the tale.

Young Sidonia, richest and fairest maid of Pomerania, loves a duke who leaves her for a princess, then hides in a convent and turns to magic for revenge. Meinhold, in Lady Wilde's translation, leaves it open whether this is history or fancy. Volume one is a dark, romantic tale of pride, love, and witchcraft.
6701-sidonia-the-sorceress-the-supposed-:
Volume two of Meinhold's Sidonia carries book three from her reception into the convent at Marienfliess to her execution on August 19, 1620. Chapters tell how Sidonia talks Dorothea Stettin out of office, wounds a rival with an axe, and prays a porter to death, until the chaplain refuses her shriving. Witch burnings, a sun-angel, and a burning at her window follow.

Diliana Bork and George Putkammer at last marry, while Sidonia, stripped of rank, is chained to the witches' tower at Saatzig. The volume closes with the sad fate of Pomerania's last princes. Volume two is the grim, gripping end of Sidonia's dark tale.
6766-the-press-gang-afloat-and-ashore:
J. R. Hutchinson tells how the press-gang came in, why it was deemed needful, what it was, and whom it might take. Chapters follow the gang afloat and ashore, at grips with victims, at play, and in its dealings with women, ending with how the gang went out. Pictures show an unwelcome visit, a seizing on Tower Hill on a wedding morning, and Jack in the bilboes.

The press-gang, which seized men for the navy, was feared and hated across Britain. Hutchinson writes with a historian's care and a storyteller's pace. The Press-Gang Afloat and Ashore is a vivid, grim account of a harsh old naval custom.
6908-the-air-ship-boys-or-the-quest-of-t:
Ned and his friends build an air ship and fly south in search of Aztec treasure, in a tale by H L Sayler. The early chapters set the scheme in motion, with Major Baldwin Honeywell, Miguel Vasquez, a contract, and liquid hydrogen for lift. A dinner party on the Placida and a newspaper man from the Kansas City Comet add color before the ship takes shape in New Mexico.

Once afloat, the boys fight Indians with a searchlight, drop a cordite bomb, and make a thrilling rescue in mid air. Camp Eagle in the mountains leads to a secret tunnel in the mesa, a turquoise temple, and the golden eagle of the Aztecs. The quest ends with a quarter of a ton of treasure, won by nerve and by flight.
695-glaucus-or-the-wonders-of-the-shore:
Charles Kingsley wrote this guide to the seashore for readers who walk the rocks at low tide and wonder what they see. First issued in 1855, it leads the reader from pool to pool, naming sea anemones, crabs, shells, and weeds, and noting how each lives, feeds, and breeds. Colour plates in later printings help the eye match the page to the shore.

Kingsley urges the reader to keep live specimens, watch them at home, and learn by close looking rather than by books alone. His tone is warm and eager, full of praise for small wonders most walkers pass by. The book helped make seaside natural history a popular pastime, and it still serves as a friendly first guide to tide-pool life.
6950-the-bobbsey-twins-at-the-seashore:
Laura Lee Hope sends the Bobbsey twins to the seashore, opening with a busy departure and a chase after a duck. Dinah climbs into the big depot wagon, Freddie brings his pet cat Snoop in a box, and Flossie guards ferns wrapped in wet paper from the sun. Mrs Bobbsey trusts Bert with a satchel holding glasses of jelly, while Nan fears someone will sit on her hat box.

Uncle Daniel readies old Bill the horse, Aunt Sarah counts boxes, and Freddie's little duck Downy in a blue shoe box nearly gets left behind. The chapter promises a holiday of small mishaps and family fun at the shore. The twins, their pets, and their elders set out in a bustle that young readers will know well.
6965-alice-sit-by-the-fire:
J M Barrie's play Alice Sit by the Fire opens with a wish to peep into Amy's diary, an octavo book with Amy in gold letters wandering across soft brown leather. The narrator notes that novels often invite readers to look over shoulders, while plays are more coquettish things. Yet the book is padlocked, though its hiding place in a lower drawer is known, and Amy's own feelings, not the author's, are the true subject.

The play that follows turns on Amy, her family, and the gap between what she thinks happened and what others think. Barrie writes with his usual blend of wit and tenderness, letting a girl's diary stand for a young mind finding its voice. The comedy grows from secrets kept, read, and half understood at home.
7008-the-city-of-fire:
Grace Livingston Hill sets The City of Fire in Sabbath Valley, a green jewel cupped in mountain hands under a serene morning sun. Clean smooth streets, white houses with green blinds, clear cut maples, a wide winged brick schoolhouse, a vine clad stone church, and a low roofed stone parsonage fill the opening view. The word manse had not yet reached the valley, and no affectations troubled its air.

Billy Gaston waits two miles away and a few degrees up the mountainside, on the little station platform at Pleasant View. A note on the text records chapters renumbered from chapter twenty four and the name Fenning changed to Fenner throughout. Hill's tale follows valley folk through fire, faith, and the testing of a quiet town.
7017-a-study-in-tinguian-folk-lore:
Fay Cooper Cole offers this study in Tinguian folk lore as a doctoral thesis for Columbia University, published in Chicago in 1915. It rests on a collection of Philippine folk tales from the Field Museum. It was gathered during sixteen months among the Tinguian, a powerful pagan tribe of the mountain districts of Abra, Ilocos Sur, and Norte in northern Luzon. In social order, government, house building, and material culture the tribe differs sharply from the neighboring Igorot.

Cole finds their religious order and ceremonies more highly developed than those of nearby tribes, a claim his tales and notes support. The study gives English readers direct access to a mountain people's stories, rites, and world view. It stands as early American field work in the Philippines, careful, plain, and rich in tale matter.
7056-along-the-shore:
Rose Hawthorne Lathrop sings along the shore in poems dedicated to G P L, opening with a verse on sky, spring wind, and souls tender as May tints. For such large ecstasies, she asks, what can we bring, save wild flowers of love laid on affection's altar to win unexcelled protection. The contents list Inlet and Shore, Impersonality, A Protean Glimpse, Power Against Power, and Life's Priestess.

Love Now, One and One, The Violin, Gertrude, and Unity in Space follow, with The Shell and the Word, The Clock Tower Bell, and Ours to Endure. Broken Waves, The Ghosts of Revellers, Life's Burying Ground, and Beyond Utterance lead to The Suicide, For Others, and Zest. Lathrop writes shore, sea, and spirit in brief, musical lyrics.
7148-lectures-on-dramatic-art-and-litera:
August Wilhelm Schlegel's lectures on dramatic art and literature open with a Herschel epigraph praising a taste for reading above all gifts. Give a man that taste and the means to gratify it, Herschel says, and he can hardly fail of happiness, unless handed a most perverse selection of books. Reading places him among the best society of every age, with the wisest, wittiest, tenderest, bravest, and purest characters who adorned humanity.

He becomes a denizen of all nations and a contemporary of all ages, with the world created for him. Schlegel's lectures, with a translator's preface and the author's own preface, then survey drama from ancients to moderns, in the romantic criticism that shaped a century. The volume remains a classic guide to the stage as literature.
7201-a-history-of-english-literature:
Robert Huntington Fletcher wrote this history as a general manual for college students and readers beyond high-school age. He aimed to outline the growth of English literature with due regard for national life. He also gave an appreciative reading of the most important authors, choosing a limited set rather than crowding the page with names.

Fletcher notes that he found no other book combining those two ends to his mind, so he wrote his own. The volume moves from early writing toward modern work, linking books to the times that made them. Its steady, classroom prose helps a student see both the line of development and the value of single writers along the way.
7397-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
Before the Curfew gathers Holmes's late poems, written when evening was coming on. At the Saturday Club recalls his circle of friends meeting by King's Chapel in Boston. Poems to Harriet Beecher Stowe on her seventieth birthday, to Lowell, and to Whittier on his eightieth, honor the writers of his generation one by one as they aged.

The volume also marks public milestones. There is a poem for Harvard's two hundred and fiftieth anniversary, a welcome to a scientist, and verses for a festival and for a volume printed in raised letters for the blind. The tone is warm and valedictory without self-pity. Holmes writes as a man still at his fireside, taking stock of friends, books, and a city he had sung for fifty years.
7479-dorothy-dainty-at-glenmore:
Amy Brooks wrote and illustrated the Dorothy Dainty books, and this volume, published in August 1917, takes Dorothy to Glenmore. A letter from Vera, answered by Dorothy on the third page, sets the story moving. The familiar pleasures of the series follow: friends, holidays, and small adventures told in a gentle, old-fashioned voice. The author's own illustrations picture the scenes.

Dorothy Dainty was a popular girls' heroine of the era, and Glenmore gives her a new setting for kindness, mischief, and growing up. Brooks writes for young readers without talking down to them, and the book's charm lies in its warmth. It belongs on the shelf with the other Dorothy Dainty volumes, a quiet story of a good girl's summer.
762-british-airships-past-present-and-fu:
George Whale, late Major in the Royal Air Force, wrote this history of British airships from their early days to the post-war years. Chapters trace private firms, army airships, and the naval airship section, from Parseval and Astra-Torres types to the non-rigids of coastal patrol and the great rigids, No. 1 and No. 9.

Whale writes as an insider, with technical detail on design, lift, and service, but in prose a general reader can follow. He covers triumphs and wrecks with equal candour. The book is a key source on the age when Britain bet on the airship, before the aeroplane won the skies, and it still serves historians of early flight.
7855-the-vision-of-desire:
Margaret Pedler's The Vision of Desire quotes the Rubaiyat on heaven as fulfilled desire and hell as a soul on fire. It follows Ann's legacy through the Brabazons of Lorne, a man with a scar, and a lady from the priory. Chapters promise rats in a trap, oldstone cottage, dream flowers, and a sprig of heliotrope.

Later headings run from an eternal triangle and a battle of wills through refusal, return, and wild oats. The teeth of the wolf, a patch of sunlight, and a vision fulfilled close the book. Through romance and mystery, Pedler asks whether desire, once seen plainly, can be kept or must be paid for.
823-the-life-of-st-declan-of-ardmore:
Rev. P. Power translated and introduced this life of St. Declan of Ardmore, edited from a manuscript in the Royal Library at Brussels. Declan, an early Irish saint, is praised in the Martyrology of Oengus as the head of a hundred thousand, a champion of battle for Erin. His life blends history with legend.

The tale follows Declan's birth, his mission, and his works in Munster, with miracles and journeys that mark the early Irish church. Power's introduction sets the text in its place and weighs its sources. The book serves readers of Irish saints' lives, and of the faith that shaped Ireland before the Normans came.
8323-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-23-eccl:
Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, and the book that follows tests every human project and finds it wind. Ecclesiastes, in Challoner's Douay-Rheims text, is the voice of an old king who tried wisdom, wealth, building, and pleasure, and watched each fade. Work, riches, and fame all end the same way, in death, and the writer says so with bleak honesty.
