Yet the book is not despair: it urges readers to eat, drink, and enjoy honest work as gifts, and closes by advising fear of God and keeping his commands. Its refrains, a time for every purpose and the wisdom of the quiet word, have passed into common speech. Ecclesiastes suits readers who want Scripture to argue with easy optimism.
8470-the-life-of-john-clare:
Frederick Martin wrote The Life of John Clare, the Northamptonshire peasant poet hailed as the English Burns. Martin's preface recalls how, some forty years before, the literary world rapturously hailed Clare's appearance. Rossini set his verses to music, and Madame Vestris recited them before crowded audiences, before neglect and madness closed his story.

Clare, a farm laborer who wrote of fields, birds, and village life, became a Romantic celebrity and then a patient in asylums. Martin's biography, an early life of the poet, tells that rise and fall with sympathy. Readers get the classic story of a working-class poet, loved, lionized, and left, in Victorian England.
8487-dame-care:
Hermann Sudermann's novel Dame Care, translated by Bertha Overbeck, opens at a hard time: just when Meyerhofer's estate is to be sold by auction, his third son Paul is born. Frau Elsbeth, haggard and melancholy, lies in her big four-post bed, the newborn's cradle near her, listening to events that will shape the family's fate.

Sudermann, a leading German dramatist and novelist, writes of care itself as a dame, a presence haunting a family through debt, birth, and loss. Readers get a naturalist novel of rural Germany, where money troubles and human feeling intertwine. The book's opening, a birth beside a ruin, sets its tone: life beginning as fortune ends.
8555-initiation-into-literature:
Émile Faguet wrote Initiation into Literature as a guide to the world's literatures, translated from French by Sir Home Gordon, with additions the author made specially for the English version. Contents open with ancient India, the Vedas and Buddhist literature, and move through the great literatures in order, giving beginners a map of what to read and why.

Faguet, a leading French critic, writes for readers who want to enter literature without a university course. The translator acknowledges Faguet's courtesy in adding material for English readers. The book suits students and self-taught readers, as a companion to a lifetime of reading, clear, opinionated, and wide-ranging.
8737-robert-elsmere:
Mrs Humphrey Ward's Robert Elsmere, published in Boston by DeWolfe, Fiske and Company. Follows a young clergyman whose faith is shaken by historical criticism and by the suffering he sees. Dedicated to two friends separated by diversity of circumstance and opinion, Thomas Hill Green, Oxford moral philosopher. Laura Octavia Mary Lyttelton, the novel links them by the love of God and the service of man. That dedication states the book's theme.

Elsmere leaves orthodox belief but not religious duty, founding a new brotherhood of service among London's poor. Ward's long, earnest novel became a sensation, debated in pulpits and drawing rooms on both sides of the Atlantic. It remains the classic Victorian novel of doubt, valuable for its portrait of a mind moving from creed to conscience. For its picture of late Victorian religion in crisis.
8894-latin-literature:
J. W. Mackail, sometime fellow of Balliol College, Oxford, writes this history of Latin literature as a tribute to his friend and master, Professor William Sellar. Sellar was to have written the volume for a series of manuals. After his death Mackail, one of his old pupils, was asked to carry out the work Sellar had undertaken. The book is offered as a last tribute to Sellar's memory, and its preface states that debt plainly.

Contents move from the republic's origins, early epic and tragedy with Andronicus, Naevius, Ennius, Pacuvius. Accius, through comedy with Plautus and Terence, to early prose, the satura, jurists, annalists, and orators, with Cato, the Scipionic circle, and Lucilius. Lucretius, Catullus and lyric poetry, and Cicero follow. Mackail's compact survey remains a clear guide for students, and a readable introduction for anyone wanting the shape of Latin letters whole.
9073-the-roof-of-france-or-the-causses-o:
Matilda Betham-Edwards wrote this travel book, the third of her published travels in France, and dedicated it to President Sadi Carnot. Its subject is the Causses of the Lozère, high limestone plateaus she calls the roof of France. She made two journeys in search of them, from Le Puy to Mende and onward.

Chapters cross the Morvan, the Rhône valley, and the Tarn canyon, with rapids shot and strange rock towns viewed. Betham-Edwards writes with a keen eye for land and folk. The book still charms as a record of rural France before the age of cars.
9154-salted-with-fire:
George MacDonald wrote this Scots novel in broad Scots speech, opening with a shoemaker, or soutar, and his daughter Maggie. Maggie runs to Stanecross for chaff to fill her father's hungry bed, while the minister is due that morning. Father and daughter spar in dialect about the minister, a man Maggie cannot abide.

The title, salted with fire, points to trial that purifies. MacDonald's Scots folk argue faith, pride, and love in their own tongue. The novel gives readers a vivid taste of Scottish village life, its humor, its kirk, and its stubborn hearts.
9813-santo-domingo-a-country-with-a-futu:
Otto Schoenrich published this survey of Santo Domingo in 1918, when the Dominican Republic was little known to most American readers. He traces the island's past from Columbus's landing in 1492 through conquest, colony, revolution, and the American influence of his own day.

After the history, Schoenrich turns to the land itself: its coasts and climate, minerals, plants, people, faith, schools, and roads. The book argues that the country had room to grow, and it still serves as a clear, fact-packed portrait of the Dominican Republic at the start of the twentieth century.
9973-yorkshire:
Gordon Home both painted and described Yorkshire in this travel book, with illustrations of the county he loved. His chapters cross the moors from Pickering to Whitby, follow the Esk valley, and trace the coast from Whitby to Redcar and to Scarborough.

Home writes as a walking companion, noting villages, abbeys, cliffs, and the light on the moors. The book belongs to the painted travel books of its age, where pictures and prose share the work. Readers planning a visit, or dreaming of one, get Yorkshire town by town, valley by valley, at a walker's pace.
a-drama-on-the-seashore:
Honoré de Balzac places his short tale on the rocky coast of Brittany, in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's translation. The narrator, walking by the sea with a companion, falls into thought about youth and ambition. They meet a poor fisherman whose worn face and silence hide a dreadful story.

The fisherman's tale, told in brief, concerns a father, a son given to crime, and a punishment the father felt God required of him. The sea and the barren shore frame the confession, and the narrator leaves shaken. Balzac packs guilt, faith, and fate into a few pages, and the stark ending has kept the story in print.
a-girl-of-high-adventure:
A Girl of High Adventure is a 1914 girls' novel by L T Meade, one of the most prolific writers of fiction for young people in her day. Its heroine, Margot St Juste, lives under the care of her Uncle John and his wife. The opening pages show the aunt lecturing the girl on gratitude, warning her that without their kindness she would be a miserable little beggar.

Margot answers her uncle's kindness easily, but life in that strict household is harder than the lectures suggest. From this constrained start, Meade builds the adventure promised by the title, in her usual manner for girl readers of the period. The book preserves a lively example of Edwardian girls' fiction and its mix of duty, spirit, and escape.
a-history-of-english-literature:
Robert Huntington Fletcher wrote A History of English Literature as a college manual, and his preface is dated August 1916. He aimed to outline how the literature grew with the nation's life, judge the chief authors fairly, and still leave students time to read the works themselves rather than books about them.

The survey runs by periods, from the Britons and Anglo-Saxons through the Norman-French age and on toward the nineteenth century, which Fletcher treats at greatest length. Chapters mix biography, criticism, and lists of cheap editions a class could actually buy. Questions and assignments at the end turn the volume into a working textbook, not just a shelf reference.
a-journey-in-other-worlds-a-romance-of-t:
John Jacob Astor imagines a voyage to Jupiter and Saturn, in a romance whose contents include a historical sketch of the world in the year 2000, given by Professor Cortlandt. President Bearwarden speaks, plans are laid, and the ship Callisto is built. Book one handles the future earth before the travelers say goodbye.

Book two explores Jupiter: mastodons, strange hunters, a Jovian Niagara, and polar discoveries. Book three reaches Saturn, where the travelers meet spirits and hear sermons on the soul's fate. Astor, one of America's richest men, mixes science guesses, hunting scenes, and theology. The novel is a curious window into what the future looked like from his decade.
a-study-in-tinguian-folk-lore:
Fay-Cooper Cole submitted this study for his doctorate at Columbia University, publishing it at Chicago in 1915, as the title page states. It rests on a collection of Philippine folk tales he gathered during sixteen months with the Tinguian, a pagan people of the mountain districts of Abra and northern Luzon. He notes their social organization and ceremonies differ sharply from the neighboring Igorot.

Cole analyzes the tales by motif and type, comparing Tinguian stories with those of other peoples to trace how folklore travels and changes. The study is technical, written for fellow anthropologists, but its subject is living story: creation, spirits, and heroes. It stands as an early, serious piece of Philippine folklore scholarship.
adventure:
Jack London's novel was taken from the 1911 Thomas Nelson edition named on its opening page. It begins with a very sick white man carried on the back of a servant in the Solomon Islands. The sick man runs a plantation, and fever has nearly finished him. A ship's arrival brings Joan Lackland, a young woman who wants to become a planter herself.

Twenty-eight chapters follow storms, labour troubles, rival traders, and the hard bargain of island planting. Joan shoots, rides, and argues as an equal, and feeling grows between her and the recovering planter. London fills the tale with trade goods, copra, disease, and the rough rules of the South Seas.
alice-sit-by-the-fire:
J. M. Barrie begins, in his stage directions, by wishing he could peep into Amy's diary. It is octavo, with Amy in gold letters across its soft brown leather covers. It lies padlocked in the lower drawer of a hand-painted escritoire. Amy is sixteen, and today she is washing her hair. Her parents are coming home from India after years away, and she has built a romance around the mother she barely knows.

Alice, the mother, finds grown children who treat her as a stranger and a daughter bent on a tragic love affair copied from novels. Barrie turns the tangle with tenderness: scenes of misunderstanding mend into recognition. The play shows the Peter Pan author writing family feeling without magic, and finding it harder.
along-the-shore:
Rose Hawthorne Lathrop gathers her poems under a shore title, dedicating the volume to G. P. L. The contents open with Inlet and Shore and run through Impersonality, A Protean Glimpse, Life's Priestess, The Shell and the Word, The Clock-Tower Bell, Broken Waves, and The Ghosts of Revellers. Sea pieces stand beside studies of grief, faith, and endurance.

Later titles — The Suicide, For Others, A Song Before Grief, The Baby, Twenty Bold Mariners, In the Artillery, The Lost Battle — show the range from lyric to narrative. Lathrop, Nathaniel Hawthorne's daughter, wrote verse of real feeling before she gave her later life to nursing the poor with cancer. The poems keep her early, literary self in view.
at-aboukir-and-acre: At Aboukir and Acre, G, a, henty's napoleonic tale, the egyptian campaign. This book preserves that historical novel. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
at-the-earth-s-core:
Edgar Rice Burroughs opens At the Earth's Core with a narrator who warns that nobody will believe his story. He tells how David Innes and inventor Abner Perry bored into the earth in a great iron mole. They emerge in Pellucidar, a hollow world lit by a central sun, where time barely moves. Dinosaurs, beast-men, and the reptilian Mahars rule there.

Enslaved, Innes meets Dian the Beautiful, escapes, and fights the Mahars, who paralyze victims in their temple before eating them. The contents promise slavery, freedom, pursuit, and a return to earth. Published in 1914, the novel launched Burroughs's Pellucidar series and mixes lost-world adventure with his usual swift, cliff-hanging pace.
beautiful-stories-from-shakespeare:
E Nesbit retold twenty of Shakespeare's plays as Beautiful Stories from Shakespeare, opening with Dr Johnson's praise that Shakespeare alone gave his country more practical wisdom than all his successors. Her preface calls his works the richest and fairest uninspired genius ever penned, instruction delivered through delight. A brief life of Shakespeare precedes the tales.

A Midsummer Night's Dream, The Tempest, As You Like It, King Lear, and Romeo and Juliet lead the contents, each play compressed into clear prose for young readers. Macbeth demanding which of them has placed Banquo's ghost in his chair shows her fidelity to the drama. Nesbit's versions, like Lamb's Tales before them, started generations toward the plays themselves.
black-bartlemy-s-treasure: Black Bartlemy's Treasure, Jeffery Farnol's pirate adventure. The treasure hunt unfolds. This book preserves that tale. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
brandes-main-currents-in-19th-century-li:
Georg Brandes opens his landmark survey of European writing with The Emigrant Literature, here in English. Exiles driven out by revolt carried new ideas from land to land after the French Revolution. The Danish critic treats their books as sparks in a broad fire.

Brandes links life, politics, and art in one flowing account. He asks how writers in exile shaped the taste of a whole continent. Later volumes would take up France, Germany, and England in turn. This first book launched a six-volume work that changed how Europe read its own nineteenth century.
british-airships-past-present-and-future:
George Whale, a late major in the Royal Air Force, surveyed British Airships from the earliest experiments through the machines of the First World War. Chapters divide the subject among private builders, army airships, and the naval airship section. Named types include Parseval and Astra-Torres ships, the coastal and C Star classes, and the great rigids numbered 1, 9, 23, and 33.

Whale gives dimensions, lifting arrangements, and frank judgments, as when the North Sea airship suffers for its badly designed propelling machinery. Written just after the war, the book also looks forward to airships' commercial future. It preserves technical detail and service gossip that official reports left out.
castle-nowhere:
Castle Nowhere, by Constance Fenimore Woolson, opens on the empty northern curve of Lake Michigan. Woolson describes a shore the school maps leave blank. A hundred miles of shore west of Point St Ignace counts as nothing, by the map makers' account. Jesuit canoes and modern propellers alike cut across and leave it alone. The railroad of the future, she notes dryly, will make British America a garden of roses someday.

Woolson sets her stories in that bypassed wilderness. A castle nowhere is a dwelling built on no route to anywhere. Isolation is her subject and her method. The Great Lakes stories collected here grew from her years on Mackinac Island. She was James Fenimore Cooper's grandniece, and Henry James's friend and rival. Her north is colder than his Europe and as carefully observed. Readers who find the map blank, she promises, are exactly the readers she wants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acre:
Acre, called Saint-Jean-d'Acre, is a Syrian Mediterranean seaport, on a plain with Mount Carmel to the south and the mountains of Galilee to the east. Though choked with sand, it ranks among the best harbours on the Syrian coast. Chanaanite-built and given to Aser's tribe, it was never conquered by them. It passed through Assyrian, Tyrian, Seleucid, and Roman hands, and Claudius granted it municipal rights as Colonia Claudii Caesaris.

Its early Christian community hosted St. Paul. The city was taken by Moslems in 638, by Crusaders in 1104, by Moslems again in 1187, by Crusaders again in 1191, and finally by Moslems in 1291. Napoleon failed before it in 1799, Egypt's viceroy took it in 1832, and the sultan retook it in 1840. Until about 1400 it held a Latin bishop, and it now has a Melchite bishop under Antioch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-in-early:
Adam matters greatly to the Fathers and to apocryphal writers of the first five Christian centuries, as their frequent allusions show. Yet his place in the liturgy is far from prominent. The calendar and one Eastern church hymn carry his name, and he fares little better in the West. The sections referring to him are Holy Saturday's first prophecy and the Genesis readings at Septuagesima time.

In literature, by contrast, Adam is treated generously and becomes hero of several books. They include the Book of the Penance or Combat of Adam and the Struggle of Adam and Eve after the Garden. They also include the Codex Nazaraeus, the Testament of Adam, the Apocalypse of Adam, and the Book of the Daughters of Adam. The Testament survives in fragments of great interest, and the entry follows these works through liturgy and legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aedh-of-kilda:
Aedh of Kildare, Leinster's king and an Irish saint, is commemorated by Colgan under 4 January, though much obscurity attaches to his life and work. The Four Masters' Annals and Ulster's agree on this monarch, who gave up his crown and eventually became Kildare's bishop. Under Aidus, Aedh's latinized form, his name appears in several martyrologies.

Colgan says he resigned Leinster's throne in 591, really 592, entering Kildare's great monastery for forty-eight years' service to God, rising successively to abbot and bishop. His episcopate ran from about 630 to 639, and he died in 639 by the corrected Ulster chronology. He must not be confused with Aedh Finn, king of Ossory, called Aedh the cleric, a contemporary who also resigned a throne for a monastic cell. Aedh of Leinster was called Aedh Dubh for his dark features, while Ossory's Aedh was fair.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aire:
Aire, also Abram, covers the Landes department's territory. Auch's suffragan under the old regime, re-establishment waited until 1822, when it again became the re-established Auch archdiocese's suffragan. The former Dioceses of Aire and Acqs, or Dax, supplied its territory; history's first mentioned bishop, Marcellus, sat at the Council of Agde in 506.

Among its sixteenth-century bishops was Francois de Foix, Count of Candale, a mathematician who translated Euclid and founded a Bordeaux mathematics chair. Mas d'Aire's Gallo-Roman crypt holds a sarcophagus preserving St. Quitteria's body, martyred perhaps under Commodus for resolving to remain a virgin. Saint-Sever owes its origin to a tenth-century Benedictine abbey built by a Gascon duke in thanks for victory over the Northmen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexandre-guy:
Alexandre Guy Pingré was a French astronomer, born at Paris in September 1711 and dead in May 1796. Educated at Senlis by the Genovefan fathers, he joined their order at sixteen and became professor of theology there in 1735. About 1749 he took the astronomy chair at the new academy of Rouen. He was famous for catching a four-minute error in Lacaille's reckoning of the lunar eclipse of December 1749. In 1753 he observed the transit of Mercury.

Pingré built an observatory at the Abbey of Ste-Geneviève and worked there for forty years, compiling the nautical almanac for 1754. He joined an expedition to Rodriguez to watch the transit of Venus in June 1761, which failed, and saw the transit from Haiti in June 1769. His Cométographie of 1783 to 1784 sifted the history of comets from ancient annals and recent works. The entry defends him against the charge that Jansenist quarrels drove him into provincial posts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alpha-and-ome:
Alpha and Omega, the Greek alphabet's first and last letters, symbolize orthodox confidence in the scriptural proofs of Our Lord's divinity from the fourth century. The Apocalypse suggested the symbol: Christ shares with the Father the titles First and Last. He is the Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. Clement of Alexandria also calls the Word Alpha and Omega.

In early monuments the symbol was most used. The earliest dated occurrence, a Roman inscription of 295, has Omega taking precedence, both letters part of the inscription. Whether the symbol in regular form predates Nicaea in 325 is unsettled; if so, rare. A mid-fourth-century fresco in the Praetextatus catacomb joins Alpha and Omega to the monogrammatic cross. The oldest inscription in traditional form dates from 364. From then on the letters were a favourite orthodox symbol, disfavoured by Arians, found across early Christendom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altars-in-scr:
The English word altar, from alta ara, describes its purpose less well than Hebrew mizbeah, from zabhah, to sacrifice, and Greek thysiasterion, from thyo, to immolate. In the Old Testament the brazen altar stood in the Temple court east of the Temple proper. Twenty cubits long, twenty broad, and ten high, it was larger than the tabernacle altar it resembled. The altar of incense served offerings the entry treats apart, where modern critics diverge from the common opinion.

In the New Testament the word covers the altar of holocaust or of incense. St. Paul argues from the ministers' share in the sacrifice that Gospel ministers should live by the Gospel. Modern critics affirm several legitimate pre-Josian places of worship, a claim the entry notes but does not examine, since only altar regulations concern it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambroise-pare:
Ambroise Paré, French surgeon born at Bourg-Hersent near Laval in 1517, died 20 December 1590. Apprenticed to a barber young, he became barber-surgeon at Paris's Hôtel-Dieu and army surgeon under Francis I. From 1545 he studied anatomy under Sylvius, became surgeon to Henry II in 1552, and first surgeon and chamberlain to Charles IX in 1563. A lifelong Catholic, he was not the Huguenot spared at St. Bartholomew's by royal command, as legend claimed.

His motto read, I treated him, but God healed him. His pioneer military surgery reformed gunshot wound treatment and revived arterial ligation after amputation, against the cauterizing of supposedly poisoned wounds with hot iron or oil. His standing beside Vesalius in anatomy marks his place in modern surgery's rise, and soldiers held him in special regard for his humanity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ampere:
Andre-Marie Ampere, born at Lyons in 1775 and dead at Marseilles in 1836, stands among the founders of the science of electricity and magnetism. As a child he showed a prodigious gift for mathematics. He taught himself Latin to read Bernoulli and Euler, and he was shaken deeply when his father was executed at Lyons during the Revolution in 1793.

After Oersted showed that a current deflects a magnetic needle, Ampere showed within a week that parallel wires carrying currents attract or repel each other. That work laid the ground for electrodynamics, and he published his mathematical theory of the subject in 1830. He also proposed an electric telegraph in 1821. He taught and served as Inspector-General of the University, and he closed his life with a wide philosophical survey of human knowledge, published after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-lefeb:
Antoine Lefebvre, Sieur de la Barre, a French colonial governor born in Paris in 1622, served France in Guiana and Canada. A judge and intendant at home, he sailed in 1664 to settle Guiana, publishing an account of the colony on his return. He later commanded in the Antilles before becoming governor-general of Canada in 1682.

In Canada he followed royal orders to curb the Iroquois and protect French trade, but his expedition to Fort Frontenac failed. Louis the Fourteenth recalled him in 1685, and he later governed Cayenne again until his death in 1690. The entry follows an able administrator whose Canadian command ended in recall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arthur-moore:
Arthur Moore, count, was born at Liverpool in 1849 and died at Mooresfort, Tipperary, in 1904, son of Charles Moore, member of parliament for Tipperary. Educated at Ushaw, he travelled in Spain, and in 1874 won election as member for Clonmel borough. In parliament he followed Butt and strongly backed land reform, better treatment of workhouse children, university access for Irish Catholics, and Home Rule. He took special interest in Catholic chaplains for the fleet.

In 1877 he married a daughter of the English baronet Sir Charles Clifford and received the title of count from the pontiff. During Gladstone's parliament of 1880 to 1885 he usually sided with Parnell, favouring land purchase as the best solution of the Irish question. He urged cottages for Irish labourers and fairer treatment of Irish emigrants aboard ship. He steadily voted for Home Rule and fiercely denounced coercion, while rejecting violent agitation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aubrey-thomas:
Aubrey Thomas Hunt de Vere was an Irish poet, critic, and essayist. He was born at Curragh Chase in County Limerick in 1814 and died there in 1902. A friend of the astronomer William Rowan Hamilton, he came through him to revere Wordsworth and Coleridge. He studied metaphysics at Trinity College Dublin, and later fell under Newman's influence. Days spent under Wordsworth's roof stayed with him as the greatest honor of his life, and he made a pilgrimage to the poet's grave while age allowed.

Study of Coleridge first moved him toward Catholicism, and he was received into the Church at Avignon in 1857, without losing his many friends. He sat as Member of Parliament for Limerick from 1854 to 1859, and his later years at Curragh Chase produced translations from Horace. The entry also records the Gothic church he built there, his slight frame, and a life unmarried to the age of ninety.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baltimore:
Baltimore is the senior see of the United States, founded as a diocese in 1789 and raised to an archdiocese in 1808. It covers Maryland west of Chesapeake Bay plus the District of Columbia, 6,502 square miles in all. Of about 1,273,000 people there, 255,000 were Catholics, chiefly of English, Irish, and German descent. Polish, Lithuanian, Bohemian, and Italian congregations also flourished, with six churches for black Catholics.

Catholic Maryland was planned by George Calvert, founded by his son Cecilius, and named for Queen Henrietta Maria. Its assembly passed the famous religious toleration act in 1649, after Catholic rule since the 1634 landing. Puritans later seized the government and curbed Catholic worship, though liberty later returned. Growth came by natural increase, immigration, and conversion, aided by Cardinal Gibbons and his book The Faith of Our Fathers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-belluno-feltr:
Belluno-Feltre is a diocesan entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, covering two joined sees in Venetia, in northern Italy. Belluno sits on a hill between the Ardo torrent and the Piave river, and its bishops once held temporal rule as counts under an imperial grant of 959. Disputes over the town ran for centuries until its people accepted Venice in 1420.

Feltre shares the later story, and the entry lists bishops, churches, and religious houses across both towns. Statistics on parishes, clergy, and schools close the picture of a mountain diocese with deep medieval roots. The piece is a compact local history built around its bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-andre: Bernard André, an Augustinian friar from Toulouse, was poet laureate of England and chronicler of Henry VII, whose reign ran from 1485 to 1509. Tutor to Prince Arthur and probably to the young Henry VIII, and blind in later life, he wrote mostly in Latin under Renaissance influence. His history of Henry VII remains a rare contemporary source for the Cornish revolt of 1497.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethlehem-in-: Bethlehem, in architecture, is a term used in the Ethiopian Church for the oven or bakehouse where the Korban, or Eucharistic bread, is baked. Coptic churches usually include one as an attachment, generally set within the church enclosure. The entry illustrates it from the plan of Mari Mina and from the monastery of Dair Abu Makar, where the oven stands among monks' cells and domestic buildings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-bernardine:
Blessed Bernardine of Feltre, a Franciscan missionary, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Feltre in 1439, eldest of nine children of the noble Tomitano family, he died at Pavia in 1494. A Lenten course preached by St. James of the Marches at Padua in 1456 moved him to take the Franciscan habit that May.

Studies at Mantua and ordination in 1463 led to a long apostolate, after a miraculous cure of a speech impediment freed his tongue. Counted among the fifteenth century's great Franciscan missionaries, he preached across Italy and founded monti di pietà, pawnshops lending to the poor without usury. The entry presents a preacher and a friend of the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-humphrey-m:
Blessed Humphrey Middlemore, an English Carthusian martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Son of Thomas Middlemore of Edgbaston, an old Warwickshire family, he was professed at the London Charterhouse, ordained, and made procurator, or steward, of the house. Prior John Houghton prized his learning and piety.

Refusal of Henry VIII's oath of supremacy brought the Charterhouse fathers to Tyburn in 1535. Middlemore died there on 19 June, hanged, drawn, and quartered with his prior and a fellow monk. The entry presents a quiet steward among the first Carthusian martyrs of the English Reformation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-byzantine-arc:
Byzantine building blends Greek and Roman forms with Eastern ones, though early on the two strains cannot be cleanly split. The western church plan, a nave on columns with an atrium, appears in fifth-century examples at Byzantium and Rome. The sixth century carried such churches to Ravenna, Istria, and Africa. Vaulted basilicas arose in Asia Minor, Syria, Africa, and Constantinople. The domed style, with barrel-vaulted aisles and transepts, won favor in the East.

That domed type leads to plans built round a center: circular, octagonal, or cross-shaped. The East favored the shape, yet Italy knew it from the fourth and fifth centuries. The apse, the narrow narthex, the eastward facing, and the sharp-cut acanthus leaf cannot be pinned to the East alone. Ravenna's churches, Saint Apollinare and Saint Vitale among them, are too quickly labeled Byzantine. Like features appear in the West as well.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-byzantine-lit:
Byzantine literature voices the mind of the Greek people of the Eastern Roman Empire in the Christian Middle Ages. It blends Greek, Christian, Roman, and Eastern strains on a Roman political base. Greek culture centers not on Athens but on Alexandria, where learned scholarship and popular Jewish-Greek life stood side by side. That split runs through the whole literature, setting a scholarly, rational strain against a romantic, popular one.

The scholarly strain, backed by the Atticizing movement that looked back to classical Athens, held the upper hand until the fall of the empire. Historians and chroniclers, encyclopedists and essayists, secular verse, church and theological writing, and popular poetry all find their place in it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-camille-lefeb:
Camille Lefebvre, apostle of the Acadians, was born at Saint Philippe, Quebec, in 1831 and died at Saint Joseph, New Brunswick, in 1895. Son of sturdy French-Canadian farmers, he taught school, studied Latin, and entered the Congregation of Holy Cross in 1852, becoming a priest in 1855. His gifts as a preacher carried him through curacies, teaching, and missions until 1864, when he took charge of Memramcook and founded Saint Joseph's College.

Since the expulsion of 1755, Acadians in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island had lived without means of schooling or advancement. They were looked down on as hewers of wood and drawers of water. In three decades Lefebvre's college changed that. His students rose in business, the professions, the bar, the legislatures, the federal parliament, and the Supreme Court bench, turning servitude into equality and freedom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonesses-re:
The Canonesses Regular of the Holy Sepulchre trace their foundation only by tradition to Saint James the Apostle, with Saint Helena said to have taken the habit from Saint Macanus of Jerusalem. The first date on record is 1276, when the Saragossa convent was founded. A house at Charleville in 1622, founded by Claudia Mouy, the Marquis de Chaligny's widow, opened a great revival in the West.

A Jesuit Father drew up constitutions, approved by Urban VIII in 1631, binding the canonesses to the Divine Office, strict fasts, the discipline, and a strict reading of poverty. Twelve professed religious were needed to elect a prioress. Susan Hawley founded the English canonesses, leading a community at Liège from 1652. After the Revolution the sisters reached England in 1794, settling at New Hall near Chelmsford, where they still run a boarding school for young ladies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-inv:
Canonical investiture names the act and the rites by which a lord once granted a fief to a vassal. From the middle of the eleventh century the word also covered the way princes gave bishops and abbots their titles. With the titles came the lands and public rights tied to their offices. The entry traces how that usage grew out of the wider feudal ceremony.

Church law books later used the word for the grant of a church office itself. Only from the thirteenth century did it settle into its modern sense, the act of putting a holder in possession of a benefice. That sense matches what canonists call corporal institution. The entry points readers to the related entries on institution and installation for the fuller picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-casanare:
Casanare is a vicariate apostolic in Colombia, run by Augustinians under the Congregation of Extraordinary Ecclesiastical Affairs. Its city on the river of the same name once belonged to the Diocese of Tunja. Created in 1893 after efforts from 1884, it forms a great triangle bounded by the Meta River, Venezuela, and the Andes. Bogotá, Tunja, and Pamplona are its neighboring dioceses.

In 1893 some 110,000 people were served by only ten priests, and the seat stands at Tamara among towns such as Nunchia, Tame, and Arauca. Jesuit pioneers had built 126 reductions and large, well-furnished churches, but their expulsion in 1767 wrecked the missions, and merchants still display candlesticks from the abandoned churches. By 1907 about thirty missionaries and three Sisters of Charity convents worked there, despite revolutions in 1895 and 1899.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-peri:
Catholic periodical literature began with the printed broadsides of the late fifteenth century. The earliest surviving sheets came from Germany. Florence's Notizie scritte, nicknamed Gazetta for the coin paid to read them, ranked among the first Italian periodicals. From the start these rudimentary sheets carried religious news, and the Jesuit Relations soon showed how early church authorities grasped the new medium.

The article traces this literature country by country across the western world, covering dailies, weeklies, monthlies, quarterlies, and annuals, not only political newspapers but every periodical form. It gives the history of Catholic journalism in each prominent country. It also gives an account of its standing in its own day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-honor:
Charles-Honore Laverdière was a French-Canadian historian born at Chateau-Richer in 1826 and dead at Quebec in 1873. Ordained in 1851, he joined the Quebec Seminary, where he had studied classics and theology, and stayed there until his death. He taught belles-lettres, physics, chemistry, mathematics, music, and drawing. Though his own writings were few, a school history of Canada and some pamphlets, he supervised the re-editing of works that are the very sources of Canadian history.

Chief among them were the Relations des Jésuites of 1858, and the Journal des Jésuites of 1871. Finally came his dearest wish, the Oeuvres de Champlain, for which he wrote the introduction. When the newly completed edition burned entirely, he calmly noted that misprints escaping his vigilance might be avoided next time. His mastery of plain-song also let him publish liturgical works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-choir-in-arch:
An entry on the choir in church architecture, a term full of ambiguity. Strictly, the choir is the part of the church holding the clergy stalls, though the word is loosely used for the whole eastern arm. At Westminster Abbey the stalls stand in the east nave, so no part of the choir lies in the eastern arm. At Canterbury it fills the western bays of the eastern arm.

Early churches such as Santa Maria Maggiore had only nave and sanctuary, with no choir between. The choir grew as the east part of the nave, fenced by low marble walls called cancelli, the source of the word chancel. Isidore of Seville and Honorius of Autun traced choir to the corona, the circle of clergy or singers around the altar. The enclosed central choir, with pulpits for reading Gospel and Epistle, was the last great change of plan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cincture:
An entry on the cincture, or girdle, an article of liturgical dress recognised as such since the ninth century. Now as then it binds the loose, flowing alb so it does not hinder the wearer. Its liturgical character shows in the prayers said while putting it on and in its symbolism of spiritual watchfulness. The Stowe Missal lists it among Mass vestments, perhaps reflecting seventh-century Celtic practice.

Celtic practice, like Greek practice today, had bishops and priests alone wear the girdle, leaving the deacon's tunic ungirded. Early survivals show narrow bands of silk and rich stuff, often embroidered. Modern girdles are preferably flax or hemp, though wool and silk are allowed. The vesting prayer, gird me, O Lord, with purity, marks it as a sign of priestly chastity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-estien:
Claude Estiennot de la Serre, a Benedictine of Saint-Maur born at Varennes in 1639 and dead at Rome in 1699, joined the Benedictines at Vendome and professed there in 1658. After teaching humanities briefly at Pontlevoy, he was sent to Saint-Germain-des-Pres in Paris, where Dom Mabillon recognised his research talent. The two became intimate friends and fellow-workers, walking through Flanders to visit its chief monastic libraries.

In 1670 Estiennot became sub-prior of Saint-Martin's at Pontoise, whose three-volume history was his first published work. His chief work, the Benedictine Antiquities, was compiled between 1673 and 1682, treating France's monastic traditions diocese by diocese. In 1684 he became procurator of his congregation at the Roman Curia and lived in Rome thereafter. En route he gathered material for Mabillon, feeding the Benedictine Annals and the Gallia Christiana, and he collected sixteen volumes of historical fragments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coimbatore:
Leo Kelly's entry covers Coimbatore, a city in Madras in British India. It stands on the River Noyel. In 1901 it held 53,080 people, of whom 3,000 were Catholics. The diocese takes in the Coimbatore district except one taluk. It also takes in the Nilgiris, parts of Malabar country, and the Nelliampathy Hills. Split from the Vicariate Apostolic of Pondicherry in 1846, it became a vicariate in 1850. It became a full diocese on 1 September 1886 under Bishop Joseph Louis Bardon.

Across a population of two and a half million, the diocese counted 37,080 Catholics. They were served by 41 European and 13 native priests, with 14 students in its seminary. Its schools ran from a second-grade college and a high school down to 67 elementary schools with 4,239 pupils. It also kept two hospitals, four orphanages, and an industrial school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-college-of-sa:
Stephen Donovan's entry covers the College of Saint Bonaventure at Quaracchi, near Florence. It stands famous as the literary center of the Order of Friars Minor. Mgr. Bernardino del Vago, Archbishop of Sardis and then minister general, founded it on 14 July 1879. Its first director, Father Fidelis of Fauna, launched the new edition of Saint Bonaventure's works. After his death in 1881, Ignatius Jeiler of Saxony took charge, and Leonard Lemmens followed him in 1902.

Under the Patres editores, the college won a name for critical scholarship. Foremost stands the Opera Omnia of Saint Bonaventure. Beside it run the Analecta Franciscana, four volumes of early order chronicles from 1885 to 1907. Two Bibliotheca series followed, plus the monthly Acta Ordinis and the Archivum Franciscano-Historicum. In 1903 the friars also began a new critical edition of Alexander of Hales.

John Hanrahan's entry follows the College of Saint Isidore in Rome. It was first founded for Spanish Franciscans under Gregory XV. In 1625 the buildings passed to Father Luke Wadding. With sanction from the General of the Friars Minor and the pope, he turned them into a college for Irish Franciscan students. Within a few years over thirty religious lived within its walls. Some years later the number had grown to fifty. Wadding drew able Irish professors, among them Hickey and Fleming.

The college flourished as a home of Irish learning in Rome. Its fortunes broke when French troops occupied Rome in 1798. The community scattered, and its precious manuscripts were moved for safety. They now rest in the order's convent at Merchant's Quay, Dublin. The entry thus joins a house of study to the wider story of Irish scholars in exile.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comte-de-mais:
Georges Bertrin's entry follows Joseph de Maistre, a French philosophical writer born at Chambéry in Savoy in 1753 and dead at Turin on 26 February 1821. His family, French in origin, had settled in Savoy a century earlier, his father presiding over the Senate. Eldest of ten, Joseph learned from Jesuits, who with his parents gave him love of religion and detestation of eighteenth-century rationalism, which he always opposed. He entered the magistracy in 1774, became assistant fiscal advocate general in 1780, and senator in 1788.

Fleeing the invading French, he served his Sardinian king on mission at Lausanne for four years. His writings, all in French, then Piedmont's literary tongue, include the 1809 Essai sur le principe générateur des constitutions politiques and the Gallican Church treatise of 1821. Bertrin praises ideas bold and penetrating, at times seemingly prophetic, in a French style among the language's ornaments. His younger brother Xavier wrote too.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coptic-litera:
Eugène Hyvernat's entry updates Coptic literature since the Egypt article, reporting new Sahidic material now published by competent scholars. The Morgan Collection dominates. The Monastery of Saint Michael's Fayûm library, discovered in spring 1910, comprised fifty-eight volumes. Most reached Paris, purchased by J. Pierpont Morgan in December 1911 for his New York library. Five thousand volumes remained in Cairo's Museum, with a few fragments. Except one Fayûmic and one Bohairic manuscript, all stands in Sahidic.

Its Bible section holds six complete Sahidic Old Testament books, the Four Gospels excepting stated passages, and Saint Paul's fourteen Epistles. Liturgy offers a complete Lectionary, and the Synaxary over one hundred homilies, discourses, eulogies, Acts, lives, and treatises for Sundays and feasts. Feasts include the Nativity, Choiac 29, 25 December, and Epiphany, Tybi 11, 6 January. An official catalogue stands in preparation, resting on the writer's cursory inspection of most manuscripts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-a:
A compact reference entry traces the councils held at Auxerre in France and what their decrees reveal about Christian life in the early Middle Ages. It presents the meetings as evidence for how bishops tried to shape behaviour among newly converted peoples and Gallo-Roman Christians living side by side.

The council of 585, or possibly 578, issued forty-five canons aimed at surviving pagan customs and superstition, while also preserving older Christian practices. A later council, dated 695 or 697, turned chiefly to the Divine Office, meaning the daily cycle of prayer, and to church ceremonies. Together the two sets of rules give a vivid glimpse of worship, discipline, and everyday morals in Merovingian Gaul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-court-in-scri:
This scripture entry untangles the many meanings of the word court in the English Bible, tracing each back to Hebrew terms for an enclosed space. It distinguishes a nomad encampment, a village protected by stockade or rampart, the courtyards of houses and temples, and, in a rarer sense, the retinue or household of a king.

Place names carry the same root: Haseroth, where Israel camped after Sinai, and Asor, the Canaanite city taken by Joshua, fortified by Solomon, and seized by Tiglath-Pileser. House courts are rebuilt from excavations in Syria and Palestine and from lasting local custom, showing an outer court between street wall and dwelling. The entry closes with temple courts and a full bibliography for deeper study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coventry-patm:
A biographical entry presents Coventry Patmore, a major nineteenth-century English poet despite his slender verse output. Born at Woodford in 1823 and dead at Lymington in 1896, he was the son of a man of letters who moved among Lamb, Hazlitt, and Leigh Hunt.

Left to earn a hard living after his father's reverses, Patmore found work in the British Museum Library, which made his marriage possible. His Angel in the House, a versified love story begun in 1854, made him famous. After his wife's death in 1862, grief became his later theme. His Unknown Eros, long neglected, is now ranked as a great English classic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-czech-literat:
A literary survey traces Czech, or Bohemian, literature from the conversion of Moravia and Bohemia in 863 through the apostles Cyril and Methodius to the early twentieth century. Except for Bulgarian, no Slav literature is older than Czech, which stayed the richest until the seventeenth century. Its story divides into four periods.

The first runs from Christianization to John Hus in 1404, fruitful in poetry, with Cyril's Slav alphabet and liturgy. The second, the golden age, centres on Hus and devotional prose. The third follows the White Mountain defeat of 1620 and Catholic renewal. The fourth is the national revival led by priests and teachers like Dobrovsky. Long lists of poets, novelists, dramatists, and theologians close the survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-delaware:
A state entry presents Delaware, one of the original thirteen United States, lying between Pennsylvania, the Delaware River and Bay, and Maryland. Its area is 2,370 square miles, of which 1,965 are land, and its fertile soil stands largely in high cultivation. History opens with Henry Hudson sailing into Delaware Bay in 1609 for the Dutch East India Company.

The bay took its name about 1610 for Lord Delawarr, Virginia's first governor. Dutch settlers planted Swaanendael near Cape Henlopen in 1631, but Indians destroyed it within months. Swedes, Dutch, and English followed, and the entry traces the colony to statehood. Sections cover population, counted near 194,479 in 1906, education from Old Swedes' Church school, Catholic progress from a few settlers to diocesan life, other religions, and legislation on religious freedom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denis-auguste:
A life of Denis Auguste Affre, Archbishop of Paris, born in 1793 at Saint-Rome-de-Tarn and killed in Paris in 1848. Trained at Saint Sulpice under his uncle, he served as vicar-general at Luçon and Amiens, then took the Paris see in 1840 after a brief spell as vicar-capitular. His years in office pushed better training for priests and freedom for Church teaching.

During the 1848 rising he sought General Cavaignac, said his own life was of little value, and walked to a barricade bearing a green branch as a peace sign. Shots broke out as he spoke, and he fell mortally wounded. Writings named at the close include a study of Church property from 1837 and a philosophical introduction to Christianity from 1846.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-divine-promis:
Promise in Scripture covers pledges between men, vows of men to God, and above all God's pledges to men. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry warns that a full study would demand a review of all Old Testament prophecy and of grace and election. Every word of grace from God is in a sense a promise, and obedience to his commands brings many assurances of favor.

When Israel was told to go in and possess the land, the land was in practice already theirs, since God had lifted his hand to give it. Their disobedience undid the promise wrapped in the command. The entry follows such examples through the Bible, showing how promise and obedience weave together in the story of God's people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dom-jacques-a:
Dom Jacques Alexandre was a learned Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint Maur, born at Orleans on 24 January 1653. He professed at Vendome in 1673 and, after studies in philosophy and theology, was sent to Bonne-Nouvelle, where he spent the rest of his life. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that he died sub-prior of the house, delicate in health yet a man of great industry.

All his leisure went to mathematics and to physical and mechanical science. He wrote much without thought of print, copying most of it into one great folio kept in the library. He is known chiefly by two works, on the tides and on clocks, including a pendulum device described by Berthoud, though it never came into practical use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dromore:
Dromore counts among Armagh's eight suffragans in Ireland, covering parts of Down, Armagh, and Antrim. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry counts eighteen parishes, two of them, Newry and Clonallon, mensal parishes held for the bishop's support. The see takes its name from Dromore, great ridge, a small town in northwest County Down on the Lagan, sixty-three miles north of Dublin.

Saint Colman, also called Mocholmoc, founded the see in the sixth century, one of more than a hundred Irish saints of that name. A prophecy ascribed to Saint Patrick sixty years before is said to have foretold it. The entry draws on Archdall, Reeves, and Healy to trace a small see with a long and tangled past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
Ecclesiastical architecture is, in the shortest and best definition, the art of building. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry stresses the word art, not merely the act of putting stones together. Good building gives a structure whatever beauty fits its purpose and its means. As one recent writer put it, there is no separate art of building well and of building badly, since good architecture is building beautifully and expressively.

The entry then surveys church building from the early house churches to the great cathedrals, weighing Romanesque, Gothic, and Byzantine manners. It doubts whether Byzantine bulk suits a great cathedral alone, yet hopes the Westminster experiment may bear fruit. For readers, it joins theory to the stones of real churches.

Ecclesiastical tenure, in the feudal system, followed the laws of temporal fiefs. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains the feudal grant: a suzerain, bishop or abbot, bestowed an estate forever on a person who thus became his vassal. At enfeoffment the grantee did homage, swore fealty, and offered the set money or object by which he held his fief. These acts were repeated whenever suzerain or vassal changed.

Churchmen granted such fiefs to princes, barons, and knights, who then owed protection to the church and domains of their overlord. The system was not confined to land, since church revenues and tithes were often farmed to laymen as a kind of fief. For tenure by incumbents of benefices, the entry points to the article on benefice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-english-liter:
English literature is likened to a great tree, rooted deep in the past, its branches spread wide and bearing fruit through storms, calms, sunshine, and rain. No short article can give its full history, the entry admits, so it traces only the main lines of its life. Nor was English literature an isolated growth: it sprang from a common Aryan root and has taken in influences from other literatures again and again.

Yet, as Freeman said, we are ourselves and not somebody else. Latin, French, Italian, Greek, and Spanish literatures have poured their influences upon English writing, yet its character, language, and literature remain unmistakably English. Its makers, the Angles, Saxons, Jutes, and Frisians, spent a hundred and fifty years, from 455 to 600, conquering the island after Rome abandoned the Britons in 410. Christianity, preached by Augustine in 597, brought education, science, and the arts as the main refining force.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-entablature:
An entablature is the horizontal superstructure that rests on columns in classical building, and this short entry defines its parts. It is split into three members: the architrave, the supporting beam carried from column to column; the frieze, the decorative band above it; and the cornice, the crowning member that projects outward. Each classical order has its own proper entablature.

Both the total height and the subdivisions follow a scale of proportion drawn from the diameter of the column, so that the whole stays in harmony with its supports. The entablature is also used, at times, to finish the upper part of a wall architecturally even where no columns stand. With pilasters, or with columns detached from or engaged in a wall, it is sometimes profiled round them, carrying its mouldings unbroken past the projection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistle-in-sc:
An epistle in Scripture began as a book or writing in general, and only later became a distinct literary form, as this entry explains. Hebrew first used a general word for book, then transitional words for writing, and finally terms of Assyrian or Persian origin that the Septuagint always renders as epistle. The Old Testament shows two stages: first the letter as a book or writing, then the letter as a form in its own right.

The dividing line is hard to fix, but in general the Hebrews shaped their notion of a letter as a specific form during the Captivity. The first written biblical message is David's letter to Joab about Uriah, sent for secrecy, like Jezebel's order about Naboth and Jehu's commands to Samaria. Later letters include Jeremiah's message to the exiles in Babylon and a false prophet's letters from Babylon aimed at undermining Jeremiah.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eugene-bore:
Eugene Bore was an Orientalist, born at Angers on 15 August 1809 and dead at Paris on 3 May 1878. From Angers he went to the Collège Stanislas in Paris, where at eighteen he won the philosophy prize against all France's colleges, one rival being Alfred de Musset. In 1829, with his brother Léon, he joined the coterie of the Abbé de Lamennais, introducing his college-mate Maurice de Guérin.

With Montalembert he tried to persuade Lamennais to submit, hoping for his return to the Church until 1851. A member of the Asiatic Society in 1833, he won fame in the Journal Asiatique. He was professor of Armenian in 1833 and 1834 at the Collège de France. After six months of study at Constantinople in 1837, he went with Father Scaffi to Erzerum in Armenia. At Tauris he started a school for Christianity, whose service was always his chief concern.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-family-of-lef:
The Lefebvre were a family of tapestry weavers in France and Flanders. Lancelot Lefebvre worked as a weaver at Brussels and Antwerp around 1655. Pierre le Fevre settled in Paris in 1630 and died in 1669. His son Philip carried the craft to Florence in 1677.

Philip's son Jean worked at the Gobelins on high-warp looms with Jans. Their workshops wove the Toilet of a Princess and a fine Flora series. They also produced histories of St Paul, Louis XIV, and Alexander. The article traces the family trade across three generations and several cities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-family-of-pet:
The Petre were an English Catholic family of courtiers and peers. Sir William Petre served as secretary under Henry VIII and Elizabeth. William, the fourth lord, died in the Tower in 1684 over Oates's Plot. Later lords worked for Catholic emancipation in the eighteenth century.

William Joseph, the thirteenth baron, ran a school at Woburn Park from 1877 to 1884. The family also gave the church bishops Francis and Benjamin Petre. Sir Edward Petre, a Jesuit, served James II as privy councillor. The pope refused requests to make him a bishop or cardinal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fathers-of-th:
The Fathers of the Holy Sepulchre are Franciscans guarding Christ's tomb in Jerusalem. Six or seven fathers, with as many lay brothers, keep the basilica's sanctuaries. Picked every three months from St Saviour's community, they live confined. Their only contact with the outside world passes through the portal aperture.

Each afternoon they lead a pilgrimage through the sanctuaries of the basilica. At midnight they process to the tomb chanting the Office and the Benedictus. Their superiors alternate among Italians, French, and Spaniards in turn. Emperor Francis Joseph's visit in 1869 won them light, air, and a bell tower.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinand-bru:
Ferdinand Brunetiere was a French critic and professor of literature. Born at Toulon in 1849, he failed its entrance examination through weakness in Greek. He joined the Revue des Deux Mondes in 1874 and became its editor-in-chief in 1893. Elected to the French Academy, he taught French literature at the Ecole Normale.

Brunetiere judged books by fixed dogmatic principles, not by mere impression. Later he applied Darwin's evolution to literary genres and forms. A convert to Catholicism, he defended the faith in speeches across France. He died at Paris in 1906, a master of conviction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-filippo-parla:
Filippo Parlatore was an Italian botanist born at Palermo in 1816 and dead at Florence in 1877. Trained in medicine, he soon gave all his time to botany, beginning with the flora of Sicily. He travelled through Italy, Switzerland, France, and England, staying longest at Kew in London. At the Florence congress of 1841 he proposed a general herbarium, which was then founded there.

Grand Duke Leopold made him professor of botany and director of the botanical garden at Florence. For more than thirty years he built up the central herbarium, to which his own collection later passed. His lifework was the Flora Italiana, five volumes of which appeared between 1848 and 1874. He also founded the Giornale botanico Italiano and wrote widely on plant geography and history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-xav:
Francisco Xavier Alegre, born at Vera Cruz in Mexico on 12 November 1729 and dead at Bologna on 16 August 1788, was a Jesuit historian and classical scholar. He entered the Society in 1747 and soon won a name for learning in everything classical. He held a chair at the Jesuit college at Havana and afterwards at Merida in Yucatan.

He left many works, mostly translations of classics. They include the Alexandriadas of 1773, the Iliad in Latin published at Rome in 1788, Homer's Battle of Frogs and Mice in Latin, fragments of Horace. A Spanish version of the first three cantos of Boileau's Art of Poetry completes the list. His work is the History of the Society of Jesus in New Spain, edited by Bustamante at Mexico in 1841. It is dignified in tone and free from attacks on Spain even though written while the order was persecuted, and indispensable for colonial Mexico and its Indian peoples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-viet:
Francois Vieta, Seigneur de la Bigottiere, known as Viete, was born at Fontenay-le-Comte in Poitou in 1540 and died at Paris in February 1603, the father of modern algebra. Son of a solicitor, he studied under the Franciscans of his town and law at Poitiers, and returned to Fontenay at nineteen. He ranked among the province's leading barristers, counting Mary Stuart among his clients.

 A barrister at Paris and councillor of the Parlement at Rennes, he fell from favour with Henry III. Then, as councillor at Tours under Henry IV, he rendered signal service by breaking the Spanish cipher. In his last years at Paris, as master of requests, he published the algebra that made letters general symbols of quantity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-french-litera:
French Literature surveys the whole growth of French letters, from spoken Latin in Roman Gaul to the modern age. The article opens with the birth of the language itself, as low Latin bent through Celtic and Frankish speech into Romance. Its earliest texts include the Strasbourg Oaths of 842 and a song for Saint Eulalia from about 880.

From dialects of oc in the south and oïl in the north, the speech of Paris rose to lead the rest in the twelfth century. Literature began with epic song, grouped in French, Breton, and antique cycles, sung by trouvères at feasts and before battles. The survey then follows poetry, prose, and drama through the centuries, naming the works that fixed the French tongue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-german-litera:
German Literature, a sweeping survey from pagan oral song to the Christian age, opens before any written monument. No German text predates the eighth century, and Ulfilas's fourth-century Gothic Bible belongs to Gothic, not German, letters. Tacitus records unwritten poetry of god-hymns and hero songs, sung in chorus with dancing in alliterative verse, plus minstrel praise songs, charms, and riddles.

Migration-age heroes like Attila, Theodoric, and Ermanric fed saga cycles that fused myth with history, the Nibelungen saga joining Siegfried's death to the Burgundians' destruction by Huns in 435. Charlemagne's collection of heroic lays perished, leaving the Merseburg Charms and the Hildebrandslied, a Fulda fragment of father-son combat written after 800. The High German sound shift of 500 to 700 split southern from northern dialects, and conversion, pressed by Boniface and sealed by Charlemagne's baptism of the Saxons, remade the literature's world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-dupr:
Giovanni Dupré was a sculptor of remote French ancestry, born at Siena in 1817, who died at Florence in 1882. A woodcarver in youth, he taught himself sculpture and won his rank with the life-size dead Abel in marble, followed by Cain in 1840. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a career that ran from academy prizes to a Paris medal of honor.

After illness came renewed vigor: the brooding Sappho of 1857, the Ferrari monument, the Grape Children, and the Addolorata for Santa Croce. In 1863 he reached his height with the Pietà for the Bichi-Ruspoli tomb at Siena. It was awarded the grand medal of honor at Paris. Later works include the Cavour monument at Turin and a bronze Savonarola, while his last St. Francis was finished by his daughter Amalia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gothic-archit:
Gothic Architecture is an article on a style whose name began as a Renaissance term of contempt. Vasari wrote of new architects building after the manner of barbarous nations in the style called Gothic, and Evelyn called it a fantastical and licentious manner without proportion, use, or beauty. A Catholic Encyclopedia article argues the name fits neither the style's nature nor its home.

Ethnically the art is Franco-Norman in origin, and between the Arian Goths and the Catholic Franks and Normans lies a racial and religious gulf. Ignorant of its true habitat, Renaissance Italians called it the German manner. Since Goth meant perfect barbarism to them, they fixed the name on a style they meant to destroy. When the nineteenth century brought new apologists, the old title was kept as the only one available.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hauteserre:
Two learned brothers share this entry: Antoine Dadin d'Hauteserre, historian and canonist, and his younger brother Flavius. Antoine, born in 1602 and dead in 1682, was dean of law at Toulouse, steeped in the Fathers and councils. He was highly esteemed by the French clergy for works on feudal and Roman law, Aquitaine's antiquities, and Gregory of Tours.

At two bishops' request he reviewed legal tracts on the appel comme d'abus in 1670 and refuted them. His Ecclesiasticae Jurisdictionis Vindictae of 1707 stands out among sixteen volumes published at Naples. Flavius, a law professor at Poitiers dead about 1670, annotated the early canonical collections of Ferrandus and Cresconius in 1630.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hebrew-langua:
Hebrew, the tongue of ancient Israel and of nearly all the Old Testament, belongs to the Semitic family stretching from the Mediterranean to Arabia, with southern, northern, eastern, and central branches. Its name for the language appears only late, in the Greek prologue to Ecclesiasticus about 130 before Christ. Isaiah calls it the language of Canaan and other passages call it the Jews' language.

Twenty-two consonant letters, written right to left, carry the language, with three-consonant roots whose vowels shift the sense, as qtl runs from he killed to slayer and slain. Early script differed from the square letters of later times, and vowels went unwritten while Hebrew lived. After its death as a spoken tongue the Massoretes built the dot-and-dash vowel system that fixed its traditional reading.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-der-:
Middle High German poet Heinrich der Glichezare, the hypocrite, in the sense of one bearing a strange name, wrote about 1180 the oldest German beast epic we possess, Reinhart Fuchs. Based on a French Renart poem older than any surviving branch, it survives complete only in a faithful thirteenth-century version at Heidelberg and Kalocsa. Fragments of the original Isengrin's Trouble were found at Melsungen in 1839.

At first the fox is outwitted by weaker beasts. Later he plays outrageous tricks, above all on Isengrin the wolf, escapes punishment by healing the sick lion at his foes' expense, and finally poisons his benefactor. Plainly told with satiric touches, it closes on craft rewarded while honesty goes unpaid. Goethe later drew his Reineke Fuchs from a Low German version of the same matter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-helen-more:
English Benedictine Dame Gertrude More, born Helen More at Low Leyton in 1606, was great-granddaughter of Thomas More and chief foundress of the Cambrai community. Her mother died young, her father raised her. Dom Benet Jones drew her into his Cambrai foundation. There she was first of nine postulants admitted in December 1623.

Scruples clouded her novitiate until Dom Augustine Baker taught her affective prayer. After that she advanced swiftly and edified the young house, her name going to Rome with Catharine Gascoigne's when an abbess was needed in 1629. Catharine was chosen, but Gertrude stayed honoured as foundress. She upheld her abbess through the vicar's interference with Baker's teaching, and died of smallpox in 1633 during the general chapter that approved her way of prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-more:
Henry More, great-grandson of the martyred English chancellor, was born in 1586 and died at Watten in 1661. Schooled at St. Omer and Valladolid, he joined the Society of Jesus, served in college posts, and was sent on the English mission. There he was twice arrested and imprisoned, in 1632 and 1640. He became provincial in 1635 and dealt with the papal agents Panzani, Conn, and Rossetti at the court of Queen Henrietta Maria.

More was rector of St. Omer from 1649 to 1652 and again from 1657 to 1660. In those later years he wrote Historia Missionis Anglicanae, his history of the English Jesuits covering 1580 to 1635 and published at St. Omer in 1660. He also translated Jerome Platus on the happiness of the religious state and a manual of meditations. He composed a life and doctrine of Christ in daily meditations, published in Latin at Antwerp in 1649 and in English at Ghent in 1656.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-sepulchr:
The Holy Sepulchre is the tomb where the body of Jesus was laid after the Crucifixion. The evangelists say it was Joseph of Arimathea's own new monument, hewn from rock in a garden near Calvary. It stood outside Jerusalem's walls yet close to the city, closed by a great stone rolled to the door. Jews allowed no burial inside the city except for kings, which confirms the site outside the walls.

No further mention of the place appears until the fourth century, but nearly all scholars hold that oral tradition preserved its knowledge. Constantine's investigations in 326 marked the site for future ages with a basilica over the tomb. An unbroken written tradition links that basilica to the church standing there today, and the entry sifts gospel evidence, tradition, and archaeology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hungarian-lit:
Hungarian literature grows from a language spoken for nearly a thousand years and now used by about twelve million people. Pithy and pliant, rich in vowel sounds, Hungarian differs fundamentally from most literary tongues. As the Jesuit Sajnovics determined in 1770, it is nearest to Vogul-Ostiak, though Hungarians parted from those speakers over two thousand years ago. With Lappish, Finnish, and others it belongs to the Ural group, and with Turkish and Mongolian to the Ural-Altaic group.

Its vocabulary gained much from neighbours: Persian and especially Turkish words before the settlement of present Hungary in 896, then Slav, German, Latin, and Italian words after it. Despite some harshness, Hungarian suits oratory and serious poetry well. The entry surveys its writers from early chroniclers to Vörösmarty, regarded by many as Hungary's greatest lyric, epic, and dramatic poet, and to Petöfi, its greatest lyricist, who fell young in war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-irish-literat:
How Ireland learned letters, and what it wrote with them, is the vast question this literary history takes up. Direct trade with Gaul may have brought writing, but McNeill's work on oghams points instead to Romanized Britons as teachers. Yet the first Irish alphabet was neither Latin nor Greek: early Irish devised their own script, built with skill on Latin letters, for carving on pillars and gravestones.

Ogham strokes run straight or slanting, long or short. They are drawn over, under, or through a stem line. They open a story that runs from stone inscriptions through monastic manuscripts to later poetry and prose. The entry weighs origins, scripts, and ages of writing, giving readers the deep background of a literature that began in carved lines before it ever reached a page. Its scale matches a national literature, not a single book.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-italian-liter:
Italy's modern tongue, grown from the Latin actually spoken on the peninsula after Rome fell, is the root of the literature surveyed here. Scholars dispute how far that spoken Latin matched classical literary Latin. They also dispute how far it was popular rustic speech. Most likely it mixed the two, with the popular strain winning as society changed. Greek words survive from Byzantine rule, Crusades, and trade, Arabic words linger chiefly in Sicily, and French and Provençal strains entered through Latin itself.

Germanic invasions, by contrast, left only a slight mark on the vocabulary despite long centuries of conquest. From those linguistic roots the entry traces a literature from early dialects toward a national tongue. It sets the language question first. Then the poetry, prose, and drama that follow read as growth from living speech rather than from books alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-bonfr:
Biblical scholar Jacques Bonfrère was born at Dinant, Belgium, on 12 April 1573. He died at Tournai on 9 May 1642. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1592. After teaching rhetoric, philosophy, and theology, he devoted himself to Scripture. He long taught Scripture and Hebrew at Douai. There he also served as superior of the Scots College.

Sweert praised him as a man of rare virtue, industry, and prudence. He also praised his penetrating mind and solid judgment. Cornelius à Lapide had introduced him to scriptural study. His Praeloquia, a general introduction to the Bible, won lasting esteem. In 1839 Migne chose it to open his complete course of Scripture. The entry presents a patient exegete whose introduction outlived him by two centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-le-fe:
French theologian Jacques Le Fèvre was born at Lisieux in the mid-seventeenth century. He died at Paris on 1 July 1716. He became archdeacon of his native city. He served as vicar-general of Bourges archdiocese. In 1674 he earned a Sorbonne doctorate in theology. His works show a conciliatory controversialist at work.

His Entretiens d'Eudoxe et d'Euchariste, published in 1674, discussed Maimbourg's histories of Arianism and iconoclasm. Its first dialogue was condemned and burned. His Motifs invincibles of 1682 argued that Catholic and Protestant teachings agree at root. Differences, he said, were slight and mostly verbal. Arnauld attacked those views. Le Fèvre answered him in 1685 with a Réplique defending his book. The entry presents a peacemaker whose peace offerings drew fire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-marie:
Celebrated pulpit orator Jacques Marie Louis Monsabré was born at Blois on 10 December 1827. He died at Havre on 21 February 1907. He was ordained a secular priest on 15 June 1851. Soon he felt a religious vocation. On 31 July 1851, St Ignatius' feast, he said his first Mass. He thought seriously of joining the Jesuits. Four days later, on St Dominic's feast, he chose the Dominicans instead. He at once wrote to Père Lacordaire seeking admission.

He waited four years for release from his diocese. The bishop held Holy See permission to delay newly ordained priests' entry into orders. In May 1855 he received his dimissorials and entered the Flavigny novitiate. He took the habit on 31 May and professed simply a year later. Days later he was sent to the Chalais house of studies. The entry opens the career of a Dominican preacher famed across France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Glaire, a French priest and Bible scholar born at Bordeaux in 1798 and dead near Paris in 1879, gave his career to Hebrew and Scripture. After study at Bordeaux he followed Saint-Sulpice courses in Paris alongside Oriental languages at the Sorbonne, and was ordained in 1822.

Glaire taught Hebrew at Saint-Sulpice, then at the Sorbonne, where he became professor of Scripture in 1836 and dean in 1841. His books corrected Gesenius's Hebrew lexicon, set out Hebrew, Chaldean, and Arabic grammar, and introduced both Testaments in a staunchly conservative key. Later scholars call much of it dated, yet honour what he did to ground French Bible study.

Molière, properly Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, was a French comic playwright born in Paris in 1622 and dead there in 1673. Son of a furniture dealer who also served the king, he studied with the Jesuits at Clermont and perhaps law at Orléans, but the stage claimed him at twenty-one.

With Madeleine Béjart he founded the Illustre Théâtre, a venture that failed and landed him briefly in debtors' prison. Years touring France taught him his craft, and from Lyons in the 1650s he began the fine comedy that made his name. His plays skewer doctors, misers, hypocrites, and snobs with laughter that still holds the stage, and he died soon after playing his own Imaginary Invalid.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-de-la-br:
Jean de La Bruyère, a French moralist born in Paris in 1645 and dead at Chantilly in 1696, was the son of a comptroller of city revenue. Trained as an advocate, he quit the bar, bought a finance post at Caen in 1673, and lived a studious life in Paris.

Bossuet's friendship brought La Bruyère into the Condé household to teach history to the young duke of Bourbon. He half succeeded as tutor but won the great Condé's friendship and a pension, staying at Chantilly till his death. His Characters, printed anonymously in 1688, pairs a translation of Theophrastus with sharp portraits of his own age that made the book a hit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-nicolas-:
Jean-Nicolas Laverlochère, a French Oblate missionary born at Grenoble in 1812 and dead at Temiscaming, Canada, in 1884, began as a lay brother before studying for the priesthood. Ordained in 1844, he left L'Acadie near Montreal for Hudson Bay country to preach to Indigenous peoples.

Laverlochère served in turn at Abitibi, Moose Factory, and other bay posts, labouring for the conversion of native tribes. Alone or with others he published devotional books in Indigenous tongues, and his letters in the Annals of the Propagation of the Faith drew wide notice across Catholic Europe. He became known as the Apostle of Hudson Bay.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-pierre-c:
Jean-Pierre Camus, bishop of Belley, was born in Paris in 1584 and died there in 1652. A Burgundian of good birth, he won fame for eloquence, and by papal dispensation became bishop at twenty-six, consecrated by Saint Francis de Sales, whose close friend he remained.

Camus ruled Belley with ardent, if sometimes hasty, zeal, and in 1614 defended church rights before the Estates-General. Longing for study, he stayed at his post at De Sales's counsel until the saint's death in 1629, then retired to Aulnay. Called as auxiliary at Rouen, he ended at Paris's Hospice des Incurables, more sympathiser than patient, and died before taking Arras.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jordanus-de-n:
Jordanus de Nemore was a thirteenth-century mathematician whose works on weights and arithmetic shaped medieval science. Nothing is known of his life, and his name in manuscripts has been read as Jordan of Nemi, suggesting an Italian. Chasles dated him no later than the twelfth century from his Algorismus.
