A fourteenth-century Dominican chronicle wrongly identified him with Jordanus Saxo, Dominic's successor as master general in 1222.

His vogue in the Middle Ages was great. Roger Bacon quoted his De ponderibus in the Opus Majus, Bradwardine and the Oxford logicians used him heavily, and his statics powerfully influenced the Renaissance. His treatises include an Algorismus on elementary arithmetic, Elements of Arithmetic printed at Paris in 1496, and works on weights and given lines. The Algorithmus printed at Nuremberg in 1534 was really by a Master Gerard, not Jordanus, whose genuine demonstrated Algorismus was only rediscovered in 1906.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-carrie:
Joseph Carrière was a French moral theologian who led the Society of St. Sulpice for fourteen years. Born near Rodez in 1795, he entered St. Sulpice in 1812, was ordained at twenty-two, and soon taught moral theology there with brilliance. In 1829 he visited America, took part in the First Provincial Council of Baltimore, and won praise for learning and simple charm.

His chief works treat marriage, justice, and contracts, and he was the first notable writer to set theology beside the Napoleonic Code. Lawyers used his clear accounts of French law as authorities. Chosen superior of the society in 1850, he held the post until his death at Lyons in 1864.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-fabre:
Joseph Fabre was the second Superior General of the Oblates of Mary Immaculate. Born at Cuges in southern France in 1824, he studied at Marseilles, joined the Oblates, and was ordained in 1847. He directed the Marseilles seminary and served as procurator before the founder's death in 1861 brought his unanimous election as superior.

During his thirty-one years in office, Fabre spread the Oblates to Italy, Spain, Holland, Britain, Canada, and the United States, and membership more than doubled. He stressed charity and humility, set up retreats for superiors and members, and left ten bishops leading vicariates when he died at Royaumont in 1892.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-henri-:
Joseph Henri Marie de Prémare was a French Jesuit missionary and China's finest early language scholar. Born at Cherbourg in 1666, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1683 and reached China in 1698. He worked chiefly in Guangxi until Emperor Yongzheng banned the faith in 1724, confined him at Canton, and then banished him to Macao.

In retirement he mastered Chinese language and letters better, sinologists judge, than any older missionary. His Notitia linguae sinicae explains both everyday Chinese and literary style, and James Legge called it invaluable. He also translated odes, maxims, and the tragedy Orphan of the House of Zhao for Du Halde's Description of China.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-saenz-:
Joseph Sáenz de Aguirre was a Spanish Benedictine cardinal and scholar who lived from 1630 to 1699. Born at Logroño, he joined Monte Cassino, directed studies for fifteen years at Salamanca's St. Vincent monastery, then became its abbot. He then taught dogmatic theology and opened the Scripture course at Salamanca University.

Aguirre's refutation of the Gallican Declaration of 1682 earned him a cardinal's hat and praise from Innocent XI. His letters to Bossuet show his fight against Quietism. His works defend Aristotle and Aquinas, comment on Anselm, and gather the councils of Spain and the New World. Overwork broke his health, and he died of a stroke.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kilmore:
Kilmore is an Irish diocese covering almost all of Cavan and about half of Leitrim, roughly matching the old territory of Breffney. This entry starts with its first known bishop, St. Fedlemid, or Felim, of the early sixth century, patron of the diocese, whose feast falls on 9 August.

From 1136 to 1445 its bishops often styled themselves bishops of Breffney. Bishop Andrew MacBrady rebuilt St. Fedlemid's church on a larger scale, making it his cathedral in 1454 with Pope Nicholas V's approval. The great church, cill mor, gave the diocese its name. Penal times brought hardship. Richard Brady was chained three times and saw his Multifarnam refuge burned over his head in 1601. A later bishop, Andrew Campbell, made visitations disguised as a Highland piper.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-knights-of-th:
The Knights of the Holy Sepulchre have no assignable founder or founding date once legendary links to Godfrey of Bouillon, Charlemagne, or St. James are set aside. The body is really a lay confraternity that grew up around Christ's tomb, the shrine the crusades were launched to free.

Godfrey took no title but Defender of the Holy Sepulchre, and princes like Bohemond and Tancred called themselves its vassals. In a broad sense any crusader knighted in its defence could claim the name, and unknighted pilgrims longed to be dubbed there above all. Even after Jerusalem's Latin kingdom fell, pilgrims kept coming, and the Franciscans, given custody of the Holy Land, kept the knighting custom and supplied the order's first grand masters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lacordaire:
Jean-Baptiste Henri Lacordaire (1802-1861) was the nineteenth century's greatest pulpit orator. Born near Dijon, he lost his father at four, trained for the bar under his lawyer mother, and shone early before the great advocate Berryer.

Having lost his faith at school and regained it, he entered the Issy seminary in 1824 and was ordained in Paris in 1827. Chaplain work bored him, and a plan to serve New York's bishop collapsed with the July Revolution of 1830. Instead he joined Lamennais's paper L'Avenir, fighting for God and Freedom, with Montalembert beside him. Their platform spurned state protection and claimed religious liberty, free speech, and a free press as rights, not favours.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lahore:
Lahore is a diocese in northern India, in the province of Agra, covering the Punjab except two small parts, plus the native state of Bahawulpur. Christianity seems never to have touched the Punjab before the sixteenth century.

At Akbar's invitation, Jesuits from Goa visited his court at Fatehpur-Sikri and Lahore in 1579 to 1581. Jahangir let Portuguese Jesuits build a Lahore church with a salary, but Shah Jahan withdrew the pension and pulled the church down. Fragments survived for the traveller Thevenot in 1665, then vanished. The region passed through the Deccan and Great Mogul vicariates, the Tibet mission, and Agra, until the Punjab became its own vicariate in 1880 and a diocese in 1886.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgical-us:
Fire in worship is one of the oldest and most vivid symbols, since ancient peoples prized its heat, light, and power, and sometimes adored it as a god. Christians kept the symbol but denied it godhead, making fire stand for a God who lights and warms humankind.

The Easter Vigil gives the symbol its grandest form. Old fire is put out, and new fire is struck from flint and blessed. A three-branched candle is lit, and the deacon sings the Exultet. The entry also notes the Greek new-fire rite at Jerusalem, Irish night fires from the sixth century, and other local customs that grew around this one element.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-christo:
Louis Christophe Leon Juchault de La Moriciere was a French general, born at Nantes in 1806 and dead near Amiens in 1865. Schooled at the Ecole Polytechnique, he joined the Algiers expedition in 1830. He won a Zouave captaincy for gallantry, and stayed seventeen years in Africa.

He built the Bureau Arabe to mediate between French and Arabs, and tribes trusted him so far that he travelled unarmed, save a stick, earning the name Bou-Aroua, father with a stick. He rose to lieutenant-general, helped force Abd-el-Kader's surrender in 1847, then turned to politics, served as war minister, opposed Louis Napoleon, and suffered arrest and nine years of exile.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-frederi:
Louis Frederic Brugere was a French professor of apologetics and church history, born at Orleans in 1823 and dead at Issy in 1888. Schooled with the Christian Brothers and at Orleans and Paris seminaries, he taught classics and philosophy at La Chapelle-Saint-Mesmin for fifteen years.

Joining Saint-Sulpice in 1862, he taught apologetics at Paris and added church history in 1868. His teaching prized tact: the apologist, he held, must first meet the seeker's own doubts and hungers, then show how Christianity fits the soul's needs, before offering miracles as proof. Moral certainty, distinct from proof in physics or metaphysics, yet free of reasonable fear of error, was his key theme.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-joseph-:
Louis Joseph Le Loutre was a missionary to the Micmac Indians and vicar-general of Acadia, born in France about 1690 and dead there about 1770. Partisan writers painted him as the Acadians' tyrant and sworn foe of England, blaming him for blocking reconciliation.

Better historians call that portrait caricature. Le Loutre, forceful and loyal to France while allegiance hung in dispute, also befriended Englishmen in need, and joined Micmac war parties mainly to curb their cruelty. Quebec's bishop in 1757 called him irreproachable in ministry and in colonial affairs. Captured en route to France, he spent years jailed in Jersey before going home to die.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luminare:
A luminare is a light shaft pierced through the roof of a catacomb passage or chamber to let in light and air. These chimney-like openings cross a thick layer of soil, widen below, narrow toward the top, and are usually square, sometimes round, in section.

Often they drop to the second or lower level, passing through the first, and one shaft may serve two chambers or a chamber and gallery at once. Jerome, recalling boyhood visits to Rome's tombs about 360, tells how a little light from above broke the dark, and Prudentius later describes such apertures in detail. The entry traces their forms, their history, and their use in burial and worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mangalore:
Mangalore was a diocese on India's west coast, suffragan to Bombay. It covered all of South Canara and part of Malabar from Ponany to Mount Deli, reaching inland to the Ghats, forty to sixty miles. Its Catholic population stood at about 93,028. South Canara held four districts under rural deans, with thirty-three churches served by resident priests, plus chapels, while Malabar held churches at Cannanore, Tellicherry, and Calicut.

Franciscans pioneered the coast early in the sixteenth century, and migrants from Salcete near Goa swelled the Christians. Portuguese decline left Canara short of clergy in the seventeenth century, and Rome stepped in. Its prelates run from Bernardine of St Agnes in 1845 to Abundius Cavadini, bishop to 1910, with Nicholas Pagani first bishop in 1886. Its institutions included St Aloysius College with 1,000 pupils, St Joseph's Seminary with 43 students, and St Anne's High School with 449 girls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matteo-libera:
Matteo Liberatore was a philosopher, theologian, and writer, born at Salerno in 1810 and dead at Rome in 1892. He studied at Naples's Jesuit college in 1825, sought Society admission a year later, and entered novitiate on 9 October 1826. His long studies ended with unusual success, and he taught philosophy eleven years from 1837 until the 1848 Revolution drove him to Malta.

His chief glory lies in reviving Thomist scholastic philosophy. He began it by publishing his philosophy course in 1840 when prevailing teaching methods, even among Catholics, gave Catholic doctrine shaky foundations. For over half a century he championed truth in philosophy and theology and Church rights, fighting Rationalism, Ontologism, and Rosminianism. Sommervogel records over forty published works and more than nine hundred Civilta articles, reviews included. Many call him his day's greatest philosopher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-moore:
Michael Moore, also called Moor, was a priest, preacher, and professor born at Dublin in 1640 who died at Paris in 1726. He learned at Nantes and Paris, then taught philosophy and rhetoric at the College des Grassins. Back in Ireland he took orders in 1684, and Archbishop Russell made him Vicar-General of Dublin.

When the Revolution of 1688 drove James II from his realms, Tyrconnell kept Ireland loyal to him. Trinity College's provost fled, Jacobites took hold of the college, and its chapel turned into a powder store, one wing into a barrack, and another into a gaol. Moore, who served Tyrconnell as chaplain and confessor, was named provost by James in 1689, the only Catholic ever to hold the post. He kept the college from further pillage, eased the prisoners' lot, and, with the librarian Father McCarthy, kept the library safe from soldiers' torches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-miserere:
Psalm 50 opens in the Vulgate with Miserere. Psalms 55 and 56 open likewise, and each of the three goes on with mei, Deus, have mercy on me, O God. Latin psalm indexes tell them apart by their fourth word. That word is secundum in Psalm 50, quoniam in Psalm 55, and miserere in Psalm 56, so Psalm 50 appears as Miserere secundum.

So liturgically and musically pre-eminent is Psalm 50, however, that it is commonly called the Miserere without further qualification. Its title is among the best authenticated of all, being found in the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin texts. The psalm, David's penitential cry after his sin with Bathsheba, has inspired countless musical settings, above all Allegri's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mitre:
The mitre is a kind of folding cap worn by bishops and certain other dignitaries. It consists of two like parts, each stiffened by a lining and rising to a peak. They are sewn together at the sides but united above by a piece of material that can fold together. Two lappets trimmed with fringe hang down from the back. The mitre is, in theory, always supposed to be white.

The official Caeremoniale Romanum distinguishes three kinds: the mitra pretiosa, the auriphrygiata, and the simplex. The first two differ only in the richness of their ornamentation, while the simple mitre is of white silk or linen. The article traces the mitre's antiquity, origin, grant to dignitaries other than bishops, and the development of its shape, including the Greek rite's liturgical head-covering.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mysore:
Mysore is a diocese in India, suffragan to Pondicherry, covering the Mysore native state, the British provinces of Coorg and Collegal, part of Wynaad and the Ossoor taluk of Salem district. It is ringed by Madras, Poona, Goa, Mangalore, Coimbatore and Pondicherry. Its Catholic population numbers about 48,202, served by 65 priests, 53 European and 12 native, caring for 123 churches and chapels.

Brothers of the Immaculate Conception and of Saint Gabriel, Good Shepherd nuns, Little Sisters of the Poor, Sisters of Saint Joseph of Tarbes and native sisters assist them. Cathedral and bishop's residence stand at Bangalore. The diocese, under the Paris Foreign Missions, grew from seventeenth-century Canarese missions and a 1703 Telugu mission founded by two French Jesuits from Vellore, checked by a sultan's fanaticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nature:
Nature, from Latin natura, to be born, like Greek physis, to bring forth, refers to the production of things, and hence carries ideas of energy and activity. The entry reduces its meanings to two classes: the natures of individual beings, and nature in general. In an individual, nature sometimes means the collection of distinctive features, original or acquired, marking him off from others.

That sense is superficial. In philosophy and ordinary speech, nature properly means what is primitive and original, what a thing is at birth, as opposed to what is acquired or added from outside. Features like height or sociability manifest a man's nature but are not his nature. The line between natural and artificial cannot be drawn precisely. The entry then treats nature in general, its causes, and its theological uses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-navarre:
Navarre, formerly one territory, now belongs to two nations, Spain and France, as it lies south or north of the Western Pyrenees. Spanish Navarre borders French Navarre in the north, Huesca in the northeast, Saragossa in the east and southeast, Logrono in the south, and the Basque provinces in the west. It lies partly in the Pyrenees mountains and partly on the Ebro banks, with Basques in the mountains and Spaniards in the south.

It counts 269 communes in five districts, Pamplona, Aoiz, Estella, Tafalla and Tudela, with Pamplona as capital. French, or Lower, Navarre belongs to the Basses-Pyrenees department, around Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port on the Nive. The two divisions share a history until 1512, when Spanish Navarre was conquered, and the entry follows both kingdoms, their kings, fueros, and church life through union with France and Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-hampshire:
New Hampshire, the most northerly of the thirteen original American states, lies between 70 and 72 degrees west and 42 to 45 degrees north. It covers 9,305 square miles, with a 1910 census population of 430,572. It borders Massachusetts in the south, the Atlantic for about eighteen miles, Maine in the east, Quebec in the north, and Vermont in the west along the Connecticut River.

The entry traces the state's geography, rivers and mountains, its settlement, colonial government, and growth into a manufacturing and farming state. It surveys its towns, schools, and religious life, with particular attention to the Catholic Church. That attention covers its early missions, the Diocese of Manchester, and its parishes, priests and religious orders. It also covers its schools and charitable institutions, and the Catholic population's share of the state's people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ointment-in-s:
Ointment in Scripture means perfumed oil used to anoint body, guest, king, and corpse from remote antiquity. The holy oil of unction, minutely prescribed in Exodus, blends olive oil with myrrh, cinnamon, calamus, and cassia, and unauthorized making or use of it counted as sacrilege.

Luke distinguishes plain oil for the head from ointment for the feet, myrrh-rich preparations dressed the dead, and spikenard, a costly unguent, anointed Jesus at Bethany. The entry follows those uses through law, prophecy, and Gospel scenes to their sacred meanings. Identical preparations, rich in myrrh, anointed both the living subject and the dead body.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-sarsf:
Patrick Sarsfield Gilmore was a bandmaster born at Ballygar in Galway on 25 December 1829 and dead at Saint Louis on 24 September 1892, a kinsman of Daniel O'Connell. Reaching Boston in 1848, he led the Suffolk, Boston Brigade, and Salem bands in turn, and in 1858 founded Gilmore's Band, later America's leading military and concert band. With war he enlisted with the 24th Massachusetts Volunteers under Burnside in South Carolina.

After bands were discharged from the field, Governor Andrews gave Gilmore their reorganisation, and General Banks made him bandmaster general. For services at Louisiana Governor Hahn's inauguration, army, navy, and New Orleans civic leaders feted him with a silver goblet holding five hundred gold pieces. To mark national peace he staged Boston's giant National and International Peace Jubilees of 1869 and 1872, among the largest popular festivals in musical history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-maximili:
Paul Maximilien Emile Littre was a French lexicographer and philosopher born at Paris on 1 February 1801 and dead there on 2 June 1881. Schooled at Louis-le-Grand, he graduated with honours and served as secretary to Count Daru. He then studied medicine, quitting near his degree when his father's death forced him to support his mother by teaching Greek and Latin. Medical interests stayed with him lifelong.

Early works treated cholera and great epidemics, and with Dezeimeris he founded the medical journal L'Experience in 1837. He translated Pliny's Natural History, Mueller's physiology handbook, and Nysten's medicine dictionary, and from 1839 to 1861 published his Hippocrates translation, winning election to the Academy of Inscriptions in 1839. Politics and positivist philosophy followed, and his great French dictionary, built on historical principles, crowns his later years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-o-sull:
Philip O'Sullivan Beare was an Irish historian in Spanish exile, born about 1590. His father was Dermot O'Sullivan, and his uncle was Donal O'Sullivan Beare of Dunboy. Spain received him in 1602, and he was schooled at Compostella by Vendamma and the Irish Jesuit Father Synnott. He served in the Spanish army, and his pen served Ireland's memory.

In 1621 he published his Catholic History of Ireland, a work the entry calls not always reliable but valuable for the Irish wars of his own day. He also produced a Life of St. Patrick, answered Gerald Barry, and replied to Archbishop Ussher's attack on his History. This short Catholic Encyclopedia entry gathers a life spent between sword and history book, ending with his death in Spain in 1660.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippe-de-l:
Philippe de La Hire was a French mathematician, astronomer, physicist, naturalist, and painter, born at Paris in 1640. Fontenelle called him an academy in himself. His father Laurent was a distinguished artist, and Philippe first studied painting at Rome in 1660 for his health, then turned on his return to classics and science. In mathematics he learned from Desargues as pupil and fellow investigator.

Elected to the Academy of Sciences in 1678, he surveyed Brittany, Guienne, Calais, Dunkirk, and Provence for a government map from 1679. He extended the Paris meridian northward in 1683 and studied the Eure's flow for Versailles's water supply. He taught at the Collège de France from 1682 and at the Academy of Architecture. His chief work lay in pure geometry, continuing Desargues and Pascal with a new way of generating conics. He died at Paris in 1718.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-berche:
Pierre Bercheure, also called Bersuire, was a learned French Benedictine, born at St. Pierre du Chemin in 1290. He joined the order at Maillezais, spent twelve years at Avignon with Cardinal Peter de Pratis, and became prior of St. Eligius at Paris in 1354. An eloquent preacher and voluminous homiletic writer, he built his fame on preachers' tools.

His Repertorium morale, a biblico-moral dictionary, arranged Scripture's chief words alphabetically with moral reflections. It appeared before 1355 and was printed again and again, from Cologne in 1477 to Antwerp in 1609, with a French version in 1584. His Reductorium morale covered all Scripture's books in thirty-four volumes, and he made the earliest French translation of Livy about 1350 for King John the Good. Collected editions ran from Lyons in 1520 to Cologne in 1669. He died at Paris in 1362.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-brugie:
Pierre Brugière was a French Jansenist priest and juror, born at Thiers in 1730. Chaplain of the Ursulines and canon at home, he lost his place for refusing the formula accepting the bull Unigenitus, spent twelve years with St. Roch's community in Paris, and broke with it over his strongly Jansenist book on devotion to the Sacred Heart in 1777. The Revolution he welcomed with enthusiasm and reform pamphlets.

Taking the Constitutional Oath on 9 January 1791, he became heart and soul of the Constitutional Church, curé of St. Paul's, defending the civil constitution against bishops and pope. Yet he fiercely condemned priestly marriage, attacked its advocates, and rebuked retracting jurors, saying Mass in French and founding a society to protect the dying Constitutional Church even after the 1801 Concordat. Imprisoned by the revolutionary tribunal, he wrote to parishioners from prison. He died at Paris in 1803.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-dore:
Pierre Doré, called Auratus, was a French Dominican controversialist, born at Orléans about 1500. He entered the order in 1514 and took his degrees at Paris in 1532 after a brilliant examination. Though elected prior at Blois in 1545, he kept preaching through the provinces.

He wrote thirty-five ascetico-theological works, some thought redactions of his sermons. Chief among them stands Les voies du Paradis, printed twice at Lyons in 1538 and again at Paris, Lyons, and Rome. His Paradoxa from St. Paul refuted the Huguenots, then he turned to ascetical commentaries on the Psalms. A Latin ode for Henry II's Paris entry in 1548 won him preaching at court and the king's ear as confessor. His celebrated defence of the Eucharist came out in 1549, with further apologies in 1551, a three-volume defence of the faith, and two works on justification closing his career. He died at Paris in 1559.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pillar-of-clo:
The Pillar of Cloud, also called the Pillar of Fire, was the sign of God's presence that guided the Israelites through the desert. It first appeared on the march from Succoth to Etham as a column, bright by night. It vanished when the people reached the borders of Canaan.

During camp it rested over the tabernacle, the tent-shrine of the covenant. When it lifted, the people broke camp, and it led the march, halting where they were to pitch tents. At the Red Sea it stood between Israel and Egypt, bright on one side and dark on the other. Saint Paul reads it as a type, or foreshadowing, of baptism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plenary-counc:
The Plenary Councils of Baltimore were the national synods that governed the Catholic Church in the United States once several provinces had replaced the single province of Baltimore. After the Seventh Provincial Council asked Rome for a plenary synod, Archbishop Kenrick of Baltimore was appointed apostolic delegate to convene and preside.

The First Plenary Council opened on 9 May 1852 with six archbishops and thirty-five suffragan bishops, plus bishops from Monterey and Toronto, and abbots and superiors of the great orders. Its decrees bound American dioceses to the Roman Ritual and Baltimore Ceremonial, forbade foreign rites, and regulated burials and episcopal residence. It also urged bishops to consult clergy advisers monthly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polish-litera:
Polish Literature surveys the writing of Poland by historical periods, from medieval Latin chroniclers to the vernacular flowering of the sixteenth century. Before Christianity in 965 few traces survive, and schools founded by clergy were wrecked by invasion until Casimir the Great founded the academy that became the University of Cracow in 1400.

Chroniclers such as Gallus, Kadlubek, and Dlugosz wrote in Latin, and even Renaissance humanists like Ostrorog kept to Latin. Polish books, translations or paraphrases, date from 1520, and under Italian influence the language matured. In the second period, 1548 to 1600, Catholic writers like Wujek, who translated the Bible, and Hosius faced Protestant rivals, while Kochanowski's poetry set a standard only Mickiewicz would surpass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pools-in-scri:
Pools in Scripture explains how the English Bible's word pool stands for three Hebrew words for water storage. Agam means a pond of stagnant water, such as sheets left by the Nile flood. Miqveh means a gathering of waters, a place where streams collect, usually behind a dam across a valley. Berekah means a wholly artificial reservoir cut from rock and lined with masonry against leaking.

Such care mattered in lands dry for most of the year, and the entry argues that most biblical pools were artificial, all being called berekah in Hebrew. It then describes the pools around Jerusalem. The Pool of Siloe was built by Hezekiah between two walls and fed by tunnel from Gihon. The Pool of Bethsaida's exact site scholars still dispute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-port-alegre:
Porto Alegre, in the usage of this entry Portalegren, covers southern Minas Geraes and part of São Paulo in Brazil. It became a bishopric by brief of 4 August 1900, with its see in the city of Porto Alegre, Minas Geraes. Its first bishop was Mgr G. Bathista Correa Nery, followed by Mgr Antonio Augusto de Assis.

The diocese proper counts sixty-two parishes, one hundred and twenty secular priests, six regular priests, and eight hundred thousand Catholics. A theological seminary founded in August 1902 trains future clergy. The Diocesan College of San José, a high school founded in 1899, stands beside it. Diocesan Missionaries of the Heart of Mary, six priests founded in 1902, work for converts. The monthly Mensageiro Ecclesiastico, edited by Father Octavia Chagas de Miranda, serves as the diocese's organ, with O Estudo from San José College beside it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-portalegre:
Portalegre, a Lisbon suffragan diocese, was set up by Julius III in 1550. Julian d'Alva, a Spaniard, served as first bishop, moving to Miranda in 1557. De Noronha followed in July 1560 and rose to Placencia in 1581. Frei Amador Arraes, author of a celebrated Dialogues, resigned in 1582 and retired to his order's Coimbra college until death.

Lopo Soares de Albergaria and Manoel de Gouveia died before their confirming bulls arrived. Diego Conra took the see in 1598 and died on 9 October 1614; he was Ceuta's bishop and nephew of Bartholomew of the Martyrs. Among seventeenth-century bishops was the Englishman Ricardo Russell, who took possession in September 1671 and later left for Vizeu. Antonio Mutinho, transferred from Caboverde in 1909, is the present bishop. The diocese counts 197,343 Catholics, 16 Protestants, 148 parishes, 286 priests, and 447 churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-porto-alegre:
Porto Alegre, capital and chief port of Rio Grande do Sul in eastern Brazil, stands at the north end of Lagoa dos Patos on the Rio Guahyba estuary. Azorean immigrants founded it in 1742 as Porto dos Cazaes. Governor José Marcellino de Figuereido made it his residence in 1770, and it took its present name in 1773.

It is the state's chief commercial centre, with a harbour for vessels up to ten feet draught. Stock-raising, first organized by seventeenth-century Jesuit missionaries, leads state industry. The municipio spans 931 square miles, and the latest census gives the city 73,574 people, mostly German and Italian. Winters are cool and bracing, summers intensely hot, and yearly rainfall tops thirty inches. The Catholic Deutsches Volksblatt is among its newspapers. Jesuits first brought Christianity in the early seventeenth century, after São Paulo slave hunters drove them from Upper Paraná.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-portuguese-li:
Portuguese grew from the rustic Latin spoken in lands once part of the Roman Empire. In form and sentence shape it is Latin remade from within, with no direct help from a foreign tongue. Its words took in Germanic and Arabic terms. In the Renaissance, book language and common speech drifted apart, and the split lasted until the nineteenth century. Then Romantic writers went back to folk poetry and daily speech, and men like Almeida Garrett and Camillo Castello Branco made the book language national again.

Early verse began at home, but the first book work came from Provence. King Alfonso III, schooled in France, quickened it, and his age left the Cancioneiro de Ajuda, the oldest store of peninsular verse. Church speech peaked in the seventeenth century, when the pulpit stood in place of the press. The recluse Manuel Bernardes wrote calmer, sweeter prose.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-premontre:
Prémontré lies about twelve miles west of Laon, in the Aisne, France, and was founded by St Norbert. The gift charter calls the place Praemonstratus, or pratum monstratum, Pré-montré, likely from a clearing in the forest, though lore reads it as a place foreshown.

Old lore says the Bishop of Laon and St Norbert came to Prémontré about mid January. The bishop gave Norbert the white habit on 25 January, feast of the Conversion of St Paul. After Liège's 1131 Council, Innocent II and St Norbert reached Laon and stayed with Bishop Bartholomew. Their Prémontré visit found about five hundred religious keeping their duties under Abbot Hugh of Fosse: priests, clerics, and lay brothers. A general chapter in 1141 bade nuns' houses stand at least a league from men's abbeys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-provincial-co:
The provincial councils of Baltimore hold a unique place in American Catholic history. The early ones legislated for nearly the whole young republic. They set the pattern for every later provincial council in the country. This encyclopedia entry picks out the decrees that show the American church's special needs in its formative years. Ten councils met between 1829 and 1849. Their full decrees are printed in the Collectio Lacensis.

The First Council of 1829 gathered one archbishop and four bishops. Its decrees touched baptismal ceremonies for converts already validly baptized, and the age for confirmation. By the Fifth Council in 1843, one archbishop and sixteen bishops sat together. They barred lay orations in churches, bound pastors to residence, and forbade priests to borrow for church purposes without the bishop's written leave. Together the councils sketch a church learning to govern itself on a continental scale.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-remigius-of-a:
Remigius of Auxerre, or Remi, was a Benedictine monk born about the middle of the ninth century who died in 908. He studied under Dunchad of Reims, the Irish teacher and author of a treatise on astronomy, and under Eric, or Heirich, himself a disciple of Eriugena. He taught at Saint-Germain in Auxerre, in Paris, and at Reims.

His writings include glossaries and marginal commentaries on the Bible, on Priscian's grammar, on Boethius's Opuscula Sacra, and on Martianus Capella's De Nuptiis, besides a theological treatise, Ennarationes in Psalmos. As a teacher he wrestled with universals, seeking a compromise between Eriugena's extreme Realism and his own teacher Eric's Anti-Realism. He probed the origin of the universe with a Christian reading of its ancient passages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-russian-langu:
Russian is a Slav language of the Indo-European family. The prehistoric dispersion of Slav tribes formed various Slav dialects. Slav dialects divide into South-Eastern and Western. To the former, culminating in Bulgarian, belong the three Russian dialects of Great, Little, and White Russia. Russian has many affinities with Bulgarian and Servian.

Lack of documents makes early Russia's language hard to define precisely. Sreznevski and Lavroff held the two nearly identical, differing in turns of expression rather than grammar. Before the thirteenth century the literary, church, and administrative language was one. In the fourteenth century church language began to differ from literary language. Russian then changed locally into Kieff, Novgorod, Vladimir, and Moscow dialects. Vareghi, Greeks, Tatars, Lithuanians, and Poles left traces on the language, and under Peter the Great many words came from German, French, and English.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-barthol:
The St Bartholomew's Day Massacre, whose victims were Protestants, occurred in Paris on 24 August 1572, the feast of St Bartholomew, and in France's provinces during ensuing weeks. It has been the subject of knotty historical disputes. First debated was whether the French Court premeditated it: Sismondi, Mackintosh, and Bordier held it had, Ranke, Martin, White, Loiseleur, La Ferriere, and Vacandard held it had not. Second debated was Rome's responsibility for the outrage.

At present only a few Protestant historians claim the Holy See was the French Court's accomplice. Solving the question means separating the attack on Coligny on 22 August, and his murder that night of 23-24 August, from the general massacre. The idea of summarily executing Protestant leaders had long existed in Catherine de' Medici's mind. Widow of Henry II and mother of three kings, she shared it with her sons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-germain:
Germain of Auxerre, born about 380 and dead at Ravenna on 31 July 448, came from one of the noblest families of Gaul. He was educated at Arles, Lyons, and Rome, where he studied eloquence and civil law. After pleading before the prefect's tribunal, he married Eustachia, a court lady. The emperor sent him back to Gaul as one of six dukes over the Gallic provinces. He lived at Auxerre in comfort until a clash with Bishop Amator over hunting trophies hung on a tree used in pagan worship.

Amator cut the tree down, then, fearing Germain's anger, had him tonsured against his will and made a deacon as his destined successor. The change transformed Germain, who gave his goods to the poor, practised austerity, and was chosen bishop in 418 after Amator's death. He built a monastery for Saints Cosmas and Damian on the Yonne and governed his diocese with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sainte-anne-d:
Sainte Anne de Beaupré, a parish church and shrine in Canada, carries a devotion to Saint Anne that sailed with the first settlers of New France. The first houses on the Beaupré hillside date from 1650, and the settlers soon planned a chapel, with Etienne Lessard giving the land. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia tells how a small chapel became a great pilgrimage goal.

On 13 March 1658 Father Vignal chose the site and blessed the foundations, and that very day Louis Guimont, crippled by rheumatism, laid three stones and rose suddenly cured. That first reported miracle opened two and a half centuries of pilgrimages from across North America. An old church begun in 1676 served until 1876, when the present church opened, and the entry follows the shrine's steady growth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salve-mundi-s:
Salve Mundi Salutare is a poem honouring the members of Christ on the Cross, limb by limb, whose authorship has been argued for centuries. A fifteenth-century manuscript gives it to Bonaventure, and Daniel thought that inspired singer of the Cross could well have written it, while the commonest ascription is to Bernard. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia weighs manuscripts against fame.

Mabillon placed the hymn among Bernard's spurious works, and Trench thought it was judged away from him on slight grounds, though no manuscript predates the fourteenth century and Bernard died in 1153. Mone judged it French in origin, and Hauréau, finding it in only three fifteenth-century manuscripts, two in Paris and one at Grenoble, doubted Bernard wrote it at all. Readers get a model of how hymn authorship is tested.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-samaritan-lan:
Samaritan language and literature form the subject of this scholarly entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, which traces a small community's tongue from Hebrew through Aramaic to Arabic. Hebrew stayed the sacred language of the Pentateuch, pronounced by tradition without vowels or written marks, and differing notably from the Masoretic pronunciation fixed by Jewish scholars.

From the last centuries before Christ into the early Arab age, Samaritans spoke a western Aramaic dialect peculiar to Palestine, and Islamic rule later brought Arabic into daily use. Petermann's 1868 study of modern Samaritan Hebrew pronunciation supplies much of the evidence. The entry then surveys Samaritan writings, showing how a tiny people kept an ancient text alive across changing empires and languages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-kil:
Kildare, Irish Cill-Dara, Church of the Oak, began as Druim Criaidh, Ridge of Clay, on the Liffey plain. Under a stately oak loved by Brigid, the foundress laid the base of what became a monastic city. Her entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a woman organiser of rare talent.

Brigid's little oratory soon grew into a great double house, one part for women and one for men. Crowds flocked from far and near on pilgrimage or to hear heavenly wisdom from the Mary of the Gael. Seeing that such a house needed a bishop to consecrate churches and ordain ministers, she chose a famous anchorite to aid her rule as bishop. Famed for virtues and miracles, he ensured that nothing should be lacking for proper order. The entry traces Kildare's school and shrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-lis:
Lismore's school, as Armagh led the north and Clonmacnoise the centre, led the south of Ireland. Carthach the Younger founded it in 635 on a picturesque slope above the Blackwater's southern bank. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia opens with an unjust eviction that became a founding.

Carthach had spent nearly forty years at Rahan monastery on Meath's southern edge, in modern King's County, a house he founded and hoped would hold his grave. But Meath's clerics and chiefs, jealous of a Munster stranger's great house in their land, persuaded Prince Blathmac to expel the aged man. Annalists call the eviction most unjust and cruel, yet under God's guidance it led to Lismore on the Avonmore's fair margin, where a celebrated school soon flourished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scripture:
Scripture is one of several names for the inspired writings making up the Old and New Testaments. Its long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia starts with the word itself. Latin scriptura appears in the Vulgate sometimes in the general sense of writing, as when God's writing was graven on the tables. Sometimes it means a private or public document, a catalogue, or a portion of Scripture.

The writer of Chronicles refers to the Law's prescriptions with the formula as it is written, rendered by the Septuagint as according to Scripture. That phrase recurs in Ezra and Nehemiah, marking the start of the later appeal to Scripture as authority. The entry then treats canon, inspiration, versions, and interpretation, giving a full Catholic account of the Bible as a book and as an authority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sculpture:
Sculpture, in the widest sense, is the art of showing in bodily form people, animals, and other things in stone, bronze, ivory, clay, and like materials, whether real or imagined. More exactly, it is the art of showing beauty in bodily form through figures wholly or partly in the round. Its long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia defines an art of form alone.

Unlike painting, which works by illusion on a flat coloured surface, sculpture imitates bodies in full, achieving its effect through form itself, called plastic beauty. It therefore leaves out landscape, plants, and light and shade, painting's great effects. Its favourite subject, against painting's crowds, is the single figure. The entry follows sculpture from antiquity through Christian ages to modern schools, with its materials and techniques.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shire:
Shire, a vicariate apostolic in the Nyassaland Protectorate of Africa, takes its name from the River Shire, which carries Lake Nyassa's waters to the Zambezi. The protectorate, once called British Central Africa, stretches about 520 miles long and covers 43,608 square miles. At most 600 white people live there, beside millions of black inhabitants. The White Fathers evangelize the five northern districts west of the lake, while Shire covers the eight districts south of it.

Propaganda entrusted the territory to the missionaries of the Society of Mary, founded by Louis Grignion de Montfort. On 28 June 1901 the first three missionaries reached Blantyre, and on 25 July they opened their first mission in Angoniland. The mission grew fast, the entry says, despite strong competition. Its peoples are the Angouis, Yaos, and Angourous, three distinct tribes, and Catholic teaching spread among them by degrees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-solimoes-supe:
Solimoes Superiore was a newly erected apostolic prefecture in the Brazilian state of Amazonas, carved out of the diocese of Manaos by a decree of May 1910. This entry maps a little-explored territory between the left bank of the Amazon and the River Jacura, crossed by countless waterways and natural canals, and still largely untouched by preaching.

Entrusted to the Capuchin Fathers, the mission belonged to a wider effort by the Holy See to reach the thinly settled regions along the Amazon's tributaries. The entry keeps its focus on geography and mission organization rather than settled history. And it captures a frontier Church at the moment it first tried to plant itself in a vast, river-cut land.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spanish-ameri:
Spanish-American literature means the writing of the Spanish-speaking peoples of Mexico, Central America, Cuba. And South America, Brazil and the Guianas excepted. And this long survey traces it from colony to republic. Its methods and ideals, the entry argues, never broke sharply from Spain's, since colonies and republics alike kept the same race, religion, and speech despite political bitterness.

Unlike North America's settlers, Latin colonists made no organized attempt to wipe out the native peoples, who survive in millions and still keep their languages in places. The survey moves country by country through poets, historians, and novelists, giving readers a map of a literature that stayed Spanish in tongue while becoming American in subject.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spanish-langu:
Spanish, a Romance tongue descended from Latin, is the speech of most of the Iberian peninsula and of much of the Americas. And this long entry follows both the language and its literature Portuguese holds the west of the peninsula, Basque the Pyrenees. And Catalan the east, while Spanish itself, carried overseas by colonization, reached over forty million speakers in South and Central America, Mexico, Cuba, and Puerto Rico.

In the Philippines it long served as the official language without displacing native dialects, since Catholic missionaries learned the local tongues to teach the faith. The entry then turns to literature, from medieval beginnings to modern writers, giving readers the full arc of a world language and the books written in it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spire:
A spire is the tapering crown of a steeple or tower, conical, pyramidal, octagonal, or hexagonal in plan, growing from the cornice and often pierced with ornamental openings. This entry, from the Anglo-Saxon spir, a stalk or shoot, explains how builders handled the junction: on the Continent steeple and spire merged into one. While in England the join was frankly masked behind a parapet or battlements.

Properly belonging to Pointed, or Gothic, architecture, spires took varied forms from the twelfth century and became the standard finish of church steeples from the thirteenth to the sixteenth. Sometimes an open lantern stood between tower and spire, and ribs, where present, were enriched with crockets, details the entry sets out for readers of church buildings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-benedict-j:
St. Benedict Joseph Labre was born on 26 March 1748 at Amettes in the diocese of Boulogne in France. He died in Rome on 16 April 1783. This entry follows the eldest of fifteen children. His parents, Jean-Baptiste Labre and Anne-Barbe Grandsire, belonged to the middle class, and so could give their many children considerable opportunities for education. His early training he received in his native village, in a school run by the parish vicar.

The account of this period in the life written by his confessor Marconi agrees with the one compiled from the official processes of his beatification. Both stress that he showed a seriousness of thought and demeanour far beyond his years. Even at that tender age he showed a marked love for mortification, with an aversion to ordinary childish amusements. From the very dawning of reason he seems to have had the liveliest horror of sin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bonaventur:
St. Bonaventure was Doctor of the Church, cardinal-bishop of Albano, and minister general of the Friars Minor. This entry follows a man born at Bagnorea near Viterbo in 1221 and dead at Lyons on 15 July 1274. Of his parents, only the names survive: Giovanni di Fidanza and Maria Ritella. How his baptismal name of John became Bonaventure is not clear.

Some trace the latter name to St. Francis's exclamation, O buona ventura, when the infant Bonaventure was brought to him to be cured of a dangerous illness. That derivation is highly improbable, resting on a late fifteenth-century legend. Bonaventure himself says that as a child he was preserved from death through St. Francis's intercession, but there is no evidence that this cure took place during Francis's lifetime, or that the name came from any prophetical words of Francis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-claude-de-:
St. Claude de la Colombière, missionary and ascetical writer, was born in 1641 to noble parents at Saint-Symphorien-d'Ozon, between Lyons and Vienne. He died at Paray-le-Monial on 15 February 1682. This entry follows a man who entered the Society of Jesus in 1659. After fifteen years of religious life he vowed — to attain the utmost possible perfection — to observe his order's rule and constitutions faithfully, under penalty of sin.

Those who lived with him testified that he kept this vow with great exactitude. In 1674 he was made superior at the Paray-le-Monial Jesuit house, where he became spiritual director of Blessed Margaret Mary. Thereafter he was a zealous apostle of Sacred Heart devotion. In 1676 he went to England as preacher to the Duchess of York, later Queen of Great Britain. Even in the Court of St. James he lived as a religious.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-colman-bis:
St. Colman, bishop of Dromore, was born in Dalaradia about 450, and his date of death is uncertain. His feast is celebrated 7 June. This entry follows the founder of the See of Dromore, its patron and presiding bishop. He studied at Noendrum, Mahee Island, under St. Mochae or Coelan, among St. Patrick's earliest disciples.

Many stories tell of his edifying life at Noendrum and the miracles he worked there. Colman went to Emly's great school about 470 or 475 to perfect his knowledge of the Scriptures, remaining some years. In time he went back to Mahee Island to see his old master, St. Mochae, staying under his guidance long as the school's assistant. St. Finian of Movilla was among his many Mahee Island pupils in the first quarter of the sixth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-fiacre:
Fiacre, Irish abbot who died in 670, carried his hermit's solitude from Kilkenny to the forests of Meaux. Ordained priest, he withdrew to a hermitage on the Nore, where Kilfiachra still keeps his name, but disciples crowded him. Seeking deeper quiet, he reached Meaux in 628, where Bishop Faro, grateful for Columbanus's blessings on his house, granted him land at Brogillum. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 18 August 670.

There Fiacre raised an oratory to Mary, a hospice for strangers, and his own cell, living in prayer, fast, vigil, and garden labour. Disciples gathered again into a monastery. Legend says Faro allowed him all the land he could ring in one day, a tale the entry reports as legend. The entry follows a hermit whose solitude kept filling with guests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-jean-gabri:
Jean-Gabriel Perboyre, Vincentian martyr of China, went from a Cahors farm family to a Chinese prison. Born at Puech on 6 January 1802, one of eight children of Pierre Perboyre and Marie Rigal, he was his companions' model of piety in childhood. Companion to a younger brother at Montauban's preparatory seminary, he felt the call to priesthood, won his father's consent, and entered the Vincentian novitiate in December 1818. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his martyrdom at Ou-Tchang-Fou to 11 September 1840.

On Holy Innocents' day 1820 he made the Vincentians' four vows. Ordained on 23 September 1825 by Bishop Dubourg of New Orleans in the Sisters of Charity chapel, he said his first Mass next day. Sent to Saint-Flour to teach dogmatic theology, he became superior of its preparatory seminary two years later. Sanctity and marvellous success marked him there, before China claimed him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-thomas-mor:
Thomas More, knight, Lord Chancellor, author, and martyr, died on Tower Hill for refusing Henry VIII's supremacy. Born in London on 7 February 1477 or 1478, only surviving son of Judge John More and Agnes Graunger, he was schooled at St Anthony's in Threadneedle Street. At thirteen he entered Cardinal Morton's household, whose notice sent him to Oxford about 1492.

There he befriended Grocyn and Linacre and mastered Greek by an instinct of genius. Called to the bar, he rose to Parliament, to Henry's council, and to the chancellorship in 1529. He wrote Utopia, a vision of an ideal commonwealth, and works defending the Church. Resigning in 1532, he refused the oath of succession and was beheaded on 6 July 1535.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stoning-in-sc:
In a rocky land, stones lay ready to hand, and this short entry explains how stoning grew from mob violence into a lawful penalty in biblical Israel. It notes early cases where thrown stones showed hatred or murderous intent, then traces the Law's regulation of the practice as capital punishment.

Deuteronomy sets the pattern: the case heard at the city gate, guilt proved by two or three witnesses, and the witnesses casting the first stones. Eighteen offences in the Pentateuch carried this penalty, from Sabbath breaking to blasphemy, though murder alone drew it under every code. Stephen, the first Christian martyr, died by stoning outside Jerusalem, as Acts records.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syriac-langua:
Syriac is an important branch of Aramaic, the Semitic group that served as official language from Asia Minor to Persia under Alexander. Aramaic split into a western dialect of Palestine and Syria and an eastern dialect of Babylonia and Upper Mesopotamia, and literary Syriac sprang from the eastern one. Edessa, capital of Osrhoene, became its religious and intellectual centre.

Under Christianity the dialect grew into the liturgical and literary tongue of churches from the Mediterranean to central Persia, its supple syntax suiting new ideas better than Greek. After the Monophysite schism Greek faded, and the mid-fifth to late seventh centuries formed Syriac literature's brightest age. Arab conquest then imposed Arabic, though Syriac lived on as a learned tongue, preserving lost Greek works in translation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-byzantine:
Eastern Rome's long survival after the empire split in two is surveyed here on a grand scale. Byzantium, or Constantinople, capital of Constantine's successors, gives the empire its name. Two divisions organise the account: Byzantine civilisation first, then dynastic history in six chronological heads.

At a distance the civilisation looks unified, but closer inspection reveals local and national variety and distinct periods of growth. Peoples of the East, Finnic-Ugrians, and Slavs pressed its borders, some as dangerous neighbours, others as converts and trading partners. Law, art, liturgy, and court life all receive treatment before emperors and dynasties take the stage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-theatre:
Stage plays, banned outright by early Christian writers, pose the puzzle at this entry's heart. Greek tragedy and comedies of Plautus and Terence survive in decent form, yet Fathers of East and West condemned all drama in the severest terms. Popular fare under the Empire, not literary drama, explains the ban: mimes most audiences loved were grossly indecent and poisonous to virtue.

Aristophanes alone shows how lax public opinion ran, even in cultured pagan ages, while Roman law branded actors with infamia, marking their degradation. Tragedies and better comedies lived as literature, read aloud among friends rather than staged. Mimus, pantomime, and church judgment through the centuries complete a frank history of faith and the stage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-eyre:
Thomas Eyre, first president of Ushaw College, was born at Glossop in 1748 and died at Ushaw in 1810. Fourth son of Nathaniel Eyre, he arrived at Esquerchin near Douai in 1758 with his brothers and studied there with credit. After ordination he stayed on as prefect and teacher of rhetoric and poetry. In 1775 he returned to England for the Stella mission near Newcastle.

There he edited the works of Gother and gathered materials to continue Dodd's Church History. In 1794 Bishop Gibson put him in charge of the northern students expelled from Douai, whom he moved from Tudhoe to Pontop Hall and then to Crook Hall, where he became president. In 1803 the college moved to the new Ushaw estate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-linacr:
Thomas Linacre, physician and clergyman, founded the Royal College of Physicians in London. Born at Canterbury about 1460 to poor and obscure parents, he was schooled at Christ Church monastery under William Selling, a pioneer of the new learning. Selling took him to All Souls, Oxford, about 1480, and then to Rome, where Lorenzo de' Medici welcomed him as a fellow student of his sons.

In Italy Linacre studied Latin under Politian, Greek under Chalcondylas, and medicine at Vicenza and Padua. Back in England he became physician to Henry VIII and attendant to Wolsey, Warham and other great men, while counting More, Erasmus and Colet among his friends. Ordained late in life, he gave his wealth to endow medical lectures and the college.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-moore:
Thomas Moore, poet and biographer, was born at Dublin in 1779 and died at Devizes, England, in 1852. His father was a grocer, later barrack-master at Dublin, and his mother trained him for society life. At Trinity College, Dublin, from fifteen, he mixed with Robert Emmet's circle, then went to London in 1799 to study law, which he soon abandoned for letters.

His Irish Melodies, begun in 1807, set new words to old national airs and won him the title he prized most, poet of the people of Ireland. Lalla Rookh followed, and his Life of Byron in 1830 became one of the most popular biographies ever written, though its portrait is not wholly true. Moore's songs kept their place in Irish homes long after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-of-can:
Thomas of Cantimpre, medieval writer, preacher and theologian, was born near Brussels in 1201 and died in 1272. His schooling began at Liege at five, where he spent eleven years on the trivium and quadrivium, the seven liberal arts. At sixteen he joined the Canons Regular at Cantimpre, and after fifteen years there he entered the Dominicans at Louvain in 1232.

He studied under Albert the Great at Cologne for four years, then at the Dominican house of St. James in Paris. Returning to Louvain in 1240, he taught philosophy and theology with distinction and preached across Brabant, Germany, Belgium and France, earning the title Preacher General. Seven works on philosophy, theology and saints' lives are ascribed to him, chief among them his book on the nature of things.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tonsure:
Tonsure, from the Latin tondere, meaning to shear, is the rite by which a baptized and confirmed Christian enters the clerical state. The candidate's hair is cut and he is vested in a surplice, sharing the rights and duties of clerics. Tonsure itself is not an ordination, nor a true order, but a setting apart for divine service.

The rite was unknown in the primitive church during persecution, and Jerome disapproved of clerics shaving their heads, since Greeks and Romans took a shaved head as a slave's mark. Monks adopted it for that very reason, and by the late fifth or early sixth century it passed to the secular clergy. In the Latin church it became a separate ceremony about the end of the seventh century. It is given by the candidate's bishop, with no set age, but only to one who knows the faith and can read and write.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-turkish-empir:
This long reference entry surveys the Ottoman realm near the start of the twentieth century. At that time it still stretched across parts of Europe, Asia, and Africa. It held about twenty-five million people, and its harbours and roads joined three continents. The survey treats the empire as a patchwork of peoples, faiths, and local rulers under the sultan at Constantinople.

Region by region, the account moves from the Balkans and Anatolia through Syria, Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Arabia. It notes leading cities, railways, trade, crops, and peoples in each part. It then turns to rule and law, schools, and the many Christian churches and missions under Ottoman power. Readers seeking a compact survey of the empire just before the First World War will find it gathered here.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-types-in-scri:
Types in Scripture are persons, things, or events in the Old Testament that point forward to something later in the New. The entry starts from the Greek word typos, which Scripture uses for a mark or print, a pattern to be copied, and a model of conduct. It argues that a true type rests on a likeness planned by God, not on chance resemblance. It also sets out how such foreshadowing differs from a mere illustration or moral example.

From there the account reviews how readers through the ages have handled types, from early church writers through medieval and Reformation scholars to modern schools. Some stretched the method too far, while others denied it outright. It weighs claims that every Old Testament event hides a New Testament meaning. It states the Catholic teaching on the typical sense, its limits, and its worth for reading the Bible as one story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tyre:
Tyre was the great Phoenician seaport of the Levant. Its Hebrew name Zor and its Arabic name Sour both mean rock. The entry sifts rival claims about its founding, noting that the Amarna tablets already name it in the fourteenth century before Christ. That date falls well before the dates given by later Greek writers. It follows the city's kings, its trade across the Mediterranean, and its founding of Carthage in 814 before Christ, the most famous of its colonies.

Prophets of Israel denounced Tyre's wealth and its traffic in captive Israelites. The city endured sieges by Assyrian kings, by Nebuchadnezzar, and by Alexander. Later it became a Christian centre, then a Crusader port, and finally a small town under Ottoman rule. The account closes with its modern church life, counting Melchite and Maronite dioceses, priests, churches, and schools, and so joins ancient grandeur to a modest present.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-wai:
Waire was an English friar executed at St Thomas Waterings, Camberwell, in July 1539, about whom almost nothing is certain. All sources agree four men suffered there together, one of them John Griffith, vicar of Wandsworth and chaplain to the Marquis of Exeter. Stow alone names Friar Waire, while Sander speaks of a monk called Mayer.

Both Wriothesley and a servant of Lord Lisle mention two friars suffering with Griffith, one of them Griffith's curate or chaplain at Wandsworth. The other was either a friar or one of Griffith's servants, according to conflicting accounts. Waire may be Thomas Wyre, who signed the surrender of the Dorchester Franciscan friary in 1538. His order is uncertain, and his death goes unrecorded in the Grey Friars' Chronicle and in English Franciscan martyrologies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicente-ferre:
Vicente Ferré was a Spanish Dominican theologian who died at Salamanca in 1682. Born at Valencia, he entered the Dominicans at Salamanca, studied at the College of St Stephen, taught in several houses of his order across Spain. Was called from Burgos to Rome, where for eighteen years he served as chief regent of the Dominican College of St Thomas at the Minerva.

Returning to Salamanca as prior and then regent of studies, he was recognized in his own day among the finest Thomists, interpreters of Aquinas, of the seventeenth century. Posterity credits his published works with extraordinary fullness, clarity, and order. He died while publishing his commentaries on Aquinas's Summa Theologica: two folio volumes on faith, hope, charity. Opposing vices, three on the first part, and three on the first part of the second part, down to question 113.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vittorino-da-:
Vittorino da Feltre, properly Vittorino de' Rambaldoni, was a humanist educator born at Feltre in 1378 and dying at Mantua in 1446. Son of a notary, he entered Padua university in 1396, studied grammar and Latin letters under Barzizza and Giovanni da Ravenna. Philosophy and perhaps theology, supporting himself by tutoring, then studied mathematics under Pelacani, serving as his household servant, until his fame as a mathematics teacher surpassed his master's.

After eighteen months studying Greek under Guarino da Verona, then Italy's best Greek scholar, he opened a private school at Padua and in 1422 succeeded Barzizza in the university rhetoric chair. Resigning after about a year, whether disgusted by the city's immorality or unable to control his students, he taught at Venice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-waterford-and:
Waterford and Lismore is an Irish diocese, suffragan to Cashel, almost coterminous with the ancient Celtic territory of Decies, covering County Waterford, much of Tipperary, and 12,000 acres of Cork. Its population is 131,636, of whom 124,367 are Catholics, served by one bishop and 122 secular priests. It has a diocesan chapter, in abeyance since the seventeenth century, revived with modifications in the last decade.

Religious houses include three Franciscan houses, a Cistercian abbey, Dominicans, Augustinians, Fathers of Charity, and the Congregation of the Divine Pastor. There are also thirty houses of nuns and ten of brothers, including the Irish Christian Brothers, whose parent house is Waterford, and the De La Salle brothers, most engaged in education. The region probably received its first Christian message from Britain before St Patrick. Later sections trace bishops of the suppression period, including Nicholas Comin, translated from Ferns in 1519 and resigning, if Brady is right, only in 1551.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wells-in-scri:
Wells in Scripture explores why fresh water mattered so desperately in Palestine, a land whose only rivers of size are the Litani and Jordan, whose perennial brooks are scarce. Its wadis run impetuously in the rainy season and dry the rest of the year. Job aptly likens faithless friends to those torrent beds, swollen in spring and vanishing in summer heat.

Five rainless months of parching summer, with the hot sirocco blowing from the desert, make life itself a burden. Only unfailing springs and uncontaminated reservoirs save shepherd, flock, farmer, and caravan from thirst, so Sirach twice lists water first among life's principal necessities. Owning a well meant, from time immemorial, possessing the surrounding country. Disputes over a well could drive men to the sword, as in Genesis, Exodus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-detre:
William Detre was a French Jesuit missionary who oversaw the Amazon missions across more than three thousand miles. Born in France in 1668, he died in South America at an advanced age on an uncertain date. After joining the Jesuits, his superiors sent him to South America in 1706. Seven years later he became superior-general and visitor of all the Amazon missions under his order.

Detre is credited with turning the catechism into eighteen tongues for the Indian peoples in his charge. He also sent Europe the famed Amazon map drawn by Father Samuel Fritz and engraved at Quito in 1707. In 1727 he became rector of the College of Cuenca, where he kept up zealous ministry. His Relation of 1 June 1731, full of curious detail on Amazon peoples, appears in volume twenty-three of the Lettres Edifiantes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-au:
William of Auxerre was a thirteenth-century Paris theologian whose Summa Aurea helped carry Aristotle into the schools. His name fills papal papers on the University of Paris from the early 1200s. He was master there, archdeacon of Beauvais, and one of three theologians Gregory IX charged in 1231 with revising Aristotle's banned works on nature and metaphysics. Their faulty translations and Arab notes had drawn the Council of 1210's ban.

Gregory's letter of 6 May 1231 praised William's labour at Rome for reforming study. His Summa Aurea, printed at Paris in 1500, is no mere digest of Peter Lombard's Sentences. In method and matter it shows real freshness, shaped above all by his teacher Praepositinus of Cremona, Paris chancellor from 1206 to 1209. William in turn taught John of Treviso, an early Dominican theologian. As one of the first summas after Aristotle's natural works arrived, it holds a key place in medieval thought.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-ty:
William of Tyre was Archbishop of Tyre and the chief historian of the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem. Born probably in Palestine to a European settler family about 1127 to 1130, he died in 1190 on an unknown date. Whether French or English is unknown. Schooled overseas in Italy or France, he mastered Greek, Latin, and Arabic well enough to write Muslim history from Arabic manuscripts, and he quotes Virgil, Horace, Ovid, Livy, and Cicero.

At Tyre by 1165, he blessed King Amaury's marriage in 1167, served as archdeacon, ran a mission to Emperor Manuel, and tutored the leper prince Baldwin. As chancellor from 1174 and archbishop after, he attended the Lateran Council of 1179 and sought a new crusade in Europe. His Historia, twenty-three books to 1184, blends older sources for the early years with personal memoir and state papers for the later, making it a first-rank source.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-wa:
William of Ware was a Franciscan thinker of the late thirteenth century, styled Doctor Fundatus for the solidity of his teaching. Born at Ware in Hertfordshire on unknown dates, he flourished from 1270 to 1300. He likely joined the Franciscans young and may be the friar noted at the London convent about 1250. He took his theology doctorate at Paris, where most of his life passed, though Pitts wrongly claims Oxford, where his name never appears among Franciscan masters.

Dugdale calls him a pupil of Alexander of Hales, and Bartholomew of Pisa with others calls him teacher of Duns Scotus, whose Cologne tomb bore the line naming William as Scotus's master. Scotus cites him twice. His Commentary on the Sentences survives unprinted in many fourteenth-century manuscripts, and his disputed questions on the Immaculate Conception, drawn from its third book, were published at Quaracchi in 1904.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-windows-in-ch:
Windows in Church Architecture traces how churches learned to let in light. Unlike ancient temples, churches gathered the faithful inside, and the warm East and South demanded large openings. Basilicas therefore bristled with windows in the raised nave, aisles, and facade. In the West later chapels hide aisle window sites, but in the East, where churches stood on open ground, windows stayed standard, placed by column spacing, with two or three grouped.

Window shape stayed constant: a rectangle, round-topped, seldom flat-linteled, often eased by a wedge-stone arch. Brick western basilicas allowed little ornament, while Syrian stone churches and Spoleto flaunted contours and ribbon carving. Germanic windows kept round arches of hollowed stone, wider below than above, and Spain, England, and France favoured horseshoe arches on slanting shafts, as at Deerhurst. By the twelfth century Romanesque windows shrank to lights with sloping reveals, framed by shafts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-xavier-de-mai:
Xavier de Maistre was a French writer of masterpieces, Joseph de Maistre's brother. Born at Chambéry in 1763, he died at Saint Petersburg in 1852. An officer in the army when France reclaimed Savoy in 1792, he shared his brother's exile and served in the allied army in 1799. He followed Suvorov to Russia, where disgrace made him paint. His brother Joseph's arrival changed his lot.

De Maistre joined the Admiralty Office, became its museum librarian in 1805, fought in the Caucasian War, rose to general, and married an empress's lady-in-waiting. He became a writer: arrested for duelling at Alessandria, he spent forty-two days confined composing Voyage autour de ma Chambre, printed by his brother in 1794. Its artless grace, humour, and dreamy philosophy charmed readers. Le Lépreux of 1811, Les Prisonniers du Caucase, La Jeune Sibérienne, and the 1825 Expédition Nocturne confirm him among France's finest second-rank authors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-yves-marie-an:
Yves Marie André was a French Jesuit mathematician and writer on beauty, kept from high office by his Gallican, Cartesian, and Jansenist views. Born at Châteaulin in Lower Brittany on 22 May 1675, he died at Caen on 25 February 1764. He joined the Jesuits in 1693; his views barred responsible posts, so he was set to science and made royal mathematics teacher at Caen for thirty-nine years. His literary essay on the Beautiful won great fame and counts as a classic.

After the Society's suppression he blamed former associates over Cardinal de Noailles and stood strongly anti-Ultramontane. He kept long correspondence with Malebranche, whose life he likely wrote. On suppression he retired to Caen's Canons Regular on a Rouen parliament pension. Beyond the Beautiful, his Treatise on Man shows real power, and eighteen works span metaphysics, optics, physics, architecture, sermons, and catechisms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zenobius-memb:
Zenobius Membré was a French Franciscan missionary, born in 1645 at Bapaume in Pas-de-Calais. A member of Saint Antony's Franciscan province, he reached Canada in 1675, and in 1679 accompanied Robert de La Salle to the Illinois country, of which he wrote a description. In 1681 he descended the Mississippi with La Salle to the Gulf of Mexico. He returned with the expedition's leader to Europe by way of Canada, and became superior of the Franciscan monastery in his native city.

In 1684 Membré followed La Salle into Texas with two Franciscans and three Sulpicians. The commander built Fort Saint Louis at Espiritu Santo Bay in 1685, but Membré tried to found a mission among the Cenis Indians and failed. After about two years of toil he was killed by the natives, along with Father Maximus Le Cerq, Reverend Chefdeville, and the small garrison La Salle had left at the settlement.

The energy folks get their data. The explorer was agreement. The data were energy. The APEX were documentation. The technical were explorer.
dorothy-dainty-at-glenmore:
Amy Brooks's Dorothy Dainty at Glenmore continues the Dorothy Dainty series for younger readers, illustrated by the author herself. Brooks also wrote the Randy books, and her Dorothy volumes run from Dorothy Dainty and Dorothy's Playmates through school, shore and city to Glenmore.

The Glenmore story opens with a letter from Vera, answered by Dorothy, and follows the girls through school and holiday adventures. Brooks writes in large, clear type for young readers, with her own cover designs and pictures. Children who enjoy wholesome girls' series fiction will find Dorothy Dainty at Glenmore gentle, cheerful and kind.
elsie-dinsmore:
Elsie Dinsmore, by Martha Finley, opens in the schoolroom at Roselands, a pleasant room in the old wing of the house. Finley seats the governess Miss Day with her six pupils. Enna, the youngest, is the spoiled darling of both parents. Her lesson is a trial to teacher and scholar alike. Elsie watches from her desk, the gentle counterweight the first chapter sets in place.

Elsie is eight, motherless, and already famous among readers for her piety. Her trials come from a strict father and a household that misunderstands her conscience. Finley's novel, the first of a long series, defined the Sunday school heroine in America. Elsie weeps, prays, forgives, and converts by example. Critics mocked the books for a century. Girls read them anyway, in the millions. Roselands' schoolroom, with its white muslin and rosewood desks, is where that readership was born.
essays-on-work-and-culture:
Essays on Work and Culture, by Hamilton Wright Mabie, asks what labor does to the laborer. Mabie's contents open with the question Tool or Man, then The Man in the Work and Work as Self-Expression. A dedication verse to Henry Van Dyke makes a confession. Our dearest thoughts travel out of reach along the slender wires of speech. That suits a book about the inner life of ordinary jobs.

Later essays take up the pain of youth and the year of wandering. Fellowship, work and pessimism, special training against general training, and concentration each get a chapter, closing with the ultimate aim. Mabie writes against the idea of work as mere wages. A trade rightly seen is self expression. A school is a workshop of character. Culture is what a man brings home from his bench besides his pay.
fashions-in-literature:
Charles Dudley Warner's literary essays are gathered here under the title of the best of them, and the volume opens with a long memorial introduction. The introducer recalls Warner as the most undogmatic of idealists, a writer who used the essay as Addison used it, for serious things handled with gayety. Thirty years of reputation, from My Summer in a Garden onward, stand behind the pieces.

The title essay treats literary taste as fashion, subject to seasons like bonnets. Warner asks why schools of writing rise, reign, and become ridiculous, and what in a book lets it outlive its mode. The companion essays apply the same lens to authors, reputations, and the reading public. It is criticism without dogma, from a man the introduction calls the most companionable of teachers.
five-thousand-miles-underground-or-the-m:
Roy Rockwood's Five Thousand Miles Underground, copyrighted in 1908, sails the airship Flying Mermaid into the earth. Professor Amos Henderson calls for his assistant Washington in the machine shed as the tale opens. Mark and Jack, the boy heroes of the Great Marvel series, join the new machine. A mysterious hole in the ocean draws them downward.

Whale attacks, a cyclone, and a mutiny delay the descent. Down into the earth they pass, many miles below, into a strange draught and a new land. Giants, a fish that walked, a snake-tree, and a temple of treasure crowd the underground world. Rockwood wrote boys' series fiction at industrial speed, under a house name. This volume is his hollow-earth entry, cheerful, impossible, and brisk. The Flying Mermaid comes home, as the last chapter promises, with wonders duly witnessed.
ginx-s-baby-his-birth-and-other-misfortu:
Edward Jenkins published Ginx's Baby in 1870, a satire on Victorian charity built around one unwanted child of the London poor. Ginx, a laborer with too many children already, tries to give the baby away. The contents divide the joke into what Ginx did with him, and what charity and the churches did with him.

Each denomination and society claims the child, baptizes him, litigates over him, and lets him fall through every crack. Chapters invoke Malthus, magistrates, and the milk of human kindness while the baby grows toward ruin. Jenkins wrote to expose real failures in poor relief, and the book's anger made it a sensation that reformers quoted for years.
glaucus-or-the-wonders-of-the-shore:
Charles Kingsley wrote Glaucus, or The Wonders of the Shore to teach Victorian beginners the pleasures of seashore natural history, first published in 1855 and reprinted for decades.
