The 1890 edition carries coloured illustrations of sea anemones and other shore creatures. Kingsley addresses the book to a young lady friend and keeps the tone inviting.

He explains dredging, describing the rope lengths, bottles, and patience the work needs, then examines what the dredge brings up under a lens. Tubulipora, anemones, and crabs become wonders rather than specimens. Kingsley, a clergyman-naturalist, saw God's workmanship in every tide pool. His book helped start the aquarium craze and still models how to make science writing warm and exact.
govdocs-archive_org-KlimovGregoryTheTerr:
Gregory Klimov, a Soviet officer who defected to the West, wrote The Terror Machine about the Soviet administration in occupied Germany after the Second World War. Klimov had served in that administration himself. Edward Crankshaw, a British Soviet expert, prefaced the English edition.

He describes arrests, deportations, informers, and the daily brutality of the occupation machine from inside its offices. The account is a defector's testimony, written in the early Cold War as warning and as evidence. Its detail is its value: names, offices, and methods, unvarnished. The book stands among the classic defector accounts that shaped the West's picture of the Soviet system.
govdocs-archive_org-NurembergAndTheOther:
A 1978 booklet from Historical Review Press, Nuremberg and the Other War Crimes Trials, surveys the International Military Tribunal of 1945 and 1946 and the trials that followed it. Historical Review Press was a revisionist publisher, and the booklet argues from that standpoint. It is a pamphlet of advocacy, not an official record.

It describes the scene at Nuremberg, the role of the OSS, and Justice Jackson's opening speech, then lists the defendants and sentences. Appendices take up Katyn, the bombing of civilians, and de-Nazification, pressing the charge that the trials were victors' justice. The booklet is a debated piece of revisionist literature, held complete for researchers of the argument.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Crossfire_Cross: A publisher's flyer promotes Crossfire: The Plot That Killed Kennedy, Jim Marrs' book arguing that President Kennedy died in a plot. The same sheet carries an advertisement for a historical mystery by John Dickson Carr, issued in the same series. Flyers of this kind were trade publicity, printed to sell forthcoming books to shops and reviewers rather than to argue the case itself.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Hosty-OswaldOne:
An FBI memorandum dated October 1, 1975 went from the Director to the Attorney General of the United States. It reports the Bureau's preliminary inquiry into an allegation concerning Lee Harvey Oswald. Twelve years after the assassination, a claim about Oswald still traveled the full height of the Justice Department.

A preliminary inquiry was the Bureau's first formal step, checking whether an allegation deserved a full investigation. That the Director himself signed off to the Attorney General shows the matter's sensitivity. The memo preserves the opening of that inquiry at the top of the department.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SheridanSquareP: nsia-SheridanSquarePress Sheridan Square Press: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
In April 2018 President Donald Trump had nominated Gina Haspel to run the CIA, and the Archive posted her torture file. Declassified documents, it said, showed she personally supervised the torture of a detainee in 2002. That torture included at least three waterboarding sessions.

Haspel subsequently drafted the cable that ordered destruction of the videotapes of the torture. The posting also charged that she served as a senior official while the agency misled presidents, Congress, and the public about whether torture worked. The file assembled the public record against her at the moment the Senate weighed her nomination.
hardscrabble-or-the-fall-of-chicago-a-ta:
John Richardson's Hardscrabble; or, The Fall of Chicago opens in April 1812 at a farmhouse on the Chicago River. Four miles from the fort, a backwoods master lingers by his blazing logs. His hunting-frock, fringed homespun, and sheath knife mark him a denizen of the forest. A grizzled voyageur in a beaded sash serves under him.

Richardson builds his tale of Indian warfare toward the Fort Dearborn massacre of August 1812, when Chicago's garrison and settlers were destroyed evacuating the fort. The farm at Hardscrabble becomes the settlers' refuge and strongpoint. Potawatomi warriors, a half-breed villain, and a kidnapped heroine drive the frontier plot. Richardson had served in the War of 1812 himself, and wrote Canada's first novels. His Chicago is no city yet, only a stockade, a river, and farms waiting for the blow he knew was coming.
here-there-and-everywhere:
Here, There and Everywhere, by Lord Frederic Hamilton, is a diplomat's memoir of people and places, published in London in 1921. Hamilton opens in India, at a tiger shoot in Cooch Behar. The Maharajah's howdahs go down in a long line to the covert side. A probable tiger is reported in the grass jungle ahead. The beat stops. Three hundred yards of jungle front must be covered before the guns are posted.

Hamilton served abroad for years and dined everywhere. His chapters move between courts, camps, and country houses with a raconteur's ease. The tiger shoot sets the pattern: ceremony first, then danger, then the anecdote told at dinner. Empire appears in these pages as a social world before it is a system. Its author knew the princes and the proconsuls personally. He writes of both as characters in a club story that happens to span three continents.
history-of-american-literature:
History of American Literature, by Reuben Post Halleck, is a school textbook from the author of a widely used English literature history. Halleck explains in his preface that requests from all parts of the United States produced the book. He studied at first hand, he says, far more than a condensed textbook can hold. Judgment and selection need that background. His chapters describe the greatest achievements in American writing from the earliest times to the present.

Halleck warns against dwelling on minor authors. Half is greater than the whole, he quotes, when the half is the essential. Great authors, literary movements, ideals, and animating principles get the attention. American writing is kept in relation to English literature throughout. The book taught several school generations their national canon. Rip Van Winkle's return illustrates the front matter. Irving, the Knickerbockers, and the Hudson valley open the story Halleck's students learned by heart.
hoadly-queries-recommended-to-the-author: Queries recommended to the authors of the late Discourse of free thinking, by Hoadly. The bishop's queries. This book preserves that pamphlet. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Time has kept the file intact through the years.
how-to-fail-in-literature-a-lecture:
Andrew Lang delivered How to Fail in Literature as a lecture at the South Kensington Museum, for a college for working men and women, and printed it in 1890 much enlarged. Lang asks why people take up writing, what success they should want, and why most of them will fail. His answer is a comedy of vocation: many feel the call, few have the gift, and the smallest class of all has both gift and will.

Advice arrives upside down, as counsel on failing well: mistake ambition for talent, scorn pains, and trust the poetic temperament. Lang, who succeeded at nearly every kind of writing, salts the jokes with real wisdom about style, reading, and work. Aspiring authors still quote it.
indian-why-stories-sparks-from-war-eagle:
Frank Bird Linderman collected Indian Why Stories from Blackfeet elders in Montana, subtitled sparks from War Eagle's lodge-fire. War Eagle tells children why the chipmunk's back is striped, how the ducks got fine feathers, and why the kingfisher wears a war-bonnet. Linderman dedicates the book to artist Charles M Russell and to George Bird Grinnell.

Many tales feature Old-man, the trickster creator, stealing the sun's leggings, outwitting animals, and getting outwitted in turn. Linderman knew his tellers personally and worried that settlement was ending their world. His preface mourns the passing frontier while the stories themselves stay lively, funny, and exact about animal nature as Blackfeet tradition understood it.
kansas-women-in-literature:
Kansas Women in Literature is Nettie Garmer Barker's survey of women writers of Kansas. Its epigraphs boast that the state's children are a nobler pride than its walls of corn. Barker counts Kansas-born and adopted women alike in her galaxy of bright names. The first portrait treats Effie Graham, head of mathematics at Topeka High School.

Graham, Barker says, found romance in arithmetic and showed others the way in her lecture Living Arithmetic. Ex-Governor Hoch called her one of the most gifted women in a state noted for brilliant women. Graham lectured on moving into the king row, other people's children, and the larger service. Barker's sketches mix biography, praise, and quotation. The book preserves a state's pride in its women of letters.
kennedy-square:
Kennedy Square is a novel by F. Hopkinson Smith, set in a Southern square of the late fifties. Smith's preface quotes his own Fortunes of Oliver Horn for the square's portrait: magnolias, glossy box, and Noah's Ark church. Kennedy Square has no church, but it has an archdeacon's house instead. Its atmosphere, he promises, matches the older book's square.

Chapter one opens some sixty years earlier, in the square's great days. Smith builds his story on the square's families, their pride, their money troubles, and their honor. The Civil War era closes around them as the novel proceeds. Smith wrote of old Baltimore society with a painter's eye and a native's affection. Kennedy Square is his tribute to that vanishing world.
king-of-the-khyber-rifles-a-romance-of-a:
King of the Khyber Rifles: A Romance of Adventure is Talbot Mundy's 1916 novel of India's frontier, here in a combined edition. Its contents list eighteen chapters without titles. Captain Athelstan King of the Indian service is the hero. He works among the tribes of the Khyber Pass country, where Britain watched the road to Afghanistan.

The Khyber Rifles, the famous frontier regiment, give the book its name and setting. Mundy's tale mixes secret missions, tribal councils, and mountain fighting. A hidden valley and a mysterious woman stand at the center of the intrigue, by common report of the novel. Mundy knew India well and wrote its frontier with an insider's love of intrigue. The book made his name in adventure fiction.
kitty-trenire:
Mabel Quiller-Couch wrote Kitty Trenire, a story for young readers in twenty-one chapters. The opening chapters bring news, a drive, and storms at home and abroad. Kitty's family and friends fill the early scenes.

Later chapters bring Anna's arrival, lessons, alarms, and an exciting night. One chapter is called Missing, and another is called Banished. A girl named Betty has an escapade of her own. The book closes with a chapter titled Good in Everything, hinting at lessons learned through trouble. Home troubles matter as much as outdoor adventures here. Kitty must carry real duties while she is still quite young.
la-grenadiere:
Honoré de Balzac set his tale La Grenadière in a small house by the Loire. Ellen Marriage translated it into English. The house stands about a mile below the bridge of Tours.

Balzac describes white stone houses among gardens and vineyards along the cliffs. The finest fruit ripens there under a southern exposure. Generations of patient work cut terraces into the rock face. Against that calm, rich setting, he places a quiet story of a woman and her sons. Place matters deeply in this tale of a mother and sons. The calm house frames lives marked by loss and duty.
lady-baltimore:
Owen Wister, author of Western fiction, set his novel Lady Baltimore in the South. He dedicated it to S. Weir Mitchell with lifelong affection. A note to readers opens the book on a playful, serious theme.

Wister quotes Burns on seeing ourselves as others see us. He wishes artists could test their work as its audience first. That wish frames a story of manners and memory in an old Southern city. A young visitor meets a proud, fading society there. Romance and gentle comedy carry the clash of old and new ways.
lady-clare:
Alfred Tennyson's poem Lady Clare appears here with twenty-two illustrations. Six artists drew them, including Frederic Schell and F. S. Church. The pictures show lilies, a white doe, and the nurse Alice.

The ballad tells of a lady who seems high born and rich. Her nurse reveals a secret about her true birth. Clare must choose between rank and honest love. She gives up wealth rather than win her lover by a lie. Tennyson's short tale in verse remains a favorite for its clear moral and music. The nurse Alice drives the plot with one spoken truth. Clare's choice, once made, is held with quiet firmness.
landmarks-in-french-literature:
Lytton Strachey published Landmarks in French Literature in London in 1912. Seven chapters carry the reader from the Middle Ages to his own era. A list of authors and a bibliography close the book.

Strachey begins with origins, then treats the Renaissance. The age of Louis XIV gets its own chapter. He moves through the eighteenth century and the Romantic movement. A final chapter covers the age of criticism. His short survey became known for clear judgments and elegant prose about French writing. A chronology at the end helps students place each author. Strachey's brisk verdicts still spark argument among readers.
latin-literature:
J. W. Mackail wrote this survey of Latin literature for a series of manuals. The late Professor William Sellar had first agreed to write it. Mackail, his former pupil, finished the task after Sellar's death.

He offers the book as a tribute to his teacher and friend. Chapters begin with the Roman Republic and its early epic and tragedy. Comedy by Plautus and Terence follows. Mackail traces Roman writing from rough starts to classical polish. Students get a compact map of a vast literature in one volume. Mackail later became known as a critic and anthologist. His survey prizes style as much as bare literary fact.
lazarre:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood published her historical romance Lazarre in Indianapolis in 1901. The Bowen-Merrill Company issued it with illustrations by André Castaigne. One caption shows a figure mounting toward the guardians of an imperial court.

That court setting signals the tale's world of rank and intrigue. Catherwood built her reputation on romances set in earlier centuries. French and colonial history often supplied her scenes and characters. Lazarre belongs to that line of richly dressed historical fiction. Readers who enjoy court danger, loyalty, and lost identity will find her manner here.
lectures-on-dramatic-art-and-literature:
August Wilhelm von Schlegel's Lectures on Dramatic Art and Literature shaped Romantic criticism. The book opens with a warm defense of reading itself. A taste for reading, the motto says, shields a person against life's ills.

Schlegel surveys drama from the Greeks to his own century. He champions Shakespeare against French classical rules. His lectures helped Europe rethink what tragedy and comedy could be. Translators carried his ideas into English literary debate. The work remains a landmark of comparative literary history. German Romantic writers reshaped taste through these lectures. English poets and critics borrowed Schlegel's terms for decades.
letters-on-literature:
Andrew Lang's Letters on Literature collect his essays on books and writers. An introductory piece treats modern English poetry. Further letters treat Fielding, Longfellow, and a friend of Keats.

Virgil, Lucretius, and Plotinus represent the ancient world here. Aucassin and Nicolette brings in a medieval French tale. Richardson and Gérard de Nerval receive letters of their own. A dedication thanks a helpful friend Lang never met in person. The book shows Lang's wide, easy learning worn lightly. Lang also wrote on books for young American hunters, he jokes. His range runs from Homer to yesterday's poetry.
lister-s-great-adventure:
Harold Bindloss published this adventure novel in 1920. Part One, called Barbara's Rebellion, opens the contents. Cartwright meddles, and Barbara vanishes in early chapters. A girl on a platform and a trip to Winnipeg Beach follow.

Lister's dissatisfaction grows until a test confronts him. Part Two, The Reckoning, brings Vernon's plot into the open. Barbara returns, and Lister clears the ground for settlement. A dissatisfied shareholder and Cartwright's scruples complicate the ending. Shillito gets away and Barbara plays a part before the reckoning. Vernon's curiosity opens the plot threads of part one.
love-under-fire:
Love under Fire is a Civil War romance by Randall Parrish, dated 1911. Alonzo Kimball painted its five color pictures. The tale opens between the lines, with a despatch-bearer hunted down. A woman, Miss Willifred, soon holds the hero as her prisoner.

Chapters bring night adventures, an overheard talk, and a captured house. The villain Le Gaire forces decisions and fights a duel. The hero even becomes, for a time, a famous swordsman. Love and duty pull the young officer in opposite ways. Parrish writes brisk, old-fashioned war romance. It is full of rides, risks, and a brave heroine.
macleod-of-dare:
Macleod of Dare is a Scottish novel by William Black, printed at New York in 1883. Black had already won readers with A Princess of Thule. The first chapter names the six boys of Dare. It opens at sunset over the lonely western seas by Mull.

Ulva, Lunga, and the Dutchman's Cap darken on the water. In Castle Dare's great hall, candles blaze over a frugal supper. An old lady of proud, fine features sits at the table's head. Faithful Hamish serves the small company in the vast room. Black fills the tale with Highland scenery and sea air. His romance joins old clan pride to modern hearts.
measure-for-measure: William Shakespeare wrote Measure for Measure, and the record holds it under his name alone. The hosted sample for this entry preserves long notes by the head of Project Gutenberg. Those notes treat old spelling in Hamlet and in print shops of the time. No readable scene of Measure for Measure itself appears in the sample. This note stays with the title, the author, and that sample limit for that reason.
meyer-us4826581-controlled-process-for-t:
United States Patent 4,826,581, granted to Stanley A Meyer on May 2, 1989, covers a controlled process for making heat from gases, plus the gear to run it. The method patent is part of his eight-piece water fuel cell family. It widens his claims from engines to heat itself.

The process takes in his fuel gas, burns it under set controls, and draws off the heat for use. The filing spells out each stage, the burners, and the apparatus in claim language. Patents attest that a method was described as new, not that it works. Meyer's fuel claims were found fraudulent by an Ohio court in 1996.
miles-wallingford-sequel-to-afloat-and-a:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote this sea novel as the sequel to Afloat and Ashore. Miles Wallingford himself tells the story in the first person. The opening scene is a rescue: Miles has fought his rival Drewett in the water. Friends haul both men aboard the Wallingford and fight to revive the seemingly lifeless Drewett.

Below deck, Lucy Hardinge waits on her knees, praying for the news she fears. Cooper mixes sea action with the claims of love, honor, and old friendship. Miles narrates with hindsight, judging his younger self as he goes. The novel continues his double life between the merchant sea and home ashore.
monsieur-beaucaire:
Booth Tarkington's romance opens at the card table in Bath, England. The young Frenchman Beaucaire has guessed that a duke will cheat. He plucks the hidden card smilingly from the big Englishman's sleeve. Six silent men step from the entryway, and the duke stands caught, scarlet and white by turns.

Beaucaire promises not murder but disgrace, laughing his clear, light laugh. Behind his manners stands a mystery: Beaucaire is a French prince traveling in disguise, working as a barber. Nash, master of Bath society, dislikes the young Frenchman in the pump room. Tarkington's tale of wit, swordplay, and wooing became a beloved stage and screen romance.
my-buried-treasure:
Richard Harding Davis swears this tale of a treasure hunt is true. Only his partner's name is changed, to Edgar Powell. Powell led the trip and still makes flannels for a living. Davis says his own share is what the story earns.

The two had known each other at college, then lost touch. Powell came back with a plan and a buried hoard in mind. Davis tells what was said and done as best he can. No pact stops him from judging his friend in print. The result is crisp adventure writing, half confession and half yarn, from a master of the short tale.
mysticism-in-english-literature:
Caroline F. E. Spurgeon studies mysticism in great English writers here. Her note, dated April 1913, sets strict bounds at once. She treats only the type that seeks ultimate reality. American letters, though rich in such thought, are left out.

A line from Plato's Phaedo fronts the book on the few true mystics. Contents move from Plato and Plotinus to English thought. Love and beauty mystics include Shelley, Rossetti, and Browning. Keats and Coventry Patmore join that company. Spurgeon quotes Traherne, Jefferies, and Thompson with care. The book maps a quiet, deep stream in English writing.
myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-volume:
Charles M. Skinner gives this whole volume to buried treasure and storied places. Captain Kidd stands first, the most widespread man in history, Skinner jokes. Kidd's pots of gold are said to dot the whole coast. Gardiner's Island, Cape Cod, and the Florida Keys all claim shares.

Hope of something for nothing drove the digging, Skinner notes. Real wealth was wasted hunting doubloons that never showed. Sea-serpents, stone-throwing devils, and lovers' leaps share the book. V1 warns readers to enjoy the tales without trusting the maps. Skinner's dry humor makes this the most playful volume of his great set.
nan-sherwood-at-rose-ranch-or-the-old-me:
Annie Roe Carr opens this Nan Sherwood tale as school reopens. Early chapters bring new girls and a curfew song. Walking the plank and an unpopular Rhoda stir the school plot. A Mexican girl named Juanita enters the tale.

The treasure of Rose Ranch is named by chapter ten. At last the girls reach the ranch and its open spaces. A round-up and an outlaw close the sample contents. V1 says an old Mexican's hidden gold sets off the hunt. Nan and her friends ride and outwit villains out west, in the bright style series readers loved.
nasa-tm-19650020117-fps-16-radar-jimsphe:
James R Scoggins and Michael Susko, in Marshall's Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory, reported wind data measured at the Eastern Test Range on July 9, 1965. An FPS-16 radar tracked a Jimsphere, a special balloon made to follow small wind changes faithfully. Launch teams at the range need accurate winds high above the pad.

Radar tracking of such a balloon gives a detailed wind profile. Those profiles help decide whether a launch can proceed safely. They also feed studies of how winds vary with height. Scoggins and Susko present the measured data from the range, in a form other launch and weather workers could use directly.
nasa-tm-19650022493-research-within-the-:
Robert E Bourdeau, of the Space Sciences Division at Goddard, surveyed research within the atmosphere, with stress on the ionosphere. That charged layer was once studied only from the ground. Rockets and satellites could now pass through the region itself. Bourdeau says those chances have greatly enriched understanding of how the ionosphere behaves.

He also credits new ground-based experiments for part of the gain. The ionosphere holds charged particles with very small thermal energies. It forms when sunlight ionizes the neutral air high above Earth. Bourdeau's survey shows a field being remade by direct measurement, a theme across space science at that time.
nasa-tm-19650025671-vacancy-formation-in:
Hubert H Grimes at Lewis Research Center measured tiny defects in gold wire under great pressure for this February 1964 article draft. A vacancy is a missing atom in a crystal, an empty site in the metal's regular pattern. Grimes used changes in electrical resistance in gold wires to count such defects. The wires were held under high hydrostatic pressure, squeezed evenly from all sides.

Defect levels affect how a metal conducts and how it ages. Pressure changes the energy needed to form a vacancy. Measuring that change tests basic theories of metals. The work was prepared for a journal of applied physics, a sign that space agency laboratories also did deep basic research.
nasa-tm-19660020100-some-studies-on-the-:
David A Evensen and Robert E Fulton at Langley presented studies in October 1965 on how thin shell structures answer sudden loads. Shells form rocket tanks, fuselage skins, and nose cones. Their response is nonlinear, meaning it does not grow in simple proportion to the load. Topics in the catalog note include flexural vibration of thin circular cylinders under motion.

Buckling of shallow, conical, and spherical shells under sharp pressure is also treated. A shell that survives steady loads can still collapse under a pulse. Dynamic stability was the theme of the conference they addressed. Their studies gave shell designers test-based guidance for a failure mode that steady analysis cannot predict well.
nasa-tm-19660021037-analysis-of-the-moti:
C R Hayleck Jr at Goddard analyzed how a satellite turns when a reaction wheel does the turning, in this December 1965 report. A reaction wheel is a spinning disk inside the satellite. Speeding or slowing the wheel rotates the craft the other way. Hayleck studies the pair as one assembly, tuned for the least weight and power that can do the job.

His case is a slewing maneuver, a planned turn from one aim point to another. The wheel and the satellite trade motion back and forth during the turn. Sizing the wheel too small makes the turn slow or impossible. Sizing it too large wastes mass and power. The analysis gives designers the trade in usable form.
nasa-tm-19660030132-the-relations-betwee:
Robert A. Bruce, of NASA's Langley Research Center, gave this talk at a training program at Wallops Island, Virginia, in August 1966. The audience was learning bio-space technology. Bruce's theme is the two-way pull between a science experiment and the spacecraft built to carry it.

He walks through the steps that connect what an experiment needs with what a spacecraft can provide. To make the links concrete, the talk uses a made-up biological experiment as its example. Each requirement the experiment sets, such as its environment, then shapes a design choice. The lecture notes preserve that lesson for mission planners.
nasa-tm-19670009442-jupiter-s-magnetosph:
J. A. Gledhill wrote this paper at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in February 1967, in its Ionospheric Physics Preprint Series. Gledhill was a senior postdoctoral research associate there. His subject is Jupiter's magnetosphere, the huge bubble of magnetic field around the giant planet. The paper asks what happens to the charged gas trapped inside it.

Jupiter spins fast, completing a full turn roughly every ten hours. If its magnetospheric plasma co-rotates with the planet, centrifugal force flings that plasma outward along the field lines. Near the orbit of the moon Io, the outward force already far exceeds gravity. Gledhill argues there is a maximum plasma density the field can hold in co-rotation at any distance. Beyond it, the plasma breaks away, carrying the field with it. He estimates that maximum density in the equatorial plane by balancing magnetic energy against rotational energy.
nasa-tm-19680018225-transport-properties:
Richard S. Brokaw of Lewis Research Center reviews transport properties of high temperature gases in this 1967 symposium paper. Transport properties include viscosity, diffusion, and thermal conductivity. They govern how gases flow and carry heat in engines and reentry flows.

For cool dilute gases, Chapman-Enskog theory already describes behavior well. Heat conduction is trickier, since rotation and vibration inside molecules add to the heat flux. Work by Mason and Monchick improved that part of the theory, Brokaw notes. At high temperatures, mobile chemical equilibria and free radicals change gas behavior further. Brokaw argues the framework can still predict properties for most practical needs.
nasa-tm-19680024873-an-implantable-multi:
C. M. Winget, J. M. Pope, and colleagues at Ames Research Center describe a tiny radio transmitter built to work inside a living body. Their paper was given at a November 1967 Boston meeting on engineering in medicine and biology. The unit reads four body temperatures at once and sends them out by radio, with no wires through the skin.

Small size and low power use suit the device for long implant tests, the authors note. A ring counter samples a reference resistor and four heat sensors in turn, each shaping the pulse timing of a small oscillator. Such readouts serve studies of daily body rhythms. The animal can be watched closely while nothing outside disturbs it.
nasa-tm-19680025079-the-dry-massive-mode:
Patrick Thaddeus of the Goddard Institute for Space Studies defends a dry, massive model of Venus's atmosphere in this paper. In that model, a deep carbon dioxide atmosphere with no water droplets or dust explains radio observations. Pressure-induced absorption then requires a high ground pressure to fit the data.

Such an atmosphere holds so much heat that nightside cooling stays slight. That creates a problem for the observed microwave phase effect, a small intensity change. Thaddeus argues a model supporter can question whether that effect is real. Measurement errors could fake so small a signal, he notes. He reviews the effect's history at two wavelengths to support the doubt.
nasa-tm-19680025201-the-structure-of-the:
Joseph S. Hogan, of the Goddard Institute for Space Studies and New York University, models the structure of the Martian atmosphere in this study. No spacecraft had yet landed on Mars, so its air had to be built from telescope data and physics. Hogan's model reaches from the surface up into the ionosphere, the charged upper layer observers had detected.

His calculations follow how sunlight is absorbed in carbon dioxide bands and how the gas radiates heat away. A separate chemistry calculation tracks how sunlight breaks carbon dioxide apart and what heating that causes. Weighing mixing against that chemistry, he sets upper and lower limits on particle density in the ionosphere. The scan text is partly garbled, but the model's scope reads clearly.
nasa-tm-19700025450-analysis-of-rendezvo:
Rendezvous radar tracking needs for Mission D are analyzed in this Houston internal note, number MSC-EG-69-6. The radar had to have its angle bias corrected while the two craft flew together. Mission D was Apollo 9, the first crewed flight of the lunar module, tested in Earth orbit.

A data book rule required fifteen minutes of steady radar tracking before any maneuver based on radar updates. The analysis asks whether that much tracking is truly needed to correct the angle bias in the guidance computer. Simulations with only ten minutes of tracking, the summary reports, showed no real fuel penalty. The standing rule, the authors conclude, is a conservative one.
nasa-tm-19700026380-investigation-of-the:
NASA issued this general working paper, number 10,044, on pilot control of gliding parachutes. It investigates what a pilot must see to steer such a parachute well. The goal was landing spacecraft on land rather than at sea, which demanded a far more guided final descent.

The study lays out the mode of operation first, then the test program objectives. Testing ran in three phases, each with its own vehicles and systems described in turn. By comparing phases, the investigators could separate what the pilot saw from what the craft itself did. The aim throughout was a firm list of visual references a pilot needs to land the parachute where intended.
nasa-tm-19710009389-an-evaluation-of-the:
J. W. Montano of NASA's Astronautics Laboratory wrote this evaluation in February 1971, issued as NASA TM X-64569. Its subject is A-286, a stainless alloy strengthened by cold working, meaning it is squeezed or rolled before use to make it harder. Montano set out to measure the alloy's mechanical strength and its resistance to stress corrosion cracking.

The report's contents lay out tensile tests, hardness checks, and low-temperature test work on bar specimens from two makers, Carpenter and Armco. Figures track longitudinal tensile specimens, notched specimens, and hardness across different amounts of cold work. Results and conclusions follow the test sections, giving engineers a compact record of how the worked alloy behaves under load and in cold service.
nasa-tm-19710013626-analysis-of-rotation:
John Zuk and Lawrence P Ludwig of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a May 1971 engineering meeting. It analyzes gas flow across the sealing dam of a noncontacting shaft face seal. Such seals limit leakage along spinning shafts in engines and pumps. Rotation of the seal faces changes the flow in ways simple formulas miss.

The authors treated steady, smooth, subsonic flow at steady temperature. They worked out leakage rates and pressure patterns across the dam. They also gave the conditions where a simpler hydrostatic formula stays valid. The error from using that shortcut is stated. Handy formulas cover leakage, opening force, and the center of pressure.
nasa-tm-19720017690-unipolar-induction-i:
Unipolar Induction in the Magnetosphere presents a new theory of how the solar wind powers Earth's magnetic bubble. Its author names are illegible in the scan. A conductor moving through a magnetic field generates electric currents, an effect called unipolar induction. The paper asks how much of the magnetosphere's activity that effect can explain.

Treating the magnetosheath as a simple ohmic conductor, the theory shows induction can energize several current flows in the magnetosphere. It explains the correlation between the east-west part of the interplanetary magnetic field and polar electric fields and magnetic variations. In the tail region it accounts for effects tied to the field's north-south part. When that field points southward, the theory allows a large energy input into the magnetosphere.
nasa-tm-19720018198-apollo-15-mission-ma:
The Mission Evaluation Team at the Manned Spacecraft Center issued this anomaly report in December 1971. It is report MSC-05805, anomaly report number one for Apollo 15. During the return to Earth, one of the command module's three main parachutes failed. The crew still splashed down safely, but NASA needed the cause. A failed parachute on a crewed flight demands a full investigation.

Investigators studied several possible failure paths in turn. They examined malfunctions in the forward heat shield area. They studied a broken riser, one of the straps tying canopy to capsule. They also studied fuel expelled from the command module's steering thrusters. The catalog record says a most probable cause was identified. The report runs to thirty two pages.
nature-and-human-nature:
Thomas Chandler Haliburton published Nature and Human Nature in 1855. Its first chapter brings back Sam Slick, his famous clockmaker, at a squire's door. Chapter heads promise clippers and steamers, a woman's heart, and a new way to learn Gaelic.

Later heads turn to a day on the lake, a foggy night, and female colleges. Others name gipsying, a betrothal, a honeymoon, and being lost at sea. Haliburton mixes outdoor sport with sharp talk on manners and love. The Pope lines on the title page set the aim: catch manners living as they rise.
news-from-nowhere:
William Morris, poet, craftsman, and socialist, wrote this tale of a dream England in 1890. It first ran in the Commonweal, the journal of his own league. Morris wrote it in part as a reply to Bellamy's Looking Backward of two years past.

A man wakes in a Thames side England where mills, cash, and slums have all passed away. Folk work at crafts they love, share goods in common, and live in a green, clean land. The book is the chief utopian tale of its decade, and a hymn to work done with joy.
no-13-washington-square:
Leroy Scott published No. 13 Washington Square in 1914, a New York tale named for a house address. Chapter one meets the great Mrs De Peyster. An amiable young gentleman enters next, and the lady stands as mistress of her house. A front picture shows a speaker who never suspected ending in such a little blaze.

A slight predicament and the honor of the name trouble the house next. Behind the blinds, the honeymooners, and the flight move the plot along. The Reverend Mr Pyecroft visits, and an attic room holds a secret. Domestic scenes and a happy family close the contents. Scott plays society manners against house mystery.
no-thoroughfare:
Charles Dickens opens No Thoroughfare with an overture, not a chapter. The date is set with care: November the thirtieth, 1835, by the great clock of Saint Paul's. It is ten at night in London. Lesser church clocks strain their metal throats around the cathedral bell.

One clock lags behind the rest, lower and nearer to the ear. It belongs to the Hospital for Foundling Children. Dickens recalls when foundlings were left, no questions asked, in a cradle at the gate. Now mothers must answer inquiries and give up all claim forever. A veiled lady flutters near the hospital gate. Mystery starts with her.
old-saint-paul-s-a-tale-of-the-plague-an:
William Harrison Ainsworth wrote this novel of plague and fire. The preface is dated November 30, 1841. The tale centers on Saint Paul's Cathedral in London. Book one opens in April 1665, plague year. A grocer of Wood Street shuts his family indoors.

Ainsworth says he followed a rare narrative by Defoe closely. That account tells how the grocer fed his household safely. Coffin makers, gamesters, and plague nurses fill the scenes. The Great Fire follows the plague in the story. Ainsworth blends fact, legend, and strong melodrama. The novel remains his popular portrait of old London.
on-the-evolution-of-language-first-annua:
John Wesley Powell wrote this study for the Smithsonian Institution. It appeared in the Bureau of Ethnology report for 1879 to 1880. The Government Printing Office issued it in 1881. Powell directed the bureau at that time. He bases the study on American Indian languages.

Powell asks how few words can express many thoughts. A word for every idea would need a vast vocabulary, he says. Language grows by shaping grammar and parts of speech. Sentences join small units into fuller meaning over time. He traces that growth in Native American speech. The paper is an early work of American linguistics.
over-here: Edgar A. Guest published Over Here in Chicago in 1918. He dedicated the poems To the Mothers Over Here. It is a home-front book for the First World War. The hosted sample shows the title page and an index of poems only. The Boy Enlists, Drafted, and A Father's Prayer appear there. So does The Complacent Slacker, and Christmas, 1918. No poem itself appears in the sample.
paul-and-virginia-from-the-french-of-j-b:
An 1851 English translation of Bernardin de Saint-Pierre's Paul and Virginia carries a remarkable preface. The unnamed translator explains that the work was done in Paris during Robespierre's tyranny. Reading and writing were dangerous then, and the translator burned one manuscript to escape the police searches.

Turning each day to the scenes of Mauritius brought relief from the terror outside. Some sonnets and part of the translation were seized and never recovered. The novel itself tells of two children raised in innocent love on the island, parted by a voyage to France. The preface gives this version a history as moving as the tale.
pericles-prince-of-tyre: The hosted sample here shows only the front matter of Pericles, Prince of Tyre, the act and scene list and the start of the persons of the play. No dialogue is visible. The list maps William Shakespeare's romance across Antioch, Tyre, Tarsus, Pentapolis, Ephesus, and Mytilene, with scenes on shipboard and before the temple of Diana. A chorus heads each act, and the persons begin with Antiochus, king of Antioch, and Pericles himself, with Helicanus and Escanes, lords of Tyre.
pieces-of-eight-being-the-authentic-narr:
Richard Le Gallienne presents a found manuscript as a true account of treasure discovered in the Bahama Islands in 1903. The book, copyrighted in 1917 and 1918, opens with a prologue set at a New York performance of Treasure Island, where the manuscript reached him in a curious way.

Inside the frame, the narrative promises sharks, sailing companions, and a pirate-style hunt, and Le Gallienne dedicates it to friends he calls fellow sailors on the pirate craft called Earth. He hopes each may find his treasure and escape hanging at the end of the trip. The tone is playful, but the story is offered to the public as authentic.
potash-perlmutter-their-copartnership-ve:
Montague Glass created Abe Potash and Morris Perlmutter. The garment trade partners whose quarrels and reconciliations fill this book of their copartnership ventures and adventures, drawn from stories copyrighted from 1909 onward. The first chapter opens in a lawyer's office, where Abe, burned by his dissolved firm of Vesell and Potash. Swears he would refuse partnership even with Andrew Carnegie: five thousand dollars of lessons stand behind the oath, which the reader knows cannot survive the chapter.

Glass built comedy from the New York cloak and suit business, its credit risks, strikes, buyers, and lawsuits, all argued in the partners' glorious dialect. Abe blusters and Morris schemes, and friendship survives every balance sheet. The stories defined Jewish-American humor for a generation, moved to the stage. Fixed a whole industry in literature: two men, one firm, and an endless negotiation between caution and nerve.
poule-noire:
La Poule Noire, The Black Pullet, is a French grimoire framed as the memoir of a Napoleonic officer. The narrator tells of learning talismanic magic in Egypt during the French campaign there. This text, dated about 1820, became the great talismanic grimoire of the French tradition.

Its teaching centers on talismans and rings said to bring riches, love, and protection. Egyptian color dresses older European magic in exotic clothes. The black hen of the title belongs to a rite for finding treasure. Readers loved the mixture of adventure story and working manual. The Black Pullet shows the grimoire changing with its century, adopting Egypt as magic's fashionable homeland.
preface-to-shakespeare:
Samuel Johnson published his annotated edition of Shakespeare's plays in 1765, and this preface. Printed with selected notes on plays from Measure for Measure to Othello, became the most famous essay on Shakespeare ever written. It opens against the worship of age: praises are without reason lavished on the dead, and the honors due only to excellence are paid to antiquity. Johnson proposes a sterner test, length of duration and continuance of esteem, what mankind have long possessed, often examined, and still chosen.

From that ground he defends Shakespeare's mingled drama, faults his careless plots and moral laxity. Dismantles the unities of time and place with one stroke: spectators are always in their senses, and know the stage is only a stage. The notes that follow apply the same common sense line by line. Criticism in English has lived in this preface's house ever since.
robert-elsmere:
Mrs. Humphry Ward published this novel with DeWolfe, Fiske of Boston, dedicating it to two friends of unlike views. They are Thomas Hill Green, late professor of moral philosophy at Oxford, who died on March 26, 1882, and Laura Octavia Mary Lyttelton, who died on Easter Eve, 1886. Ward links them by the love of God and the service of man.

Book one, Westmoreland, opens on one bright afternoon late in May. The spring had been cold and late in the lonely valley of Long Whindale. Warmth had only just reached its bare green recesses, where scattered trees rushed into leaf and March flowers lingered by the stream. Robert Elsmere's story of faith and doubt begins in that country quiet.
salted-with-fire:
George MacDonald opens Salted with Fire at Chapter I in broad Scots speech, in a shoemaker's house on a fine morning. The soutar, or shoemaker, looks up from his work and asks his daughter Maggie where she is off to, standing in the doorway with her shoes in her hand. Maggie answers that she is going over to Stanecross, with his leave, to ask the mistress for a handful or two of chaff. The straw under her father, she insists, has grown hungry-like and thin. It is her part, she says, to look after her own father and see there be no knots in his bed or his porridge.

Father and daughter spar with warmth about the minister, who will call that morning. Maggie cannot abide him and calls him an argle-bargling body, a man fond of wrangling talk.
samoa-a-hundred-years-ago-and-long-befor: George Turner, LL.D., of the London Missionary Society, wrote Samoa a Hundred Years Ago and Long Before. The book was first printed at London in 1884. It was reprinted in 1984 by the Institute of Pacific Studies at the University of the South Pacific. Pictures show a Samoan woman and a Samoan man in costume of the past.
santo-domingo-a-country-with-a-future: Otto Schoenrich wrote Santo Domingo, A Country with a Future, dated 1918, with front pages signed O. S. at New York in January 1918. The pages shown here list sources rather than narrative. They include publications of the Bureau of American Republics and the Pan-American Union. They also include annual reports of the General Receiver of Customs of the Dominican Republic, sent to the Bureau of Insular Affairs from 1907 to 1917.
sea-warfare:
Rudyard Kipling published this group of wartime sketches with Macmillan in London in 1916. Kipling wrote while the First World War was still being fought at sea. The book holds three parts: The Fringes of the Fleet, Tales of the Trade, and Destroyers at Jutland.

Songs open the first part, honoring small armed boats crewed by fishermen, chapel men, and old engineers. Kipling honors plain men doing hard, dull, risky work far from the great battle fleets. His pages gave home readers a close look at patrol craft, merchant routes, and the men who kept them going under fire.
seneca-letters-lucilius-gummere:
Seneca wrote his 124 Moral Letters to Lucilius near the end of his life, around 65 AD, after retiring from Nero's court. Richard M. Gummere's Loeb translation, made between 1917 and 1925, is the text here. The letters look like private mail; they are really a course in Stoic living.

Nearly every letter handles one knot: time wasted, fear of death, anger, wealth, crowds, or pain. Seneca answers with short drills, sharp examples, and orders to practice daily. He admits his own faults as he writes, which keeps the advice human. The letters are still the warmest guide to Roman Stoicism we have.
shakespeare-and-precious-stones-treating:
George Frederick Kunz, a noted gem scholar, wrote this study of the precious stones named in Shakespeare's works. Title pages nearby advertise Kunz's companion books on the lore of gems and the magic of jewels and charms. His name carries weight in the gem trade and in gem history alike.

Kunz gathers the known mentions of stones across the plays and poems and treats each in turn. Birth stones, lucky stones, and stones of healing all fell within his wider work. Readers curious how Shakespeare's age prized rubies, pearls, and other gems get a learned guide written by a man who knew stones by hand and by book.
shakespeare-s-play-of-the-merchant-of-ve:
Charles Kean arranged this acting version of The Merchant of Venice for the Princess's Theatre, where it first played on Saturday, June 12, 1858. Kean adds history and notes to explain the text. The cast list names Kean himself as Shylock, with Mr. Graham as Antonio and Mr. Ryder as Bassanio.

Princes of Morocco and Arragon sue for Portia in this staging, while Launcelot Gobbo clowns as Shylock's servant. Kean's cuts and settings show how Victorian London liked its Shakespeare: grand, careful, and built around a star. Students of the stage can see a famed production fixed in print.
sidonia-the-sorceress-the-supposed-destr:
Lady Wilde translated this German tale of Sidonia von Bork, the Pomeranian canoness tried for witchcraft; volume one appeared in 1894 as part of a two-volume set. A companion tale, Mary Schweidler, called The Amber Witch, by William Meinhold, travels with the work. The German edition honors Lady Lucy Duff Gordon, that tale's translator.

A preface calls Sidonia's trial among the most famed of all witch trials. She stood accused of blighting births in great houses and killing the noblest heirs of Pomerania by sorcery. Romance and record blend here, in a dark tale of beauty, envy, and fear.
sir-thomas-more:
An unknown sixteenth-century company wrote this play on Sir Thomas More, ascribed in part to William Shakespeare. First printed in 1844, it stands here re-edited from the Harleian manuscript 7368 in the British Museum. A long cast list names the Earls of Shrewsbury and Surrey, Erasmus, and More's son-in-law Roper.

John Lincoln, a broker, leads London prentices against foreign Lombards in the cast. A cut-purse, a goldsmith, players, and the hangman all appear. The play follows More from wit and office to the Tower, giving the crowd scenes and the statesman's fall in the rough, lively manner of its age.
sir-walter-scott-as-a-critic-of-literatu:
Margaret Ball published this study of Scott as a critic with the Columbia University Press in New York in 1907. Contents open with an outline of Scott's literary career, then weigh his fitness as a critic. Later chapters treat his work as student and editor in literary history.

The medieval field comes first: the Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border, studies in the romances, and other medieval pieces. Ball shows Scott shaping taste for old tales and poems across Britain. Scholars get a careful map of Scott the editor and reviewer, a giant half-hidden behind Scott the novelist.
social-pictorial-satire: George Du Maurier, author of Trilby and The Martian, wrote Social Pictorial Satire, dated MDCCCXCVIII, that is, 1898. The front picture shows Mr. and Mrs. Candle, from a drawing by John Leech, and the lower part of it had never been printed before. The list of pictures names John Leech and Charles Keene, a snowstorm of January 2, 1867, street arabs, and scenes of sport, trade, and hints dropped to landlords.
stammering-its-cause-and-cure: Benjamin Nathaniel Bogue wrote Stammering: Its Cause and Cure, as a stammerer of almost twenty years. Bogue calls himself the maker of the Bogue Unit Method of restoring perfect speech, founder of the Bogue Institute for Stammerers, and editor of the Emancipator, a journal for perfect speech. He gives the book to his mother, whose unflagging courage held him to the task. The contents open with his life as a stammerer, then turn to the causes of stuttering and stammering.
stolen-treasure:
Howard Pyle wrote and illustrated Stolen Treasure, dated MCMVII, or 1907, gathering four tales of pirates and hidden gold. The contents list With the Buccaneers, Tom Chist and the Treasure-Box, The Ghost of Captain Brand, and The Devil at New Hope.

Pyle, already known for Men of Iron and Twilight Land, fills the pages with sea rovers, sudden violence, and greed that turns men against each other. His own drawings, with captions drawn from scenes of shooting, shouting, and secret plots, match the brisk, old-fashioned storytelling. The tales suit readers who like their adventure salted with legend, ghosts, and the lure of buried wealth.
stories-of-american-life-and-adventure:
Edward Eggleston wrote Stories of American Life and Adventure for the American Book Company, with printings dated 1895 and 1923. Eggleston also wrote Stories of Great Americans for Little Americans and school histories of the United States, and he shaped this book as a reader for the schoolroom.

His preface lists three aims. The first is to make school reading pleasant with plain, direct matter. The second is to build a taste for tales of fact full of action. The third is to steer boys and girls away from cheap fiction. The stories draw on early American life, wild country, and bold deeds, taught through incident rather than dry summary.
studies-in-early-victorian-literature:
Frederic Harrison's Studies in Early Victorian Literature came out at London and New York under Edward Arnold in 1895. The essays had run in the Forum during 1894 and 1895 and were revised and partly rewritten for the book, after hearing critics on both sides of the Atlantic.

Harrison aims at a mature estimate of the lasting worth of the chief prose writers of the Queen's earlier reign, leaving living authors and all poetry, philosophy, and science aside. After a chapter on the age's traits, he takes up Carlyle, Macaulay, Disraeli, Thackeray, Dickens, Charlotte Bronte, Kingsley, Trollope, and George Eliot in turn. His judgments are firm, personal, and meant to fix each writer's place.
studies-in-literature:
John Morley's Studies in Literature gathers essays first printed elsewhere. They had appeared in the Nineteenth Century, the Fortnightly Review, and other places. The printing at hand is dated 1907. Morley's own note of October 1890 thanks the owners for leave to reprint.

The contents open with Wordsworth. Morley first wrote it as the introduction to an 1888 edition of the poet's works. It tells the life from a Cockermouth birth in 1770. It ends with death at Rydal Mount in 1850. Aphorisms, an essay on Maine's Popular Government, words on French models, and the famous lecture On the Study of Literature follow, with pieces on Hugo's Ninety-Three and Browning's Ring and the Book. Morley writes as a critic who treats books as forces in public life.
suzanna-stirs-the-fire:
Emily Calvin Blake, author of Marcia of the Little Home, wrote Suzanna Stirs the Fire, printed at Chicago by A. C. McClurg and Company in 1915, with illustrations by F. V. Poole. An early illustration shows the heroine announcing that she has adopted herself out to Mrs. Reynolds and come to stay.

Book I opens with chapters called The Tucked-In Day and The Only Child. Suzanna is a girl who walks into other people's houses and troubles and stirs them, as the title says, like a fire: poking at cold arrangements until warmth and honesty come up. Blake writes warm domestic fiction about children mending the grown-up world by plain affection and persistence.
tales-from-shakespeare:
Charles and Mary Lamb's Tales from Shakespeare retells the plays as prose stories for young readers. The preface explains the method: the tales are meant as an introduction to the study of Shakespeare, and his own words are used whenever they could possibly be brought in.

Whatever the Lambs added to give the stories a connected form was chosen with diligent care to avoid words that entered English after Shakespeare's time. In the tales from the tragedies, they note a pattern. Shakespeare's words recur very often there. They recur in narrative as well as dialogue. In the comedies the case differs. The Lambs could scarcely ever turn his speeches into prose without loss. Mary Lamb took most of the comedies and Charles the tragedies, though the title page joins their names without division.
the-age-of-shakespeare: Algernon Charles Swinburne wrote The Age of Shakespeare. Harper and Brothers printed it in New York and London in 1908. A sonnet in memory of Charles Lamb stands at the front. Chapters listed treat nine playwrights of the age. Christopher Marlowe heads the list. John Webster, Thomas Dekker, and John Marston follow. Thomas Middleton, William Rowley, and Thomas Heywood come next. George Chapman and Cyril Tourneur close the set.
the-air-ship-boys-or-the-quest-of-the-az: H. L. Sayler wrote The Air Ship Boys. Its subtitle is The Quest of the Aztec Treasure. It is a boys' tale of flight and gold. Chapters open with The Departure of the Overland Limited. Ned's Meeting with Major Baldwin Honeywell follows. Building an Air Ship stands midway. Fighting Indians with a Searchlight comes later. A Thrilling Rescue in Mid-Air follows that. The Secret Tunnel in the Mesa closes the parts shown.
the-altar-fire:
Arthur Christopher Benson published The Altar Fire in 1907, taking its title words from a Latin line about fire falling and eating up a burnt offering. In his preface Benson calls his subject a sick spirit. He argues that pain of heart and soul should be spoken of openly, much as illness of the body now is.

Benson holds that hiding grief makes it worse, since lone pain cuts a person off from help. Shared words about suffering, he writes, can give others strength to bear their own. The book thus treats sorrow as a real part of life, not a fault to be locked away in quiet rooms.
the-art-of-the-moving-picture: Title pages and the start of a contents list present Vachel Lindsay's The Art of the Moving Picture, in its 1922 revision of a book first issued in 1915. Lindsay dedicates it to George Mather Richards, in memory of art student days when the Metropolitan Museum was their picture-drama. The title page offers the book first to the new art museums rising across the country. It offers it next to universities. It also addresses critics and writers. Makers of sculpture, building, and painting are addressed as well.
the-autobiography-of-mark-rutherford-edi:
Mark Rutherford's life story, edited by his friend Reuben Shapcott, was printed by Hodder and Stoughton in a 1913 edition. Chapter headings begin with childhood and preparation, then move to Water Lane. Edward Gibbon Mardon, Miss Arbour, Ellen, and Mary all have sections named for them.

Later chapters are called Emancipation and Progress in Emancipation, ending with Oxford Street. Those headings suggest a man breaking away from early limits and testing new beliefs and work. A preface to the second edition follows the contents. The book presents a quiet, inward life in the form of a friend's careful edition.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-23-ecclesias:
Ecclesiastes, in Douay-Rheims English drawn from the Latin Vulgate, in the revision Bishop Richard Challoner finished across 1749 to 1752. Rheims in 1582 supplied the New Testament, Douay in 1609 and 1610 the Old Testament. Its speaker weighs human labour under the sun and finds a repeated emptiness. A fragment in the opening says all is vanity.

What has a man, chapter one asks, from all his labour under the sun? Generations pass, work continues, and gain looks thin from that height. The book's voice is not a storyteller but a preacher testing riches, work, and pleasure by their end. Readers meet hard questions early, before any counsel. That bleak opening gives the later call to remember God its force.
the-bobbsey-twins-at-the-seashore:
Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins at the Seashore, an early book in her set for young readers. The first part is called Chasing the Duck. It starts as the Bobbsey clan loads a depot cart for a trip from the country to the shore. Dinah climbs in first, then Freddie with a box that holds Snoop, his pet cat.

Flossie has wrapped her ferns in wet sheets so the sun will not kill them. Bert must bear a bag with jars of jelly in it, and Nan fears her hat box will be crushed. At the last moment Freddie's duck, Downy, is missed. Bert runs back for the blue shoe box on the sofa. The book then tells who the twins are: Nan and Bert, age eight, dark, and Flossie and Freddie, age four, fair.
the-chemistry-of-hat-manufacturing-lectu: Watson Smith, F.C.S., F.I.C., then a lecturer in chemical technology at Owens College, Manchester, gave these lectures before the Hat Manufacturers' Association. Albert Shonk revised and edited them for the 1906 London edition from Scott, Greenwood and Son, with sixteen pictures. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here. The first lectures treat textile fibres, chiefly wool, fur, and hair.The story, if any, begins beyond what is present.
the-city-of-fire:
Grace Livingston Hill opens this novel in Sabbath Valley, a town cupped like a green jewel in the hand of the mountains. Morning sun picks out clean streets, white houses with green blinds, a brick school house, a vine clad stone church, and the little stone parsonage. The telling stresses that the word manse had not yet reached the place, and that Sabbath Valley had no affectations.

Two miles away, Billy Gaston stands on the station platform at Pleasant View, waiting for the morning train. He is fourteen, and he looks down on the beauty at his feet with a blind sense of its loveliness. A thrill of wonder and devotion runs through him as he gazes. Hill builds her tale of faith and danger on that valley contrast: a sheltered town seen from a boy's height above it.
the-condition-elevation-emigration-and-d:
A study of the condition, elevation, emigration, and destiny of the colored people of the United States was published in 1852, with a preface and a long run of chapters. The contents open with the condition of many classes in Europe, then a comparative chapter on colored people in America. American colonization is treated next, before the argument turns home.

Later chapters press a claim of place. Their titles run: our elevation in the United States, means of elevation, the United States our country, and claims of colored men as citizens. Warriors, citizens, business men, and mechanics among colored Americans each get a chapter's proof. Literary and professional colored men and women, and students of various professions, close what is present.
the-confessions-of-nat-turner-the-leader:
Printed in Baltimore in 1831 and published by Thomas R. Gray, the pamphlet gives Nat Turner's own statement about the Southampton, Virginia, slave revolt he led. Gray says Turner spoke freely in the prison where he was held. He owned the statement when it was read back to him before the Southampton court at Jerusalem on November 5, 1831.

Alongside the confession, the pamphlet promises a full account of the revolt itself. It lists the white people killed and the Black people brought before the court and sentenced there. A copyright notice filed in the District of Columbia on November 10, 1831, opens the work, with Edmund J. Lee named as clerk.
the-damnation-of-theron-ware:
Harold Frederic opens The Damnation of Theron Ware on a crowd scene without match in the building's eight years. People wedge the seats, pack the aisles, overflow the galleries, and mass about the doors in the shadows. Gas-jets in tin-lined circles light a thousand uplifted faces, all held by one strong feeling and fixed on a single point.

The gathering is no trial or lottery, as a watcher might guess from the mix of hope and dread. It is the closing session of the annual Nedahma Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church. The Bishop, a slow, near-sighted old man, rubs his spectacles with care. He silently rehearses the list of ministerial appointments for the coming year, while the clergymen around him grind their teeth and shuffle their feet.
the-divine-fire:
May Sinclair's novel The Divine Fire, dated 1904, opens with Horace Jewdwine and a find he ranks as his best yet, though he must check it with his cousin Lucia. Four books shape the tale, with titles that hint at a poet's scattered parts, a woman's path, a house of bondage, and the man himself. Warm praise from Punch heads the front pages.

Jewdwine is a bookseller with a sharp eye for rare finds. The story follows a young poet whose gift the trade cannot price. Sinclair writes of art, money, and love with calm wit and care.
the-drama-of-the-forests-romance-and-adv: Arthur Heming's The Drama of the Forests, subtitled Romance and Adventure, was printed in 1921 by Doubleday, Page and Company. Only the title matter is present here. Heming drew its pictures himself, from paintings held by the Royal Ontario Museum. A frontispiece shows a strange winged shape crossing a lake on long feet. The book is set for Mr. and Mrs. David A. Dunlap. No tale text appears.
the-egyptian-conception-of-immortality-t:
George Andrew Reisner's The Egyptian Conception of Immortality was the Ingersoll Lecture of 1911. Its front pages print the will that set up the lectureship. Five thousand dollars went to Harvard for a yearly talk. The talk's theme is the immortality of man. Any faith or trade may supply the speaker. The talk stands apart from the fixed courses. Caroline Haskell Ingersoll's gift honoured her father's wish.

Reisner, who dug Egypt's tombs for Harvard, tells how the Nile folk pictured the soul's life after death. Tombs, spells, and grave goods give his proof. The talk stays short, clear, and grounded in the field.
the-enchanted-island-of-yew-whereon-prin:
L. Frank Baum's The Enchanted Island of Yew tells whereon Prince Marvel met the High Ki of Twi and other surprising people. Its contents open with the fairy bower and the king of thieves. Then come the royal dragon of Spor and King Terribus. The gift of beauty follows. The list ends at the hidden kingdom of Twi, with its doubled rulers.

Later heads name a tyrant, a book of magic, the queen of Plenta, and the red rogue of Dawna. A fairy prince in knight's form roams Yew righting wrongs. Baum fills the isle with strange lands and tests of wit.
the-essays-of-arthur-schopenhauer-on-hum:
Arthur Schopenhauer's essays On Human Nature, in T. Bailey Saunders's English rendering, hold six pieces: Human Nature, Government, Free-Will and Fatalism, Character, Moral Instinct, and Ethical Reflections. Saunders says he drew them from Schopenhauer's Parerga and his posthumous papers, cut a few dated parts, and split long chapters into named parts for ease.

Truths of the body may be checked by all, he begins, but truths of mind need a keener test. Schopenhauer's bleak wit weighs why men act as they do. The essays show his thought at its most plain and quotable.
the-gentleman-from-everywhere: James Henry Foss wrote The Gentleman from Everywhere as the tale of his own life, printed in 1903. The book is given to his beloved. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The heads run from the launching of his life boat to a first voyage. They pass through school days and work as a teacher. They pass through a stint as a preacher, shadow land, and mosquito land. They end with a run on the political stump. No chapter text shows up in these pages.
the-golden-lion-of-granpere:
Anthony Trollope wrote The Golden Lion of Granpere. Chapter I sets the scene among the Vosges mountains in Lorraine. The village of Granpere lies just outside Alsace. It stands some thirty miles from the baths of Plombieres. A fine new road runs through it. The road was made under the late imperial rule in France.

Trollope notes that a diligence now runs daily from Granpere. It runs to Remiremont, where the railway begins. The railway puts the village in the middle of everything. Yet the folk of the hills feel that city ways have come near enough. That balance of old rural life and new roads frames the tale. The tale centers on the village inn, the Golden Lion. It centers on the people whose lives turn on it.
the-golden-snare:
James Oliver Curwood wrote The Golden Snare. Chapter I opens with Bram Johnson. Bram is an unusual man, even for the northland. He is a creature of his place and of need. At times he is a man with a soul. At other times he is a brute with the heart of a devil.

Curwood asks the reader not to blame Bram too much. He traces Bram's line back three generations. That was before the Johnsons went north of Sixty. The tale's ground is the far north, reached by canoe. The route runs up the Lower Athabasca to Great Slave Lake. It runs down the Mackenzie to the Arctic. There the peoples change. The quick Chippewa gives way to the slower Cree. Against that hard land, Bram's tale, the girl's, and the other man's will play out.
the-great-events-by-famous-historians-vo: Rossiter Johnson was editor-in-chief of The Great Events by Famous Historians. Charles F. Horne and John Rudd were associate editors. This record is Volume VIII. The National Alumni published it in 1905. Only front matter is present here: a note on the binding and the title page. The binding copies a mosaic design in the British Museum. Antoine Michel Padeloup made it about 1710 for Francoise Marie de Bourbon, daughter of Louis XIV. No contents list is present. The volume's events cannot be told from what is here.
the-happy-venture: Edith Ballinger Price wrote The Happy Venture, published by The Century Co. in 1920 and 1921, and she drew the pictures herself. She is named as the author of Blue Magic, Us and the Bottleman, and Silver Shoal Light. Chapter titles include Tales in the Rain, Havoc, Up Stakes, The Fine Old Farmhouse, The Wheels Begin to Turn, and The Sea Is a Tyrant. Only the title page, contents, and chapter heading are present here, so the story itself does not appear.
the-helmet-of-navarre: Bertha Runkle wrote The Helmet of Navarre, with pictures by Andre Castaigne, published in New York by The Century Co. in 1901. A verse from Lord Macaulay's Ivry stands at the front, about pressing on where a white plume shines amid the ranks of war. The contents list chapters such as A Flash of Lightning, At the Amour de Dieu, Rapiers and a Vow, A Matter of Life and Death, and A Divided Duty. No text past the front matter is present here.
the-home-acre:
E. P. Roe wrote The Home Acre. The contents list chapters on tree-planting, fruit-trees and grass, the garden, the vineyard and orchard, the raspberry, the currant, strawberries, and the kitchen-garden. Chapter one, Tree-Planting, opens by calling land hunger a natural craving that artificial city life can weaken but seldom kill for good.

For tens of thousands of city bread-winners, Roe says, a country home is the dream and reward of life's toil. More workers now join rural pleasures to business life, and quick transit helps. A cottage with deed in hand, ringed by trees, flowers, lawn, and garden, gives the tired man rest through a full change of thought.
the-house-of-the-vampire:
George Sylvester Viereck wrote this novel. His poems appeared as Nineveh and Other Poems. Moffat, Yard and Company published the novel in New York. Copyright dates from 1907, with a reprint the same year. The opening scene sits in a fashionable restaurant. A Sicilian conductor thrashes his wand through the air. The room watches someone else entirely. Reginald Clarke smiles like a conqueror. He guides a wistful young poet toward the exit.

That pairing sets the book's terms. Clarke carries himself as a man of the world. Silver just shows in his dark hair. The boy beside him has a poet's lucid eyes. Viereck builds a tale of draining influence from such contrasts. A brilliant older talent feeds on a younger one. Charm and unease arrive in equal measure.
the-house-that-jill-built-after-jack-s-h: E. C. Gardner wrote this illustrated book on home architecture. W. F. Adams Company published it in Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1896. His other books include Homes and How to Make Them. Only the title page and contents are present here. The advice itself does not appear. The chapter titles show his method. One names a wise father and a glad son-in-law. Another offers moral suasion for malarial marshes. Many fires make small dividends, says a third. A later chapter asks what happens when floods beat and rains descend.
the-influence-of-old-norse-literature-on:
Conrad Hjalmar Nordby wrote this study of Norse influence on English writing. It appeared in 1901. A stanza from the Hávamál opens it, in Thorpe's rendering. Cattle die and kindred die, it says. We die ourselves as well. Fair fame never dies for the man who earned it. A prefatory note tells the book's sad history. It is the only literary work its author left. A few planned pages are missing. It never got his final revision.

His friends published it as a memorial. Nordby was born in Christiania in 1867. His family brought him to New York at age four. City schools and the College of the City of New York formed him. He taught school, then joined his college staff. Graduate study at Columbia followed. He died in October 1900. The book carries his Norse heritage into English literary history.
the-interdependence-of-literature:
Georgina Pell Curtis published this survey in 1917. B. Herder issued it in St. Louis and London. Her epigraph comes from De Quincey. The literature of knowledge teaches, it says. The literature of power moves its readers. One is a rudder, the other an oar or a sail. Her preface is dated at Chicago in June 1916. The subject had no exclusive treatment before, she believes. Schoolmen had left it alone.

She writes in narrative style, not as a textbook. Interest in the theme is her first aim. A larger, fuller account may someday follow, she hopes. The contents move across the ancient world. Babylonian and early Hebrew writing come first. Sanskrit, Persian, and Egyptian literatures follow. Greek and Roman chapters carry the story onward. Heroic poetry, Scandinavian, and Slavonic traditions close the list. No nation's letters grow up alone, she argues.
the-interest-of-america-in-sea-power-pre:
Captain A. T. Mahan of the United States Navy gathered these papers. Sampson Low of London issued them in 1897. His title page lists the works that made his name. The Influence of Sea Power Upon History leads them. A companion volume on the French Revolution follows. Lives of Farragut and Nelson complete the list. Nelson is praised as British sea power embodied.

The preface admits the book's patchwork nature. The papers appeared at wide intervals over years. No plan linked them at first. Later publication together came as an afterthought. Their interest hangs partly on their dates, Mahan argues. The state of affairs at each writing matters too. Copyright pages layered from 1890 to 1897 confirm the magazine origins. Assembled here, the essays argue for American naval power.
the-land-of-fire-a-tale-of-adventure:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote adventure tales drawn from his own travels in America, and his last tale appeared after a life that began in Ireland in 1819. A preface tells how Reid left a planned church career, sailed to New Orleans, and volunteered for the United States in the war with Mexico.

The preface lingers on the storming of Chapultepec castle outside Mexico City. Reid led grenadiers and marines up the hill under heavy fire when the attack stalled. Readers meet the author as a soldier first, which sets up the daring mood of the adventure that follows.
the-land-of-heart-s-desire:
W. B. Yeats wrote his short fairy play in 1894, and the revised seventh edition appeared in 1912. The scene is a cottage room in the barony of Kilmacowen, County Sligo, at a remote time. Maurteen, Bridget, and Shawn Bruin sit by the hearth with Mary Bruin and Father Hart.

A faery child completes the cast listed on the opening pages. The household expects an ordinary night, yet the forest shows through the open door in moonlight. Yeats sets a plain Irish home against a strange, calling world just outside it. The quiet room makes that call feel stronger.
the-lee-shore: R. Macaulay published her novel in London in 1912, with a dedication to P. R. and an epigraph on the deep division between those who have and those who have not. Only the title page and contents are present here, listing chapters on a hereditary bequest, choice of a career, hopes, and Hilary, Peggy, and the boarders. Later titles promise the loss of a profession and the loss of an idea. The novel itself does not appear in this record.
the-life-of-john-clare:
Frederick Martin published his life of John Clare at London in May 1865, a year after the poet death. His preface recalls the rapture that greeted a new poet billed as the Northamptonshire Peasant and the English Burns. Rossini set his verses, and leading reviews praised him in chorus.

Fame lasted nine days, Martin says, and poverty, neglect, and suffering broke Clare heart. He died in spring 1864 at the Northampton Lunatic Asylum. Martin drew on masses of letters and Clare own memoirs, giving rare detail for a man born in the lowest rank of the people.
the-life-of-st-declan-of-ardmore:
P. Power edited the life of Saint Declan of Ardmore from a manuscript in the Royal Library at Brussels and translated it from the Irish. His introduction starts with place, at a rocky headland east of Youghal Harbour on the south Irish coast. Maps call it Ram Head, while its real name is Ceann-a-Rama.

Ruins there hold a round tower, a cathedral church, a second church by a holy well, an early oratory, and ogham stones. Power notes that no Irish saint holds local memory like Declan, yet scholars dispute his period sharply. Text and place together anchor the saint cult.
the-life-of-st-mochuda-of-lismore:
P. Power edited the life of Saint Mochuda of Lismore from a manuscript in the Royal Irish Academy library and translated it from the Irish. His general introduction calls Irish saint lives a distinctive class of old Irish writing. Annals, tales, and poetry found editors, he says, while the lives stayed a mine unworked.

Power admits the common charges in part. The lives hold wild legends, broken chronology, and miracles multiplied until marvel feels ordinary. He answers that all old writing needs reading by the light of its own times, and that these lives keep real historical value.
the-lion-s-share: Arnold Bennett published his novel in 1916, after a long run of Five Towns books and fantasias. Only the title page and Bennett own book list are present here, naming novels from Anna of the Five Towns and The Old Wives Tale to Clayhanger and The Price of Love. Fantasias such as The Grand Babylon Hotel and short story sets fill the list as well. The novel itself, set among artists and a woman seeking a fuller life, is not included in this record.
the-little-colonel-s-chum-mary-ware:
Annie Fellows Johnston's The Little Colonel's Chum: Mary Ware carries a 1908 copyright from L. C. Page and Company of Boston, with illustrations by Etheldred B. Barry. The front matter includes a letter from Johnston to the boys and girls who already know the Little Colonel books. In it she explains that when she finished the eighth volume, The Maid of Honour, she thought she had reached the end of the series.

The letter speaks directly to loyal young readers before the story begins. The title itself carries the news: a new companion, Mary Ware, joins the Little Colonel as her chum. Readers who follow the Kentucky series get both a word from the author and the start of another friendship in the Little Colonel's world.
