the-madonna-of-the-future:
Henry James's The Madonna of the Future appears here in the 1887 Macmillan edition. The tale is framed at a dinner table, where talk turns to masters who achieved a single masterpiece, artists and poets who touched perfection only once. The host shows a charming cabinet picture by an unknown painter who afterward relapsed into obscurity. A guest named H--- says he has seen such a case: a poor fellow who painted his one masterpiece, and did not even paint that.

H--- then tells the story, which reaches back to his youth in Italy. Arriving late in Florence, he wandered from his hotel into a moonlit piazza facing the Palazzo Vecchio. There he approached the gleaming sculptures at its base and recognized Michelangelo's David. James frames an artist's failure inside talk about art, memory, and Florence itself.
the-man-made-world-or-our-androcentric-c:
Charlotte Perkins Gilman titled her book Our Androcentric Culture, or The Man Made World. Its fourteen chapters move from humanness and the man-made family through health and beauty, men and art, and masculine literature. Games, ethics and religion, education, society and fashion, law, crime, politics and warfare, and industry follow. The survey ends with A Human World. Chapter one begins, disarmingly, with sheep. Gilman surveys the sheep from every side: religious symbol, painter's stock, diet staple, source of clothing, and emblem of bashfulness and stupidity.

In some regions sheep destroy grass and forest by nibbling; on great plains, shepherds go insane from loneliness and monotony. The scientific mind, she notes, studies the sheep's sequacity, its habit of following automatically. From an animal famous for following, she builds toward an argument about a culture shaped by one sex.
the-meadow-brook-girls-afloat-or-the-sto: Janet Aldridge published The Meadow-Brook Girls Afloat, subtitled The Stormy Cruise of the Red Rover, in 1913. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The contents open with scenting a mystery and a discovery by Crazy Jane, then move to setting up housekeeping aboard. Later chapters promise a mysterious night journey, an island of delight, and a tramp club alarmed by the girls' doings.
the-mettle-of-the-pasture:
James Lane Allen published The Mettle of the Pasture in New York in 1903 and dedicated it to his sister. Allen, author of The Choir Invisible and A Kentucky Cardinal, opens Part First at a supper table in the evening light. A young woman refuses supper and sinks back into a stately oak chair. In her drooping hand she clasps a dark red rose, which Allen calls an inverted torch of love.

Glass doors behind her open to stone steps, a lawn, gray pines, and a flower garden beyond. Scarlet strawberries and frozen cream are set before her grandmother at the table's head. The girl rises with an apology, torn between company and solitude. Love bids her go and bids her linger at once, Allen writes. She longs for the garden's privacy to think of her great happiness, now fast approaching.
the-mintage-being-ten-stories-one-more:
Elbert Hubbard's The Mintage, copyrighted in 1910, announces itself as ten stories and one more. Hubbard takes his title from Goethe: 'Tis here you'll find the mintage of my mind. The contents mix sketches and tales: Five Babies, Simeon Stylites the Syrian, the Battle of the Little Big Horn, Cleopatra and Caesar, and John the Baptist and Salome. A motto adds that all success consists in doing something for somebody.

The first story, Five Babies, begins on a Grand Trunk Railway train between Suspension Bridge and Chicago. Hubbard recalls a sight so trivial it seems unworthy of mention. Three weeks later he still remembers it, so he relates it to be rid of it. Such little incidents, he suggests, are the items that make or mar existence.
the-mutiny-of-the-elsinore:
Jack London's novel The Mutiny of the Elsinore was published in London by Mills and Boon in 1915. Only title page and a bare contents list are present here, so the sea story does not appear. London held the United States copyright himself, as the title page notes. Thirty-three chapters are listed, numbered in Roman numerals with no titles.

That numbered skeleton is all these pages show. No narrator, shipboard character, or line of dialogue is included. Readers are left with the frame alone: a long novel in thirty-three parts, and a London publisher in Rupert Street. The title promises a crew rising against its officers aboard the Elsinore.
the-natural-history-of-wiltshire:
John Aubrey's The Natural History of Wiltshire, written between 1656 and 1691, opens with an editor's dedicatory letter to George Poulett Scrope, Member of Parliament. The editor, who signs no name in the pages shown, thanks Scrope warmly. Scrope had advocated publication and helped bear its cost for the Wiltshire Topographical Society. Without him the book might never have been printed.

Obsolete in science, the letter concedes, Aubrey's work still teems with curious facts that characterise both the writer and his age. Had Aubrey revised and printed it himself, it might have ranked with Plot's Staffordshire or Morton's Northamptonshire. The editor despairs instead of Wiltshire gentry and clergy, whose apathy toward local history let appeals from Aubrey onward go unanswered.
the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendell-hol: Before the Curfew gathers late occasional poems of Oliver Wendell Holmes, bracketed as Volume 3 of the 1893 set. Here only the contents and the opening poem's first line appear; the poems themselves are absent. Titles include At My Fireside, At the Saturday Club, and Our Dead Singer. Two poems to Harriet Beecher Stowe at seventy appear, plus birthday pieces for Hedge, Lowell, and Whittier. Later entries name a Harvard anniversary poem and The Flaneur, written during the 1882 transit of Venus. A piece on President Garfield's death appears as well.
the-poor-clare: Elizabeth Gaskell's The Poor Clare is shown here through the front matter of a modern reprint from Melville House Publishing, dated 2013. Here only the copyright pages and contents appear, so the story itself is absent. The edition notes that the tale first appeared serially in Dickens's Household Words in 1856. It is reprinted from Lizzie Leigh and Other Tales, published by Macmillan and Co. in 1896. Its contents list only three chapters. A sibling record carries the opening chapter itself, dated December 12th, 1747.
the-port-of-adventure: Charles Norris Williamson and Alice Muriel Williamson's The Port of Adventure, dated 1913, was published in Great Britain under the title The Love Pirate. Here only the title pages, a list of the authors' joint novels, and the start of the contents appear, so the story itself is absent. Early chapters are In a Garden, Nick, The Anniversary, A Girl in Mourning, and What Happened in the Night. Later entries promise a police mystery and The Gold Bag Comedy.
the-prelude-to-adventure: Hugh Walpole's The Prelude to Adventure was issued by Macmillan and Co. in London, in a new edition dated September 1919. Walpole is named as author of Mr. Perrin and Mr. Traill, and the book is dedicated to R. A. Streatfield. A transcriber's note about odd spellings and accented names stands at the head of the pages shown. The contents list chapters with striking titles: Last Chapter first, then Bunning, The Body Comes to Town, and Margaret Craven. Stone Altars, The Watchers, and Terror follow. The chapters themselves are not shown.
the-press-gang-afloat-and-ashore: J. R. Hutchinson's The Press-Gang Afloat and Ashore is presented through its contents and a list of illustrations. The chapters themselves are not shown. Twelve chapters trace the life of the press-gang system. They ask how it came in, why it was necessary, and what the gang was. Later chapters cover whom it might take, what it did afloat and ashore, and how men evaded it. Women and the press-gang get a chapter, and the last tells how the gang went out.
the-principles-of-success-in-literature:
George Henry Lewes opens The Principles of Success in Literature with the nervous system. As organisms develop, it assumes an imperial character, and an animal's rank is set by it, not by bulk or strength. In the social organism, Thought likewise grows imperial, and Literature turns into a fine gauge of how a society evolves. Barbarous societies, he says, show literary life only in germ. Advancing civilisation frees the mind from immediate wants, and leisure creates both the demand and the means of new activity.

Literature is at once cause and effect of social progress. It stores the race's accumulated experience and feeds successive generations. Books have become our dearest companions, silent instructors and solace in sorrow. Friendships form with men long dead, and their little ways grow endeared like those of family. Those once thrilled by this delight naturally aspire to excite it in turn.
the-prophet-of-berkeley-square:
Robert Hichens's Prophet of Berkeley Square keeps his great telescope in the bow window of Number One Thousand Berkeley Square. It points at bright December stars over frosty London, each seemingly guarding some neighbour: an ex-premier, a belted earl, a famous actor and actress. The butler Ferdinand opens the windows, makes up the fire, and sets out Malkiel's Almanac in pink and silver brocade. The chapter is titled Mrs. Merillia Is Carried to Bed.

The drawing-room speaks respectfully of past generations, free of gim-crack modern furniture. Over the mantel stands a marble bust of the Prophet as a boy. Miniatures of his numerous grandmothers line the walls: a ship-builder's wife, a Bath beauty from Jane Austen's day, and a lady who knew Byron. Another, Lady Sophia Green, wears black with a Roman nose and knew her own mind.
the-real-adventure: Henry Kitchell Webster's novel was serialized in 1915 and issued by Bobbs-Merrill at Indianapolis in 1916, illustrated by R. M. Crosby. Book one is called The Great Illusion, with chapters on a point of departure, Frederica's plan, Rosalind Stanton, a big horse, and Rodney's experiment. Here only the title pages and opening of the contents list are present, so the adventure itself does not appear.
the-rocks-of-valpre: Ethel M. Dell wrote The Way of an Eagle. She published this romance in 1913. She dedicated it to her mother with feeling. A Southey verse on love fills the dedication. Contents open with a prologue at the head. A knight of a magic cave follows it. Destiny, a rope of sand, and divine magic come next. A birthday treat and a spell fill the middle. An Englishman closes the prologue's chapter list. Part one reaches a precipice and a conquest afterward. Only the title pages and dedication are present here.
the-roof-of-france-or-the-causses-of-the: M. Betham-Edwards called The Roof of France the third of her published travels in France. She inscribed it, with respect, to President Sadi Carnot. Its subject is the Causses of the Lozère. Here only the dedication and contents have been preserved. The travel narrative itself is left out. The contents divide the book into two journeys. The first moves through Le Puy, Mende, and Rodez. The second passes through the Morvan and Lyons. It continues to Avignon, Millau, and the cañon of the Tarn.
the-ruling-passion-tales-of-nature-and-h:
Henry van Dyke subtitled The Ruling Passion as tales of nature and human nature. He opens the volume with a writer's request of his master. He asks never to tag a moral to a story. He also asks never to tell a story without a meaning. Words and people are both alive, he says. A writer must deal honestly with each.

His preface argues that every worthy life has a ruling passion. He calls it the very pulse of the machine. Romantic love holds its season in almost all lives. Yet other passions often give a life-story its distinctive hue. Van Dyke lists music, nature, and children. He adds honour, strife, revenge, and money. Pride, friendship, loyalty, and duty complete his list.
the-san-francisco-calamity-by-earthquake:
Charles Morris, LL. D., edited The San Francisco Calamity by Earthquake and Fire. Its title promises a complete and accurate account told by eye witnesses. It speaks of panic and lawlessness in the great city. It also counts 300,000 homeless people and a world-wide rush to the rescue. Accounts of other great earthquakes and volcanic eruptions are included.

Morris's preface says earthquake, famine, fire, and sudden death came together in California. They came as a hideous quartette, he writes. The full measure of the catastrophe can probably never be taken, he warns. Panic and confusion made statistics impossible at the time. Later, details merged into one mass of misery. The book aims to record those awful days faithfully, for contemporaries and for their posterity.
the-sleuth-of-st-james-s-square:
Melville Davisson Post's The Sleuth of St. James's Square lists sixteen pieces in its contents. The thing on the hearth opens the book. The lost lady, the cambered foot, and the man in the green hat follow. A hole in the mahogany panel and the pumpkin coach appear later. A satire of the sea and the house by the loch close the list.

The first story opens with a line spoken to an Excellency. The first confirmatory evidence of the thing was the print of a woman's bare foot, the speaker says. No more of that story is shown here. Post lets a single footprint stand as the volume's threshold. The contents carry the rest of the promise, from rewards to yellow flowers.
the-snare: Rafael Sabatini's The Snare is dated 1917 in its header. The pages shown give a contents list of eighteen chapters and no story text. The affair at Tavora opens the book. The ultimatum, Lady O'Moy, and Count Samoval follow. Miss Armytage's pearls and the intelligence officer appear partway through. The challenge and the duel come at chapters eleven and twelve. The wallet and bitter water follow. Fool's mate closes this list. A sibling record carries two further chapters, The Truth and The Resignation, beyond this list's end.
the-soldier-boy-or-tom-somers-in-the-arm:
Oliver Optic wrote The Soldier Boy, or Tom Somers in the Army, a story of the Great Rebellion. Hurst and Company published it in New York. The dedication is signed by William T. Adams and addressed to William Lee, Esquire. Optic's preface explains the book's character. It is not altogether a military romance, he says.

The volume contains the adventures of a noble-hearted, patriotic young man, the preface continues. He went from a home of plenty to fight for his imperilled country. Its incidents are stirring yet within probability, Optic claims. Hundreds of gallant soldiers paralleled them in experience, he adds. He consulted authorities on both sides, loyal and rebel. He also took down the living words of participants. No full battle picture is attempted, only the hero's own movements.
the-story-of-a-picture:
Douglass Sherley published this dainty trifle for his lady love with John P. Morton and Company of Louisville in 1884. Its subject is a coloured crayon portrait. The portrait hangs in a crowded shop window. Everyone passes it by except one youth of the town. He leans over the guard-rail with hope in his heart. He studies the pictured face long and earnestly.

The portrait shows a pretty dark-haired girl in a white gown, a letter in her uplifted left hand and a pen in her right above a spotless page. She sits by a marble chimney-piece carved with Cupids. Treasures from India and China surround her. A Flemish master's work hangs near. Garden roses blush on the table beside her. Sherley's praise dwells on every detail.
the-story-of-grenfell-of-the-labrador-a-: Dillon Wallace, author of Ungava Bob, wrote this boy's life of Wilfred T. Grenfell, the Labrador medical missionary, illustrated and copyrighted in 1922 by the Fleming H. Revell Company. Presented here are a transcriber's note on the spelling of St. Johns, the title pages, and the first line of a contents list opening with a chapter called The Sands of Dee, so Wallace's biography itself does not appear.
the-treasure:
Kathleen Norris opens The Treasure in the Salisbury household, where the one servant, Lizzie, happens to be wasteful. That is nearly her sole fault, her mistress thinks, besides sauciness under stress, bold holiday requests, and rage at anyone entering her immaculate kitchen. Mrs. Salisbury, twenty years a suburban housekeeper and not an exacting mistress, can forgive words spoken before a company dinner. Waste she cannot afford to tolerate.

She likes to inspect icebox and pantry each morning and decide the day's stores herself, but Lizzie flounces, mutters, and rattles dishes against any supervision. Bills have soared alarmingly in three months, while husband Kane mutters 'bad management' over his pipe. Norris builds a domestic comedy of class and housekeeping, where the real treasure is a household that runs without waste or friction.
the-vampyre:
John Polidori, Lord Byron's young doctor, wrote this tale of a vampire lord in 1819. It grew from the famed ghost tale game at Lake Geneva in 1816, the same game that gave us Frankenstein. The tale first came out in a magazine, with Byron's name wrongly put to it.

Lord Ruthven is cold, proud, and fair, and he feeds on the lives of those who trust him. A young man who roams with him learns his secret and is bound by an oath not to tell. The tale is the first of the vampire lord in English books, a form that rules to this day.
the-vedanta-sutras-with-the-commentary-b: Part one of the Vedânta-Sûtras carries the commentary by Sankarâchârya, translated by George Thibaut for the Sacred Books of the East. A companion record holds part three with Râmânuja's rival commentary in the same series. The pages present here give the title, contents, and a transliteration note, so the sûtra text does not appear. Contents headings show an introduction and two adhyâyas, each split into four pâdas. The note explains the series' transliteration scheme, with slashes marking italic letters.
the-victorian-age-in-literature: G. K. Chesterton's Victorian Age in Literature forms number sixty-one in the Home University Library of Modern Knowledge. Henry Holt published it in New York, with copyright dated 1913. Series editors named on the title pages include H. A. L. Fisher and Gilbert Murray. The material present here is front matter plus the start of a contents list, so Chesterton's argument does not appear. An introduction begins at page seven, and chapter one, The Victorian Compromise and Its Enemies, at page twelve. That title alone states the book's governing idea.
the-village-in-the-mountains-conversion-:
Three religious narratives share one title page: The Village in the Mountains, the Conversion of Peter Bayssiere, and the History of a Bible. The first follows a Paris merchant, his name withheld, touring manufactories in the mountain country of the Loire and Puy de Dôme. His road back toward Lyons mixes pasture, vines, and cornfields with factories, furnaces, and exhausted coal-pits.

Spring scenery surrounds a working landscape where looms rattle over streams and Mont Blanc shines in the distance. Seeking a shorter mountain track, the travellers stop at a decent house to ask the way. There a coal-cart nearly crushes a small child in the street, and the merchant's companion rushes to snatch the infant to safety.
the-vision-of-desire: Margaret Pedler, author of The Hermit of Far End, published The Vision of Desire with a motto from the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam. Heaven, the motto says, is the vision of fulfilled desire. Hell is the shadow from a soul on fire. Pedler dedicates the novel to Bunty, F. Mabel Warhurst, with her love. The pages present here hold the dedication and a partial contents list, so the story does not appear. A prologue precedes chapters on Ann's legacy and the Brabazons of Lorne.
the-voice-on-the-wire:
Eustace Hale Ball opens his mystery in a club grill-room, where Captain Cronin feels out of place among the Flemish tables. He has come to meet Monty Shirley, a wealthy idler who greets him with a hand-crushing grip. Shirley confesses a month of bridge, handball, and yarns has made him a nervous wreck from having nothing to do.

Cronin, who left the police force eleven years earlier to run a detective agency, offers rescue. His newest case, he promises, carries millions, murders, and mysteries, with every frill Shirley likes. The job is too big for the agency alone. Shirley is tickled to death, and chapter one, titled When Three Is a Mystery, sets the partnership moving.
the-well-of-saint-clare: Anatole France's Well of Saint Clare appears in Alfred Allinson's English translation, published by John Lane the Bodley Head in 1909. A dedication to Madame Arman de Caillavet honours her wit, kindness, and sense of beauty. The pages present here give the dedication and contents only, so the tales themselves do not appear. Fifteen stories are named. Lucifer, Saint Mael Amabilis, and Saint Satine open the collection. Later titles include Signora Chiara's Temptations, Messer Guido Cavalcanti, Leslie Wood, and Brother Giovanni Jocondo.
the-whitehouse-cookbook-1887-cooking-toi:
Mrs. F. L. Gillette and Hugo Ziemann compiled the White House Cook Book, dated 1887, as a comprehensive cyclopedia of information for the home. Cooking, toilet and household recipes, menus, dinner-giving, table etiquette, care of the sick, and health suggestions fill its scope. Ziemann is identified as steward of the White House, and the volume is dedicated to the wives of the presidents.

A publishers' preface claims the book represents the culinary art's present perfection more fully than any previous work. Ziemann had catered for a Prince Napoleon, served as steward of Paris's Hotel Splendide, and run New York's Brunswick Café before winning Chicago gourmets at the Hotel Richelieu. Gillette is praised as no less proficient, and the preface turns to her credentials.
the-world-s-desire: H. Rider Haggard and Andrew Lang wrote The World's Desire together, and its contents list spans three books here. Odysseus, called the Wanderer, threads through the chapter titles. Queen Meriamun's story and vision occupy early chapters. Egyptian soul terms, the Ka, Bai, and Khou, appear. The last fight of Odysseus closes book three. The chapters themselves do not appear in the pages given here.
the-world-s-great-snare: E. Phillips Oppenheim's The World's Great Snare, dated 1896 in its heading, is shown through a partial contents list. A 2017 edition page calls it a thriller classic. Book one chapters mention the Blue River and a western love. Mr. James Hamilton's laugh gets a chapter. Christopher Skein is named as a villain. A debauch and a tragedy also appear. The novel's chapters themselves do not follow in the pages present.
thoughts-moods-and-ideals-crimes-of-leis:
W. D. Lighthall, an advocate, published Thoughts, Moods and Ideals, subtitled Crimes of Leisure, at Montreal in 1887. He dedicated the volume to his friends. Its first poem, The Confused Dawn, stages a dialogue between a young man and a seer.

The young man asks about a vision and cry haunting the new Canadian soul. The seer answers that mountains, forests, and trees awaken into a native land stretching from Brittany's shore toward Vancouver. Readers get early Canadian verse and prose where national feeling is treated as a dawn still taking shape.
tom-slade-s-double-dare: Percy Keese Fitzhugh's Tom Slade's Double Dare was published by Grosset and Dunlap at New York in 1922, illustrated by R. Emmett Owen and approved by the Boy Scouts of America. A frontispiece shows Hervey running desperately toward one remaining light. Contents begin with the light going out, a bridge, an important mission, a tree, and win or lose. Shadows of the night and the light that failed follow. The front pages and opening contents are what is present here, so Fitzhugh's story itself does not appear.
tom-slade-with-the-boys-over-there: Percy K. Fitzhugh took Tom Slade overseas in a Grosset and Dunlap book copyrighted in 1918, illustrated by R. Emmett Owen and approved by the Boy Scouts of America. A frontispiece quotes Tom announcing himself as American. Fitzhugh dedicated the book to F. A. O., called the real Tom Slade. The dedication says the real Slade's own adventures on land and sea outdo these tales by far. The front pages are what is included in this record, so Fitzhugh's war story itself is not shown.
traditions-of-the-tinguian-a-study-in-ph:
Fay-Cooper Cole, assistant curator of Malayan ethnology, published his study of Tinguian traditions in 1915. Contents divide the tales into mythical period stories, ritualistic and explanatory tales, fables, and abstracts, after a preface and introduction. The mythical tales open with a reconstruction of the culture.

Cole explains that leading actors recur under many names, sometimes several titles in one tale. He lists fourteen principal characters with relationships, starting with Aponitolau and his sister and wife. Six storytellers from four towns supplied the first twenty-six myths. Readers get Philippine folklore presented as comparative ethnology, attentive to naming and variation.
turkey-a-past-and-a-future:
A. J. Toynbee's Turkey: A Past and a Future, dated 1917 in Roman numerals, divides its subject into three parts: the past, the present, and the future. Chapter one begins by asking what Turkey is. No formula, Toynbee answers, can embrace the variety of lands marked Ottoman on the map.

He ranges from the monsoon coast of Yemen to the desert rim of the Hedjaz and the green strip of Mesopotamia. Armenian highlands, the Anatolian steppe, and Mediterranean coast-lands each get their portrait. The cities differ as much: Adrianople, Constantinople, Smyrna, Konia, and Aleppo. Wartime readers in 1917 met an empire described as many countries wearing one name.
uncle-bernac-a-memory-of-the-empire:
Uncle Bernac, a memory of the Empire, opens its contents with the coast of France, a salt-marsh, and a ruined cottage. Men of the night, a secret passage, and the camp of Boulogne follow. Later chapters promise Josephine and the reception of the Empress. No author is named on the pages shown.

Chapter one begins with the narrator rereading his uncle's letter for the hundredth time aboard a lugger. He knows it by heart, yet takes it from his pocket again as the French coast nears. The letter draws a young man back from England into Napoleon's France, where his uncle holds the chateau of Grosbois and a cousin, Sybille, waits in the story's path.
under-the-trees-and-elsewhere: Hamilton Wright Mabie wrote the nature essays in Under the Trees and Elsewhere. Dodd, Mead and Company issued the book in New York, with the title page dated 1904. The pages here give the title page, dedication, and contents only, so the essays themselves do not appear. Fourteen chapter titles sketch a year outdoors. They name an April day, apple boughs, open fields, earth and sky, the mystery of night, a mountain rivulet, and a climb to the heights.
valerius-terminus-of-the-interpretation-:
Francis Bacon left the fragments called Valerius Terminus as part of a great planned work on the interpretation of nature. Robert Leslie Ellis, who wrote the preface here, explains that the pieces first saw print in 1734, in Stephens's edition of Bacon's letters and remains. Some are full chapters, some are scraps, and an outline covers chapters twelve through twenty-six of the first book.

Ellis notes one firm link between the parts: the sixteenth chapter, on the doctrine of idols, appears in both the fragments and the outline. He guesses at Bacon's odd pen name, too. Terminus, the Roman god of boundaries, may hint that the new philosophy would end man's long wandering in search of truth. Readers get both Bacon's early sketches for reforming knowledge and an editor's careful map of what survives.
varney-the-vampyre:
Thomas Peckett Prest wrote this vast tale of a vampire for the penny press in 1847. It ran in cheap weekly parts, the penny dreadfuls of the Victorian poor. Its full name adds the grim words 'The Feast of Blood' to the name of Varney.

Sir Francis Varney dies, rises, and feeds on the blood of the living through a long chain of tales. The fangs, the two small wounds, and the fixed stare of the vampire all start in this book. Crude and vast, it is the root stock of the vampire tale in cheap print.
washington-square: Henry James's 1880 Washington Square: Catherine Sloper, her father, and her fortune hunter. His most perfect novella, ironic and moving. A quiet masterpiece. Catherine's quiet rebellion is James's triumph, the perfect novella, James's quiet and perfect masterpiece.
when-the-world-shook-being-an-account-of: The opening here gives the contents and the start of a dedication letter for H. Rider Haggard's When the World Shook, but no chapter text. Haggard tells of Bastin, Bickley, and Arbuthnot and their great adventure. The contents promise a cyclone, an island in a lake, and dwellers in a tomb. One chapter counts a span of two hundred and fifty thousand years. His letter to Curzon, written at Ditchingham in 1918, recalls a false charge made against Haggard more than thirty years before.
who-goes-there: Nothing but the title page and a long contents list is present here for B. K. Benson's Who Goes There?, a story of a spy in the Civil War, printed in 1900. The contents open with an advance and a shameful day. The spy breaks his musket, meets a personage, and serves in camp with a doctor. Later chapters name the line of the Warwick, Fort Willis, and the lines of Hanover. A great battle and Captain Haskell fill the late list.
wildfire:
Zane Grey opens Wildfire at Bostil's Ford, on the edge of the desert. Lucy Bostil, eighteen, has stolen away on a forbidden horse to a high perch. She feels deep thanks for her full life, yet also a strange unrest and longing. Something must happen, she feels, even if it proves terrible, so long as it is wonderful.

Below her spread the hamlet, the sage plain, and the Colorado river thundering in its gorge. Indians ride the river trail in bright colors, and an eagle hangs on the air. Lucy loves all the horses except her father's great racer, the Sage King. Grey sets a wild horse tale in a grand, harsh land.
with-clive-in-india-or-the-beginnings-of:
G. A. Henty told the rise of British India in With Clive in India, or The Beginnings of an Empire. A full chapter list heads the book, running from a boy leaving home to the siege of Pondicherry. Clive arrives in chapter six, and the siege of Arcot follows. The Black Hole of Calcutta and two chapters on Plassey mark the high points.

Henty's preface promises a vivid picture of ten packed years. At their start, Madras sat in French hands and Calcutta lay at Bengal's mercy under its Nabob. English power in India seemed near its end. By the close, Henty says, England had won in both Bengal and Madras. A young clerk turned soldier carries the tale.
woman-as-she-should-be-or-agnes-wiltshir:
Mary E. Herbert published this moral novel in Halifax in 1861. Chapter one finds Agnes Wiltshire at her chamber window on a Sunday evening. She sits lost in painful thought. Below her lies a garden that young hands once kept bright with flowers. Those hands are long dead, and the plot lies neglected, yet still lovely.

That faded garden mirrors a household touched by loss. Herbert frames Agnes as a model of quiet, dutiful womanhood. The story promises trials at home rather than public adventure. Readers get a gentle domestic tale with a clear moral aim.
women-wage-earners-their-past-their-pres: Helen Campbell wrote this 1893 study of working women, with an introduction by economist Richard T. Ely. Pages present here hold the title page, a dedication to a friend named Alice, and the start of a contents list. The first chapter is called A Look Backward. No chapter text appears in these pages. Campbell's earlier books on poverty, named on the title page, show her long focus on poor women's lives and pay.
yorkshire: Gordon Home painted and described this tour of Yorkshire. Pages present here hold a contents list covering thirteen chapters, but no chapter text or pictures. The route starts across the moors from Pickering to Whitby. Later chapters follow the Esk valley, the coast to Redcar and Scarborough, and the Cleveland Hills. Dales get full treatment near the end, with Richmond, Swaledale, and Wensleydale named. The travel writing itself stays absent here.
